Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 1:

﴿Ha Mim﴾

The discussion of its counterparts and its occurrences has already preceded, before the mention of the Qur'an and its sending down.

[Page 160]

Ibn ʿĀshūr's commentary on Sūrah 43, verses 2–3:

﴿By the Clear Book.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an, that you might understand.﴾

He swears by the Clear Book, which is the Qur'an, that God made the Qur'an Arabic, clear in its indication. It therefore deserves to be believed, if they were not stubbornly obstinate. But because of their obstinacy, they were like those who do not understand. The oath by the Qur'an is an honouring of its status and an emphasis on what the answer to the oath contains. The oath here does not serve to refute those who deny it, since they do not believe that the one swearing is God, Exalted is He. Those addressed by the oath are the deniers, as shown by His saying, "that you might understand," and by the consequence in His words, ﴿Shall We then withhold the Reminder from you, turning away?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 5], which follows from it. The emphasis of the answer with *inna* (indeed) adds further emphasis to the assertion that the Qur'an is from God's making.

In making the sworn-by object the Qur'an, described as "clear," and making the answer of the oath that God made it clear, there is a unique honouring of the Qur'an. He made the thing sworn by the same as the thing sworn about. This is a rare and original method, because it indicates that what is sworn about has reached the utmost of nobility. If one wishes to swear to the establishment of a nobility for something, he will not find anything more fitting to swear by, because of the harmony between the oath and what is sworn about. The author of al-Kashshāf (al-Zamakhsharī) counted among this kind the verse of Abū Tammām:

*And your front teeth: indeed they are freshly-strung pearls, and pearls, and a lightning-flash that gleams.*

Al-Zamakhsharī took the clause "indeed they are freshly-strung" as the answer of the oath. This was followed by al-Ṭībī and al-Qazwīnī in their commentaries on al-Kashshāf, and it is also what al-Tibrīzī explained in his commentary on the Dīwān of Abū Tammām. However, al-Taftazānī rejected this in his commentary on al-Kashshāf and made the clause "indeed they are freshly-strung" a resumptive clause (*istinaf*), that is, a parenthetical clause (*iʿtirāḍ*) explaining why her teeth deserve to be sworn by. He took the answer of the oath to be his saying, three verses later:

*The waves of the calamities of time have overwhelmed me, and I know not which of them to plunge into.*

In literary subtleties and refinements, an acceptable possibility is sufficient. His saying before it:

*And the twitching of sleep in your eyes during slumber, in its varieties, and in my eye there is no dimness.*

could be a second oath, so that the verse would be its answer.

The name "Book" is applied to the Qur'an because God sent it down to be written, and the community is commanded to write it down, even though its descent upon the Messenger ﷺ was in oral form, not written. This points to the fact that it would be written in the codices (*maṣāḥif*). By "the Book" is meant what had been revealed of the Qur'an before this sūrah, which the scribes of revelation had written down.

The pronoun in "We have made it" refers to the Book; that is, "We have made the Clear Book a Qur'an." *Jaʿl* (making) means bringing into existence and creating, and it takes one object.

The meaning is that it is to be recited without the presence of a written book. This implies that it is preserved in hearts. Were it not so, there would be no benefit in informing that it is to be recited, since every book is suitable to be read. The description of the Book as "Qur'an" is an intensification of its being recited, that is, made easy to recite, as in His saying, ﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ [al-Qamar: 17], His saying, ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyāmah: 17], and His saying, ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 9].

Thus this description establishes that the Book sent down upon Muḥammad ﷺ combines two qualities: that it is a Book, and that it is recited upon the tongues of the community. This is among the things peculiar to the Book of Islam.

[Page 161]

"Arabic" is an attribution to the Arabs. Since what is attributed is a book and something recited, the attribution implies that its connection to the Arabs is that of speech and language to its people. That is, it is among the things which the Arabs utter with similar words and with various kinds of constructions.

"Qur'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the object of "We have made it."

The meaning of making it an Arabic Qur'an is that it was formed according to the way the Arabic language was formed. God, in His dazzling wisdom, made this Book a Qur'an in the language of the Arabs, because it is the most noble of languages and the widest in indicating many meanings. He sent it down among the people of that language, because they understand its subtleties best. For this reason He chose His Messenger from the people of that language, so that the means of indication and understanding would support one another, and they would be the ones conveying God's intent to the nations. Since this Qur'an is of such a station, none would refuse to accept it except people who are extravagant in falsehood, far from fairness and rectitude. But God wished their guidance, so His remembrance is not cut off from them until His purpose is fulfilled and the spread of His religion is complete. They must therefore return to their reason and consider their sincerity, for God will not hold them to account for their past extravagance if they turn back to their rectitude.

The purpose of describing the Book as Arabic has two aims. The first is to honour the Qur'an and praise it, as it is woven in the pattern of the most eloquent language. The second is to rebuke the obstinate among the Arabs, when they were not moved by its meanings, by saying that they are like one who hears speech in a language other than his own. This confirms what is contained in the two disjoined letters with which the sūrah opens, namely the meaning of challenge: this is a Book in your language, and you have been unable to produce its like.

The particle *laʿalla* (perhaps, so that) is used figuratively in the sense of intention (*irādah*). A similar instance was discussed in His saying, *laʿallakum tattaqūn* (that you may be mindful), at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah.

*ʿAql* (understanding) means comprehension.

The purpose is an indirect reproach: that they neglected to reflect upon this Book, and that its perfection in clarity and explicitness deserves care, not turning away from it. His saying *laʿallakum taʿqilūn* therefore implies that they did not understand.

The meaning is: We made its understanding easy for you, so that you might understand. But you turned away and did not understand its meanings, although a great quantity has been sent down which, if they had reflected upon it, they would have understood. Thus this statement is used for indirect reproach by way of metonymy (*kināyah*).

[Page 160]

﴿وإنَّهُ في أُمِّ الكِتابِ لَدَيْنا لَعَلِيٌّ حَكِيمٌ﴾

It is a conjunctive clause (*ʿatf*, coordination) upon the sentence ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3]. It adds a second commendation of this Book, to exalt its status in rank and guidance.

*Umm al-Kitab* means the origin of the Book (*asl al-kitab*). What is meant by *Umm al-Kitab* is the knowledge of God, Exalted, as in His saying ﴿and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39] in Surah al-Ra'd, because *umm* means origin, and *kitab* here means the written, that is, the established and confirmed. This is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for the truth that does not accept alteration, because when they wanted to confirm a covenant over a long period, they would write it down in a document. Al-Harith ibn Hillizah said:

*Wary of tyranny and of disputes; and can desires undo what is in the scrolls?*

*ʿAliyy* originally means elevated, and it is used here figuratively (*mustaʿar*) for the nobility of the attribute, and this is a common metaphor (*istiʿarah*).

*Hakim* originally describes the one whose opinion has wisdom (*hikmah*) as an attribute, so it is here a figurative usage (*majaz*) for that which contains wisdom through what it includes of the betterment of souls' conditions and of the laws that sustain the order of the community.

The meaning of this being in God's knowledge is that God knows it to be so, and what God knows admits no doubt. Its meaning is that what the Qur'an includes of meanings is from God's intent and proceeds from His knowledge.

It is also possible that this conveys a testimony to the exaltedness and wisdom of the Qur'an, in the manner of their saying in oaths: "God knows," and "God has known."

The emphasis of the statement with *inna* (indeed) is to refute the denial of those addressed, when they denied that the Qur'an was revealed by God.

*Ladayna* is a stable adverbial phrase (*zarf mustaqarr*) which is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) either from the pronoun in *innahu* or from *Umm al-Kitab*.

[Page 163]

The purpose is to increase the confirmation of the report and the honouring of the subject of the report.

The majority of readers read *fi Umm al-Kitab* with a *damma* on the hamza of *umm*. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a *kasrah* on the hamza of *imm al-kitab* in connected reading (*wasl*), following the *kasrah* of *fi*. So if one pauses (*waqf*) on *fi*, one does not vocalise the hamza with a kasrah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 5:

﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you altogether, because you are a people who exceed the bounds?﴾

The fa' (فاء) here is for the sequencing (tafri') of the rhetorical interrogation (istifham inkari) upon the statement ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an, that you may understand﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 3]. That is, do you think that your turning away from what has been revealed of this Book would move Us to cut off from you the renewed reminding by sending down some other part of the Qur'an? So when the re-reminding of them was intended, and they had already been given the reminding which, had they reflected and contemplated, contained their guidance, and since the re-reminding was marked in their view by little benefit, He made clear to them that the persistence of their aversion would not be a cause for cutting off guidance from them, because Allah is Merciful to them, desiring their correction, and their excessive denial does not prevent Him from increasing the advancement of admonitions and guidance to them.

The interrogation is one of denial (inkari), meaning: it is not permissible that We turn the Reminder away from you altogether because of your excess.

Ad-darb (ضرب) is in its literal sense the striking of one body against another. It has well-known uses, the most famous of which is: he struck the camel with a stick (qara'a al-ba'ir bi-'asa). Here it is used metaphorically for the meaning of cutting off and diverting, taken from their saying: "he drove the strangers away from the watering-place" (darab al-gharaib 'an al-hawd), meaning he drove them off and diverted them because they do not belong to the people of the water. So they used darb for diverting and driving away. Ṭarafa said:

"Shall I turn away from you the worries that come upon you, as you strike the horse's forelock with a sword."

Page 164
Adh-dhikr (الذكر) means the reminding, and what is meant by it is the Qur'an.
As-safh (الصفح) is turning away by turning the face to one side (safh al-wajh), which is its side; it is the most intense form of turning away from speech, because it combines leaving off listening to it and leaving off looking at the speaker.

Ṣafḥan (صفحًا) is in the accusative as a substitute for the adverb of place, meaning "in a place of turning away," as one says: "put it aside" (ḍa'hu janiban). It may also be that ṣafḥan is the verbal noun of ṣafaḥa 'an kadha (he turned away from such-and-such) when he turned away, in which case it is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul muțlaq) to specify the kind of striking, in the sense of diverting and turning away.

Al-israf (الإسراف) means excess and over-abundance, and its most common use is for excessive doing of a harmful action. Hence it is said: "there is no excess in good" (la sarafa fi al-khayr). The context indicates that they exceeded the bounds in turning away from the Qur'an.

Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read in inna kuntum with a kasra on the hamza of (إن), so that (إن) is conditional. Since the general usage of conditional (in) is to occur with a condition whose occurrence is not expected, unlike (idha), which is for a condition whose occurrence is certain, the use of (in) in His words ﴿if you are a people who exceed the bounds﴾ aims at placing the addressees, whose excess is known, in the position of one who doubts their excess, because the abundance of proofs for the truth of the Qur'an should remove their excess. In this there is confidence in the truth of the Qur'an and a form of rebuke for their persistence in turning away from it.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the hamza of (أن), making (أن) a verbal particle (masdariyya), with the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil) understood as elided, meaning: "because of your excess"; that is, we do not abandon reminding you because you are excessive, but rather we continue to repeat the reminder out of mercy to you.

The insertion of qawman before musrifin serves to indicate that this excess has become a disposition for them, and their peoplehood is sustained by it, as we have noted at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Surely there are signs in that for a people who understand﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 6–8:

[Page 165]
﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples?﴾ ﴿But no prophet came to them except that they used to mock him.﴾ ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might, and the example of the earlier peoples has passed on.﴾

When he (Allah) mentioned their extravagance in turning away from listening to the call of the Qur'an, He followed it with a statement addressed to the Messenger ﷺ as consolation for what he encounters from them, in the midst of their turning away, of harm and mockery, by reminding him that his situation in this is the situation of the Messengers before him and the sunnah (established way) of Allah concerning the nations, and as a promise to the Messenger ﷺ of victory over his people, by reminding him of the sunnah of Allah concerning the nations that denied their messengers.

The first part of this statement was made for consolation, by the indication of the shift from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of absence in His saying: ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them﴾, as will come, and this contains an implicit rebuke to them for their extravagance in turning away from reflecting on the Qur'an.

So the clause ﴿And how many a prophet did We send﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 3] and what follows it up to here, as a conjunction of narrative upon narrative.

And (kam) is a noun denoting an indefinite large number, and the position of (kam) is accusative as the object of (arsalna), and its fronting is obligatory because its origin is an interrogative noun, so it was transferred from interrogation to informing by way of metonymy.

Its use in this sense became widespread until informing about abundance became one of the meanings of (kam). The reason for employing a large number is that the frequency of occurrence of this ruling is more effective in rebuking them against the like of it, and more effective in consoling the Messenger ﷺ and producing his patience, because the frequency of its occurrence indicates that it is a sunnah that does not fail, and that is more deterrent and more consoling.

And (al-awwalin) is the plural of (al-awwal), and it is used here in the sense of the past predecessors, as in His saying: ﴿And most of the earlier peoples had already gone astray before them﴾ [as-Saffat: 71], for those who were destroyed had perished, regardless of whoever might have succeeded them among the nations.

The exception in His saying: ﴿except that they used to mock him﴾ is an exception from states, meaning: no prophet came to them in any of their states except that their mockery accompanied the prophet's coming to them.

[Page 166]
The clause ﴿But no prophet came to them except that they used to mock him﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to (al-awwalin), and this circumstance is the intended purpose of the statement.

The clause ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might﴾ is a consequence and a causal result of the clause ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples﴾.

The pronoun in (stronger than them) refers to (a people who were extravagant), whose address had preceded, and He turned away from continuing the address to them to directing it to the Messenger ﷺ, because the more important aim of this statement is the consolation of the Messenger and the promise of victory to him. This entails an implicit allusion to those who denied him, for this statement reaches them as mentioned earlier.

It is apparent that the change in the mode of pronouns following the change in the direction of address does not negate considering it an iltifat (shift) in the pronoun, because the criterion of iltifat is the unity of the referent of the two pronouns together with the possibility of confining oneself to the first mode of pronoun. Is not the change in the direction of speech only a strengthening of what the transfer of the pronoun requires? The subtle point produced by iltifat is not lost, namely the renewal of the listener's attentiveness, rather it grows in strength with the growth of its requirements.

The words of al-Kashshaf are clear that the transfer of the pronoun here is an iltifat, and on this his commentators established it. However, the scholar al-Taftazani said: "Such a thing is not iltifat at all." It seems he holds that the difference of direction of address in which the two pronouns occur is a method other than the method of iltifat. The words of al-Kashshaf admit of some possibility, and the particularities of eloquence are wide-ranging.

Those who were stronger in might than the disbelievers of Makkah are those whom He referred to as (al-awwalin) and who were described as mocking whoever came to them as a prophet.

This is a wondrous construction in conciseness, for His saying: ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might﴾ implies an omitted statement whose estimate is: "So We are not incapable of destroying the extravagant, though they are less in might."

This has the sense of His saying: ﴿And how many a town, which was stronger in power than your town that expelled you, have We destroyed, so there was none to help them﴾ [Muhammad: 13].

[Page 167]
And (batsh) is harm that is forceful.

(Batshan) is accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of the relation of the superlative.

And (mathal al-awwalin) means their astonishing condition. And the meaning of (mada) is: passed away, i.e., they departed entirely, so the passing of the example is a metonymy for their annihilation, because the passing of conditions occurs through the passing of their owners. It has the sense of His saying: ﴿So the root of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾ [al-An'am: 45]. The mention of (al-awwalin) is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, due to the prior mention of His saying (among the earlier peoples).

The purpose of its being explicit is that the report about them should be explicit and run in the manner of a proverb.

This entails an implicit allusion to those who denied him, for this statement reaches them as mentioned earlier.

It is apparent that the change in the mode of pronouns following the change in the direction of address does not negate considering it an iltifat (shift) in the pronoun, because the criterion of iltifat is the unity of the referent of the two pronouns together with the possibility of confining oneself to the first mode of pronoun. Is not the change in the direction of speech only a strengthening of what the transfer of the pronoun requires? The subtle point produced by iltifat is not lost, namely the renewal of the listener's attentiveness, rather it grows in strength with the growth of its requirements.

The words of al-Kashshaf are clear that the transfer of the pronoun here is an iltifat, and on this his commentators established it. However, the scholar al-Taftazani said: "Such a thing is not iltifat at all." It seems he holds that the difference of direction of address in which the two pronouns occur is a method other than the method of iltifat. The words of al-Kashshaf admit of some possibility, and the particularities of eloquence are wide-ranging.

Those who were stronger in might than the disbelievers of Makkah are those whom He referred to as (al-awwalin) and who were described as mocking whoever came to them as a prophet.

This is a wondrous construction in conciseness, for His saying: ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might﴾ implies an omitted statement whose estimate is: "So We are not incapable of destroying the extravagant, though they are less in might."

This has the sense of His saying: ﴿And how many a town, which was stronger in power than your town that expelled you, have We destroyed, so there was none to help them﴾ [Muhammad: 13].

[Page 167]
And (batsh) is harm that is forceful.

(Batshan) is accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of the relation of the superlative.

And (mathal al-awwalin) means their astonishing condition. And the meaning of (mada) is: passed away, i.e., they departed entirely, so the passing of the example is a metonymy for their annihilation, because the passing of conditions occurs through the passing of their owners. It has the sense of His saying: ﴿So the root of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾ [al-An'am: 45]. The mention of (al-awwalin) is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, due to the prior mention of His saying (among the earlier peoples).

The purpose of its being explicit is that the report about them should be explicit and run in the manner of a proverb.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 6–8:

[Page 165]
﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples?﴾ ﴿But no prophet came to them except that they used to mock him.﴾ ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might, and the example of the earlier peoples has passed on.﴾

When he (Allah) mentioned their extravagance in turning away from listening to the call of the Qur'an, He followed it with a statement addressed to the Messenger ﷺ as consolation for what he encounters from them, in the midst of their turning away, of harm and mockery, by reminding him that his situation in this is the situation of the Messengers before him and the sunnah (established way) of Allah concerning the nations, and as a promise to the Messenger ﷺ of victory over his people, by reminding him of the sunnah of Allah concerning the nations that denied their messengers.

The first part of this statement was made for consolation, by the indication of the shift from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of absence in His saying: ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them﴾, as will come, and this contains an implicit rebuke to them for their extravagance in turning away from reflecting on the Qur'an.

So the clause ﴿And how many a prophet did We send﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 3] and what follows it up to here, as a conjunction of narrative upon narrative.

And (kam) is a noun denoting an indefinite large number, and the position of (kam) is accusative as the object of (arsalna), and its fronting is obligatory because its origin is an interrogative noun, so it was transferred from interrogation to informing by way of metonymy.

Its use in this sense became widespread until informing about abundance became one of the meanings of (kam). The reason for employing a large number is that the frequency of occurrence of this ruling is more effective in rebuking them against the like of it, and more effective in consoling the Messenger ﷺ and producing his patience, because the frequency of its occurrence indicates that it is a sunnah that does not fail, and that is more deterrent and more consoling.

And (al-awwalin) is the plural of (al-awwal), and it is used here in the sense of the past predecessors, as in His saying: ﴿And most of the earlier peoples had already gone astray before them﴾ [as-Saffat: 71], for those who were destroyed had perished, regardless of whoever might have succeeded them among the nations.

The exception in His saying: ﴿except that they used to mock him﴾ is an exception from states, meaning: no prophet came to them in any of their states except that their mockery accompanied the prophet's coming to them.

[Page 166]
The clause ﴿But no prophet came to them except that they used to mock him﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to (al-awwalin), and this circumstance is the intended purpose of the statement.

The clause ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might﴾ is a consequence and a causal result of the clause ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 9:

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing."﴾

When His saying, ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 6], was directed at the Messenger ﷺ for consolation and for the promise of victory, He followed it with a direct address to the Messenger ﷺ in His saying, "And if you asked them," etc., for the purpose of expressing wonder at the state of those who denied him. They denied him only because he called them to worship one God and to abandon the worship of idols, and they regarded this as strange, even though they acknowledge that God, exalted is He, is the Creator of the worlds and what is in them. Does anything deserve to be worshipped other than the Creator of those who worship? Moreover, the idols are among the things God created from stones on the earth. So if the Messenger ﷺ, in his argument with them, had asked them about the Creator of creation, they could not have done otherwise than affirm that it is God, exalted is He.

The clause "And if you asked them" is conjoined to the clause "And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples" [al-Zukhruf: 6] by way of conjunction of purpose (ʿaṭf al-gharad), and it is a transition to arguing against the invalidity of associating partners with God, through their implicit acknowledgement that their idols lack the attribute of deserving to be worshipped.

The emphasis of the speech by the lam of oath preparation (al-lam al-mutawwi'a lil-qasam), the lam of the response (lam al-jawab), and the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid) is to affirm that they would answer thus. This treats one who does not doubt the report as if he were doubtful, and this treatment is a metonymy for the appropriateness of their condition to be marvelled at, for the derangement of their thinking and the contradiction of their beliefs. The disclosure of their belief was framed in the form of asking them about their Creator to indicate that they are heedless of it in the course of their affairs, their acts and their supplications; so that when the questioner asks them about their Creator, they do not hesitate to answer that it is God, and then they return to their polytheism.

The address in "you asked them" (sa'altahum) is to the Prophet ﷺ, which is the apparent context of consolation; or the address may be to an unspecified addressee, so as to include every addressee who can be imagined as asking them.

"Al-'Aziz al-'Alim" is God, exalted is He. The mention of these two attributes is not part of the content of their answer; rather, their statement is reported in meaning, i.e., "they would surely say, 'He who created them is the One to whom these two attributes belong,'" whereas they actually say, "God created them," as is reported of them in Surah Luqman: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "God."﴾ This is what is established from their speech, both prose and poetry, in the pre-Islamic era.

He turned away from the name "Allah" to the two attributes only to add to their confounding: that the One from whose Oneness in worship they turned away is All-Mighty and All-Knowing. Therefore He is the One whom people must hope in for hardships, because of His might, and whom they must sincerely devote their inner selves to, because nothing of their secrets is hidden from Him, unlike their partners, which are abased and know nothing. And they do not dispute His being described as "the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing."

The singling out of these two attributes from among the rest of the divine attributes is because they are contrary to the attributes of the idols, for the idols are unable to repel the hands (of those who would harm them).

The estimated meaning is: "And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, 'God.'" And if you asked them, "Is it the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing?"

*[p. 169]*

This is a statement addressed from God, Exalted, and it is a transition (takhallus) from the argument for His singularity in divinity, based on His being the sole creator of the heavens and the earth, to the argument based on His being the sole bestower of the blessings by which the stability (qiwam) of people's lives is sustained. The sentence is therefore a resumption (istina'), in which the subject has been omitted, and the implied reading is: *He* ("huwa") *is the One who made the earth for you a bed (mihad)*. This resumption falls between the clause ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 9], and the clause ﴿And they have attributed to Him a portion of His servants﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 15].

The relative pronoun (ism al-mawsul) is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose implied form is: "He is the One who made for you." This is an omission of the subject (hadhf al-musnad ilayhi) that follows the usage that al-Sakkaki (d. 626 AH) named in his terminology. The omission occurs because the discussion about God preceded this clause. Bringing in the relative pronoun serves to make known the content of its clause (sila), so it has the same force as a proper name in identifying its referent.

Two clauses are mentioned, and in them there is an indication of the sole possession of great power and of the blessing bestowed upon them. For this reason the word *"for you" (lakum)* is inserted in both places. It is not said, "the One who made the earth a bed and made in it paths," as in His words: ﴿Have We not made the earth a bed, and the mountains as pegs?﴾ [al-Naba': 6-7], because that is the context of arguing against those who deny the resurrection. Therefore the argument is directed to them by means of the origination of great created things, in comparison with which the re-creation of man is not a strange matter.

The relative pronoun is not repeated in His words ﴿and made for you in it paths﴾, because the two clauses are combined under a single imaginative category (al-jami' al-khayali), since both are among the conditions of the earth. Thus their making is like one making. The eleven second-person pronouns occurring in the four verses from His words ﴿the One who made for you the earth a bed﴾ up to His words ﴿capable of subduing them﴾ are not a case of iltifat (shift in grammatical person), but proceed according to what the outward meaning requires.

*Mihad* is a noun for something that is spread out (yumahhad), that is, made level and easy for what settles upon it. It was discussed earlier in His words ﴿For them, from Hell is a bed﴾ [al-A'raf: 41], in Surat al-A'raf. The aspect of favour (imtinan) is that He made the outward surface of the earth expanded, and this expansion is for the benefit of the humans who dwell upon it. This does not contradict the fact that the body of the earth is spherical, as is evident, because its sphericity is not a benefit to people.

Asim read *mahdan* without an alif after the *ha'*, and it is intended to mean *mihad*.

*Subul* is the plural of *sabil*, which means a path. The word *sabil* is also applied to the means (wasilah) of a thing, as in His words ﴿They say, "Is there any way of return?"﴾ [al-Shura: 44]. Both meanings may be intended here, because there are on the earth routes that can be travelled: the plains, the slopes of mountains, and their ravines. That is, He did not make the whole earth mountains, which would make it difficult for walkers to traverse, but He made in it easy paths, and He made mountains for another wisdom. And the earth is suitable for making well-trodden roads that are travelled.

The meaning of God's making those routes in this sense is that He made it possible for people to know how to move across the earth, and for some to follow the traces of others, until the roads become paved and easy for them, and the traveller knows which of those paths will bring him to his destination.

In facilitating the means of travel across the earth there is great kindness, because through it comes the facilitation of gathering together, of getting to know one another, of bringing benefits, and of seeking help in repelling calamities and harms. Travel across the earth, whether near or far, is among the greatest manifestations of human civilization. Also, God has placed in the earth the means of subsistence of people, such as plants, fruits, leaves of trees, truffles (kam'a) and mushrooms (faq'), which are means of livelihood, so these are metaphorical paths (subul majaziyya). A parallel to this verse was mentioned earlier in Surat Ta-Ha.

*Al-ihtida'* is the reflexive form (mutawi') of *hadahu*, so *fa-ihtada* means "he was guided." The literal meaning of *hidaya* is guidance to the intended place, and from this the one who points out the paths is called *hadi* (guide). It is also applied to making true realities known, and from this is His words ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]. The intended meaning here is the second, that is, the hope that you will attain knowledge of God's oneness and of what is due to Him. This was discussed earlier in ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6].

The meaning of hope derived from *la'alla* (perhaps/so that) is a subordinate metaphorical allegory (isti'ara tamthiliyya taba'iyya), in which the state of one for whom the means of a thing are present before him is likened to the state of one who is hoped to attain what he seeks through those means.

The passage moved from the argument and the favour (imtinan) shown in creating the earth to the argument and favour shown in creating the means of livelihood within it, namely rain water, by which the earth produces what is fit for people's sustenance.

The relative pronoun was repeated (﴿والَّذِي﴾) to give this clause special emphasis, making it independent so that its presence does not come to mind together with the two preceding clauses, and so that no imagined connection links it to them. The discussion of its counterpart appeared earlier in Surat al-Ra'd and elsewhere, and the relative pronoun was repeated because its referent (mişdaq) is the agent of all of them.

Al-insha' means al-ihya' (giving life), as in His words: ﴿ثُمَّ إذا شاءَ أنْشَرَهُ﴾ [Abasa: 22].

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he disapproved of those who read ﴿كَيْفَ نَنْشُرُها﴾ with a fatha on the nun and a damma on the shin, and he recited ﴿ثُمَّ إذا شاءَ أنْشَرَهُ﴾ [Abasa: 22]. The original sense of the hamza in it is transitivity (ta'diyah), and its unaugmented verb (nashara) means "to come to life," as in the saying: nashara al-mayyit, with the dead man as the subject. Al-A'sha said:

Until the people say, at what they saw: "How strange, the dead man who has risen!"

The root meaning of al-nashr is spreading out what was folded, and from this arise the meanings of return and dispersal.

Here nashr is figurative (majaz), because the giving of life to the earth is figurative. What makes it more fitting here is that it serves as an introduction to His words: ﴿كَذَلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ﴾.

The pronoun in fa-ansharna is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the first person. Al-mayyit is the opposite of al-hayy (the living).

Describing the town (al-baldah) with it is a common figurative usage; God says: ﴿وآيَةٌ لَهُمُ الأرْضُ المَيْتَةُ أحْيَيْناها﴾ [Ya-Sin: 33].

The town, which is feminine, was described with al-mayyit, which is masculine, because it follows the pattern of descriptive adjectives whose origin is a verbal noun, such as 'adl and zur. So omitting the feminine marker is acceptable, and the modified noun has a figuratively feminine form.

The clause ﴿كَذَلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the two conjoined clauses. It is a digression (istitrad) in argument supporting what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought concerning the affirmation of the Resurrection. It arises in connection with the argument for God's sole divinity, through proofs some of which indicate the possibility of resurrection and refute their claim that it is impossible.

The demonstrative "thus" (dhalika) refers to the dispersal (inshar) derived from fa-ansharna. That is, in the likeness of that dispersal you will be brought out from the earth after your annihilation. The point of comparison is the bringing of the living into existence after its death.

The purpose of the comparison is to show that the thing compared is possible, as in the words of Abu al-Tayyib:

If you surpass mankind while being one of them, then musk is indeed a part of the blood of the gazelle.

The majority of readers (al-jumhur) read ﴿تُخْرَجُونَ﴾ in the passive voice (al-bina' lil-na'ib). Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir read ﴿تَخْرُجُونَ﴾ in the active voice (al-bina' lil-fa'il), and the meaning is the same.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 43, verses 12–14:**

﴿And He who created all the pairs and made for you ships and cattle on which you ride,﴾ ﴿so that you may sit firmly upon their backs, then remember the favour of your Lord when you are seated on them, and say: "Glory be to Him who has subjected these to us, though we could not have subdued them ourselves.﴾ ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we shall surely return."﴾

This transition is from proof and grace through the creation of the means of life, to proof through the creation of the means of earning a livelihood for the maintenance of living. He mentioned among them the means of production, and followed them with the means of earning through travel for trade.

The repetition of the relative noun (ism al-mawsul) refers back to what preceded it in its counterpart just before.

*Al-azwaj* is the plural of *zawj*, which is whatever makes the single one a second, so each of the two is called a *zawj* for the other, like *al-shaf'* (the even). The word *zawj* became the common term for the male and female of animals, as in ﴿eight pairs﴾ [al-An'am: 143] in Surah al-An'am. It was then extended so that *zawj* was applied to a kind, as in His saying: ﴿And of all fruits He made in it two pairs﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3]. Both usages are valid here. In the pairs of livestock there are benefits in their milk, wool, hair, flesh and offspring.

Since what comes first to mind from *al-azwaj* at first glance is the pairs of livestock, and since among the most important of these for them were the mounts, He joined to them what is among them as means of transport on land, and included with them the means of travel by sea.

So He said: ﴿and made for you ships and cattle on which you ride.﴾ Here, with respect to the livestock, what is meant by *ma tarkabun* is the camel, because it is the means of journeys. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin: 41], ﴿and We created for them of its kind that which they ride﴾ [Ya-Sin: 42]. And they have said: "The camels are the ships of the desert."

[Page 173]

The verb *ja'ala* (made) is used out of consideration that ships are manufactured rather than created, while livestock are known to be created, by the inclusiveness of His saying *khalaqa al-azwaj* (He created the pairs), which covers them. The meaning of Allah's making ships and livestock to be ridden is that He created in man the power of reflection by which he is led to use existing things for his benefit. So he devised how to build ships and ride in them, and devised how to tame livestock and ride them.

He placed ships before livestock because the word *azwaj* did not include them. Thus mentioning them is mentioning a different favour. Had He mentioned livestock, their mention right after *azwaj* would have been like a repetition. When He mentioned ships under the heading of their being ridden, He joined livestock to them, so the mention of livestock came as something the soul anticipated, because of a new connection. This is like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if I had never ridden a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets;*
*nor had I poured the red wine for the bay horse, nor said to my horses, "Turn back once more after the rout."*

He followed the mention of riding the steed with the mention of embracing the maiden because of the connection, and did not follow it with his saying "nor said to my horses, 'Turn back once more'," because the states of the two rides differ: the ride for pleasure and the ride for war.

The literal meaning of *al-rukub* (riding) is mounting a beast for travel. It was applied to being within a ship, because they liken the ship to a beast by the common factor of travel. So riding a beast takes its object directly, while riding a ship takes it with *fi* (in), to distinguish the original from the derived sense. This was discussed under His saying: ﴿And he said, "Embark therein"﴾ [Hud: 41] in Surah Hud.

The phrase *min al-fulk wa al-an'am* (of ships and livestock) explains the ambiguity of the relative *ma* in *ma tarkabun*. The returning pronoun of the relative clause was omitted, because it is connected and in the accusative, and omitting such a pronoun is common in speech. Since the object of *tarkabun* here is specified by *al-fulk* and *al-an'am*, the verb should have taken one of them directly and the other with *fi*. The direct transitivity prevailed over transitivity through a particle, because the intended meaning is clear, and the pronoun was omitted on the basis of that prevalence.

The use of the verb *tarkabun* here is one of the uses of a word in its literal and figurative senses.

*Al-istiwa'* means *al-i'tila'* (mounting, sitting upright). *Al-zuhur* is the plural of *zahr* (back). The back belongs to livestock, not to ships, so this too is a case of prevalence (*taghlib*). The meaning is: "upon their backs and in their bellies." The pronoun in *zuhurihi* refers back to the relative *ma*, which covers both ships and livestock, as the nature of the explanation requires.

Moreover, great ships have upper surfaces (*zuhur*), namely their high decks, shaped like roofs, to shield the riders from rain and from the severity of heat and cold. For this reason, the plural *zuhur* is from the plural of what is shared (*jam' al-mushtarak*), and the transitivity by the particle *'ala* (upon) was built on the basis that a ship has a back. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when you and those with you have settled upon the ship﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 28].

His saying ﴿so that you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾ is made as a preparation and paving for alluding to the mention of Allah's favour in His saying: ﴿then remember the favour of your Lord when you are seated on them﴾, that is, at that time. For the remembrance of a favour while one is engaged with its benefits is more striking to the soul and more compelling to give thanks for it, and more fitting for not forgetting it. That is, He made this a favour for you so that you would feel it and thank Him for it. So *al-dhikr* here means remembering with thought, not mentioning with the tongue.

This is an allusion (*ta'ridh*) to the polytheists, who lived amid the blessings of Allah yet gave thanks to others, since they took partners with Him in divinity, though they had no share with Him in the livestock.

The mention of the favour is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for giving thanks for it, because the thankfulness of a benefactor is customarily required by the bestowal of a favour. Nothing diverts from it except forgetting it. So when one remembers it, one gives thanks for the favour.

He joined to His saying ﴿remember the favour of your Lord﴾ the saying ﴿and say: "Glory be to Him who has subjected these to us"﴾. That is, so that you give thanks to Allah in your souls and proclaim the thanks with your tongues. So He taught them a formula of thanks out of care for it, just as He taught them the formula of praise in Surah al-Fatihah and the formula of supplication at the end of Surah al-Baqarah.

He began this verbal thanks with *tasbih* (glorification), because it comprises praise, since *tasbih* is the declaring of Allah free from what is unfitting. It indicates explicitly His transcendence above deficiencies and implicitly affirms perfections for Allah in the context of address.

The invocation of the Divine Name through the relative form (*mawsuliyya*) serves to indicate the reason for glorification that the relative clause implies, so that the praise which *tasbih* conveys becomes thanks, since it is explained as being in return for His subjecting these to us.

[Page 175]

The demonstrative *hadha* (this) refers to the mount, at the moment the rider utters this statement, whether a beast or a ship.

*Al-taskhir* means making something submissive and compliant. Allah's subjecting of beasts is His creating them capable of being trained and understanding the rider's intent. The subjecting of ships is achieved by the totality of: creating the sea suitable for ships to sail upon its water; creating winds that blow and push the ships over the water; creating human ingenuity to build ships, to observe the directions of the winds, and to set sails and oars. Without all this, human strength would not reach the employment of these mighty things.

For this reason, He followed with His saying ﴿though we could not have subdued them ourselves﴾, that is, could not have been capable of them, that is, by bodily strength alone, that is, had it not been for the subjecting mentioned. So the clause ﴿though we could not have subdued them ourselves﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relative to the pronoun in *lana* (to us). That is, He subjected them to us in a state of our weakness, in that His subjecting them stood in place of strength.

[Page 176]

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 43, verses 12–14:**

﴿And He who created all the pairs and made for you ships and cattle on which you ride,﴾ ﴿so that you may sit firmly upon their backs, then remember the favour of your Lord when you are seated on them, and say: "Glory be to Him who has subjected these to us, though we could not have subdued them ourselves.﴾ ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we shall surely return."﴾

This transition is from proof and grace through the creation of the means of life, to proof through the creation of the means of earning a livelihood for the maintenance of living. He mentioned among them the means of production, and followed them with the means of earning through travel for trade.

The repetition of the relative noun (ism al-mawsul) refers back to what preceded it in its counterpart just before.

*Al-azwaj* is the plural of *zawj*, which is whatever makes the single one a second, so each of the two is called a *zawj* for the other, like *al-shaf'* (the even). The word *zawj* became the common term for the male and female of animals, as in ﴿eight pairs﴾ [al-An'am: 143] in Surah al-An'am. It was then extended so that *zawj* was applied to a kind, as in His saying: ﴿And of all fruits He made in it two pairs﴾ [al-Ra'd: 3]. Both usages are valid here. In the pairs of livestock there are benefits in their milk, wool, hair, flesh and offspring.

Since what comes first to mind from *al-azwaj* at first glance is the pairs of livestock, and since among the most important of these for them were the mounts, He joined to them what is among them as means of transport on land, and included with them the means of travel by sea.

So He said: ﴿and made for you ships and cattle on which you ride.﴾ Here, with respect to the livestock, what is meant by *ma tarkabun* is the camel, because it is the means of journeys. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin: 41], ﴿and We created for them of its kind that which they ride﴾ [Ya-Sin: 42]. And they have said: "The camels are the ships of the desert."

[Page 173]

The verb *ja'ala* (made) is used out of consideration that ships are manufactured rather than created, while livestock are known to be created, by the inclusiveness of His saying *khalaqa al-azwaj* (He created the pairs), which covers them. The meaning of Allah's making ships and livestock to be ridden is that He created in man the power of reflection by which he is led to use existing things for his benefit. So he devised how to build ships and ride in them, and devised how to tame livestock and ride them.

He placed ships before livestock because the word *azwaj* did not include them. Thus mentioning them is mentioning a different favour. Had He mentioned livestock, their mention right after *azwaj* would have been like a repetition. When He mentioned ships under the heading of their being ridden, He joined livestock to them, so the mention of livestock came as something the soul anticipated, because of a new connection. This is like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if I had never ridden a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets;*
*nor had I poured the red wine for the bay horse, nor said to my horses, "Turn back once more after the rout."*

He followed the mention of riding the steed with the mention of embracing the maiden because of the connection, and did not follow it with his saying "nor said to my horses, 'Turn back once more'," because the states of the two rides differ: the ride for pleasure and the ride for war.

The literal meaning of *al-rukub* (riding) is mounting a beast for travel. It was applied to being within a ship, because they liken the ship to a beast by the common factor of travel. So riding a beast takes its object directly, while riding a ship takes it with *fi* (in), to distinguish the original from the derived sense. This was discussed under His saying: ﴿And he said, "Embark therein"﴾ [Hud: 41] in Surah Hud.

The phrase *min al-fulk wa al-an'am* (of ships and livestock) explains the ambiguity of the relative *ma* in *ma tarkabun*. The returning pronoun of the relative clause was omitted, because it is connected and in the accusative, and omitting such a pronoun is common in speech. Since the object of *tarkabun* here is specified by *al-fulk* and *al-an'am*, the verb should have taken one of them directly and the other with *fi*. The direct transitivity prevailed over transitivity through a particle, because the intended meaning is clear, and the pronoun was omitted on the basis of that prevalence.

The use of the verb *tarkabun* here is one of the uses of a word in its literal and figurative senses.

*Al-istiwa'* means *al-i'tila'* (mounting, sitting upright). *Al-zuhur* is the plural of *zahr* (back). The back belongs to livestock, not to ships, so this too is a case of prevalence (*taghlib*). The meaning is: "upon their backs and in their bellies." The pronoun in *zuhurihi* refers back to the relative *ma*, which covers both ships and livestock, as the nature of the explanation requires.

Moreover, great ships have upper surfaces (*zuhur*), namely their high decks, shaped like roofs, to shield the riders from rain and from the severity of heat and cold. For this reason, the plural *zuhur* is from the plural of what is shared (*jam' al-mushtarak*), and the transitivity by the particle *'ala* (upon) was built on the basis that a ship has a back. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when you and those with you have settled upon the ship﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 28].

His saying ﴿so that you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾ is made as a preparation and paving for alluding to the mention of Allah's favour in His saying: ﴿then remember the favour of your Lord when you are seated on them﴾, that is, at that time. For the remembrance of a favour while one is engaged with its benefits is more striking to the soul and more compelling to give thanks for it, and more fitting for not forgetting it. That is, He made this a favour for you so that you would feel it and thank Him for it. So *al-dhikr* here means remembering with thought, not mentioning with the tongue.

This is an allusion (*ta'ridh*) to the polytheists, who lived amid the blessings of Allah yet gave thanks to others, since they took partners with Him in divinity, though they had no share with Him in the livestock.

The mention of the favour is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for giving thanks for it, because the thankfulness of a benefactor is customarily required by the bestowal of a favour. Nothing diverts from it except forgetting it. So when one remembers it, one gives thanks for the favour.

He joined to His saying ﴿remember the favour of your Lord﴾ the saying ﴿and say: "Glory be to Him who has subjected these to us"﴾. That is, so that you give thanks to Allah in your souls and proclaim the thanks with your tongues. So He taught them a formula of thanks out of care for it, just as He taught them the formula of praise in Surah al-Fatihah and the formula of supplication at the end of Surah al-Baqarah.

He began this verbal thanks with *tasbih* (glorification), because it comprises praise, since *tasbih* is the declaring of Allah free from what is unfitting. It indicates explicitly His transcendence above deficiencies and implicitly affirms perfections for Allah in the context of address.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 15:

﴿And they have attributed to Him a portion from His servants. Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful.﴾ This is connected to His saying: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 9], meaning: and if you asked them about the Creator of things, they would certainly acknowledge Him, and yet they have attributed to Him, alongside that acknowledgment, a portion.

So the waw is for coordination with the clause ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 9]. It may also be for the circumstantial (ḥāl) clause, meaning: "and yet they have attributed to Him a portion from His servants." The sense of the circumstantial clause conveys astonishment at them, at the contradiction in their opinions and statements and their inversion of realities. This is a confusion in judgment that afflicts the followers of misguided doctrines, because they patch together their beliefs from the varied opinions of the callers (to those doctrines), so that the follower gathers from the opinions of those who differ in their reasoning what, if each of those who follow them had come to know the opinion of the others, he would have nullified it or retracted the opinion opposed to it.

Thus the polytheists acknowledge that God is the Creator of all things, and yet they have attributed to Him partners in divinity. How can it be proper for the created to be a god? And they attributed daughters to God, while filiation necessitates similarity in essence. How can it be proper for the Creator of all things to have daughters? For they are necessarily created by Him; and if they were not created, it would follow that they would be existing by His existence, so how could they be His daughters? The indication of this contradiction is in His saying: (from His servants), meaning: from His created beings. Or, true servitude is nothing but the servitude of the created, (a portion), meaning a piece.

The (juz') is a part of a whole and a fragment of it. A child is like a portion of the parent because it is separated from it, and for this reason the child is called a (ḍaḍʿah) (a piece of flesh). Thus they combined the belief that the angels are originated, which is the implication of their being servants of God, with the belief in their divinity, which is the implication of their being daughters of God, since filiation necessitates sharing in essence.

Since the belief of the polytheists was known to them and known to the Muslims, the intended meaning of (juz') was:

Page 177
the daughters, in accordance with the saying of the polytheists that the angels are daughters of God from the (sarawāt) of the jinn, meaning their mothers were (sarawāt) of the jinn, that is, noble women of the jinn; so (sarawāt) is the plural of (surriyyah).

al-Qurtubi relates that al-Mubarrad said: "The juz' here means daughters; it is said: 'the woman bore a portion' (ajza'at al-mar'ah) when she gave birth to a female."

In Lisan al-'Arab, from al-Zajjaj, he said: "I recited a line of verse to the effect that the meaning of juz' is the meaning of females, and I do not know whether the line is ancient or fabricated," and it is:

If a free woman bears a female one day, there is no wonder, for the free woman sometimes bears a male.

In Taj al-'Arus it is stated that this line was recited by Tha'lab, and in Lisan it is stated that Abu Hanifah recited:

I married her to a daughter of al-Aws, one who bears daughters, ∗∗∗ for whom in her dwellings the moist thornbush has a rustling sound.

al-Mawardi attributed it in his tafsir to the people of lexicography. But the author of al-Kashshaf asserted with certainty that this meaning is a lie against the Arabs and that the two lines are fabricated.

The making (ja'l) here means: passing a judgment on a thing with an attribute, a judgment without any basis, so that it is as if it were a product made by hand, and the making by hand is what the term (ja'l) applies to.

The clause ﴿Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) that indicates the denunciation of what they claimed, as being severe disbelief. And by (al-insān) is meant these people specifically.

Al-Mubin: the one who makes clear his disbelief in his explicit statements concerning the disbelief of God's blessing.

[Page 178]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verses 16–17:

﴿Or has He taken daughters from among what He creates, and chosen sons for you?﴾ ﴿And when one of them is given the good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness, his face becomes darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ "Am" (أمْ, "or") is for transition (al-idrab, a change of subject), and here it is transitional (intiqali), because the discourse moves from refuting their belief in the angels being the children of God, by showing what that entails in terms of the breakdown of the reality of divinity, to refuting it by what it requires of deficiency that contradicts the perfection which divinity demands. The discourse after "am" is an interrogation, and it is a denunciatory interrogation (istifham inkari), as indicated by His saying: ﴿and chosen sons for you﴾. The point of the argument is that females are hateful to them, so how do they attribute to God female children? Why did they not make them males? They have no excuse for the corruption that follows from their belief, by either of the two approaches, because the first refutation is theoretical and certain, and the second refutation is dialectical and self-evident. God says: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ [al-Najm: 21] ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾ [al-Najm: 22]. This is a decisive argument against them, because it is well known among them.

When Sajah bint al-Harith claimed prophethood among the Banu Tamim during the time of the Ridda (apostasy wars), and before her Musaylima al-Hanafi, al-Aswad al-'Ansi and Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi had claimed prophethood, 'Utarid ibn Hajib al-Tamimi said:

"Our prophetess has become a female, around whom we circle,
and the prophets of the people have become males."

The verb (ittakhadha, "took") is chosen here because it includes taking [a child] by birth, that is, by the formation of a separation from the Essence of God through union with the chiefs of the jinn, and it also includes what is less than that, which is adoption (al-tabanni). So, under both hypotheses, the denial is directed at the idea that what belongs to God would be inferior to what belongs to them, as God said: ﴿And they attribute to God what they dislike﴾ [al-Nahl: 62]. His saying ﴿and chosen sons for you﴾ points to this. This is an ascent in refuting their belief, by refuting the supposition that God adopted the angels, closing off for the polytheists the door of interpretation and of disowning the corruption of attributing daughters to God. Perhaps they would say: "We only intended adoption," just as they disowned their position when the proofs of the falsehood of the divinity of the idols overwhelmed them, and they said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18].

Know that what "am" implies wherever it occurs, namely the supposition of an interrogation after it, here is an interrogation in the sense of denial, and the denial is directed at taking daughters, while the daughters have not been mentioned before, because it is known from the polytheists' attributing a part to God that the thing attributed as a part is the angels, and that they make the angels female. This is known from their speech.

The clause ﴿and chosen sons for you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

The negation that results from the denunciatory interrogation applies to the restriction of the circumstance, and so two proofs refute God's taking daughters. For giving them sons is an established fact, so negating its association with His taking daughters for Himself requires the negation of His taking daughters. The intent is that the denial is conjoined with this restriction.

By this it becomes clear that the waw (و) in the clause ﴿and chosen sons for you﴾ is not the waw of conjunction, because denying that He chose sons for them does not require negating male offspring from God.

The address in ﴿and chosen sons for you﴾ is directed to those who attributed to Him a part of His servants, and in it there is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person, so that the denunciation and reproach fall upon them more forcefully, by confronting them with it.

The indefiniteness of (banat, "daughters") is because indefiniteness is the original form for names of kinds. As for the definiteness of (al-banin, "the sons") with the article, it is the definiteness of the kind, which was preceded in His saying "All praise is due to God" in surat al-Fatiha. Its intent here is to point to what is known to them, the thing they compete for in having it. This was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿He bestows female [offspring] on whom He wills and bestows males on whom He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 49], in surat al-Shura.

The mention of the daughters is placed before the sons because mentioning them is more important here, since it is the purpose toward which the discourse is directed. This differs from the context of His saying: ﴿Has your Lord then chosen sons for you and taken for Himself daughters from the angels?﴾ [al-Isra: 40], in surat al-Isra. And because placing them first contains a refutation of the polytheists in their belittling of daughters and their pessimism about them, similar to what was discussed in surat al-Shura.

Al-isfa' (إصفاء) means giving the choice (safwa), which is the best of something.

The clause ﴿And when one of them is given the good news﴾ may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the object pronoun in ﴿Has your Lord then chosen sons for you﴾ [al-Isra: 40]. The apparent expectation is that the pronoun of address would be used in His saying "one of them" (ahadahum), but He turned away from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of the third person, by way of iltifat, so that they become a people whose condition is reported to others, in wonder at the corruption of their saying and in condemnation of it, since they attributed daughters to God rather than sons, which is a deficiency. They were among those who hate daughters and belittle them, so attributing them to God leads to diminishing the dignity of divinity.

The meaning is: Do you attribute to God daughters from what He creates, and choose sons for yourselves, when one of you is given the good news of that which he has set up as a likeness to the Most Merciful, his face becomes darkened?

[Page 179]

It may also be that the clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradan) between the clause ﴿Or has He taken daughters from among what He creates﴾ and the clause ﴿Or one who is brought up among ornaments?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 18].

The use of the term "good news" (bisharah) here is sarcastic toward them, like His saying: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21], because "good news" is the announcement of the occurrence of something that delights.

The (ma, "that which") in His saying ﴿that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness﴾ is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), meaning: he is given the good news of the kind which he set up, that is, made as a likeness and an equivalent to God in divinity. Since they made the female kind a part of God, that is, separated from Him, the thing given good news of is the female kind, and the kind is not specified. So there is no need to assume: "given the good news of something similar to what he set up as a likeness to the Most Merciful."

The (mathal, "likeness") is the equivalent.

The (darb, "setting up") is making and fashioning. From it comes "minting a dinar" (darb al-dinar), and their saying "a necessary striking" (darbatu lazib). So the referent of ﴿that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness﴾ is the females.

The meaning of (zalla, "became") here is "became," for the five defective verbs with which the chapter of defective verbs opens are used in the sense of "became."

The blackening of the face is from intense anger and rage, as the blood rises to the face so its redness turns to blackness. The meaning is: he became enraged.

Al-kazim (كظيم) means one who holds back, that is, from speech, out of distress and grief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verses 16–17:

﴿Or has He taken daughters from among what He creates, and chosen sons for you?﴾ ﴿And when one of them is given the good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness, his face becomes darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ "Am" (أمْ, "or") is for transition (al-idrab, a change of subject), and here it is transitional (intiqali), because the discourse moves from refuting their belief in the angels being the children of God, by showing what that entails in terms of the breakdown of the reality of divinity, to refuting it by what it requires of deficiency that contradicts the perfection which divinity demands. The discourse after "am" is an interrogation, and it is a denunciatory interrogation (istifham inkari), as indicated by His saying: ﴿and chosen sons for you﴾. The point of the argument is that females are hateful to them, so how do they attribute to God female children? Why did they not make them males? They have no excuse for the corruption that follows from their belief, by either of the two approaches, because the first refutation is theoretical and certain, and the second refutation is dialectical and self-evident. God says: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ [al-Najm: 21] ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾ [al-Najm: 22]. This is a decisive argument against them, because it is well known among them.

When Sajah bint al-Harith claimed prophethood among the Banu Tamim during the time of the Ridda (apostasy wars), and before her Musaylima al-Hanafi, al-Aswad al-'Ansi and Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi had claimed prophethood, 'Utarid ibn Hajib al-Tamimi said:

"Our prophetess has become a female, around whom we circle,
and the prophets of the people have become males."

The verb (ittakhadha, "took") is chosen here because it includes taking [a child] by birth, that is, by the formation of a separation from the Essence of God through union with the chiefs of the jinn, and it also includes what is less than that, which is adoption (al-tabanni). So, under both hypotheses, the denial is directed at the idea that what belongs to God would be inferior to what belongs to them, as God said: ﴿And they attribute to God what they dislike﴾ [al-Nahl: 62]. His saying ﴿and chosen sons for you﴾ points to this. This is an ascent in refuting their belief, by refuting the supposition that God adopted the angels, closing off for the polytheists the door of interpretation and of disowning the corruption of attributing daughters to God. Perhaps they would say: "We only intended adoption," just as they disowned their position when the proofs of the falsehood of the divinity of the idols overwhelmed them, and they said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18].

Know that what "am" implies wherever it occurs, namely the supposition of an interrogation after it, here is an interrogation in the sense of denial, and the denial is directed at taking daughters, while the daughters have not been mentioned before, because it is known from the polytheists' attributing a part to God that the thing attributed as a part is the angels, and that they make the angels female. This is known from their speech.

The clause ﴿and chosen sons for you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

The negation that results from the denunciatory interrogation applies to the restriction of the circumstance, and so two proofs refute God's taking daughters. For giving them sons is an established fact, so negating its association with His taking daughters for Himself requires the negation of His taking daughters. The intent is that the denial is conjoined with this restriction.
