Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 18:

﴿Is one who is brought up in ornaments, and who in dispute is not clear [in expression]?﴾

This is a conjunction of one denial upon another. The waw is a conjunctive particle joining one clause to another, and it is placed after the interrogative hamza because the interrogative holds the front position; the original order is: "And is one who is brought up [yunasha'u]..." The interrogative clause is conjoined to the denial implied after "am" in His words: ﴿Or has He taken daughters from what He creates?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 16]. Accordingly, "one who is brought up in ornaments" is in the accusative position, governed by a verb omitted that is indicated by the verb "has taken" in His words: ﴿Or has He taken daughters from what He creates?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 16]. The sense is: "Has He taken one who is brought up in ornaments...?" You may also make "one who is brought up in ornaments" an apposition (badal) to His words "daughters," an appositive that agrees with it in full, and the governing verb in the appositive is made explicit to emphasize the sense of denial, especially since it was omitted from the thing replaced.

Since denial applies only to the predicate of the statement, the object of the second denial differs from the object of the first denial, even though the one described by both attributes, to which the denial pertains, is a single described entity, namely the female.

The "nash' of a thing in a state" means that the beginning of its existence coincides with that state, so that for the thing it is like a container. For this reason the particle "fi" (in), which indicates the sense of location, is brought in, though it is in fact used figuratively for the sense of accompaniment and association. The meaning of "one who is brought up in ornaments" is: one for whom ornaments are provided from the earliest times of his existence and who is never without them, for a girl is adorned from the beginning of her life and is kept in that state through all her stages. It suffices as evidence that her ears are pierced so that earrings may be placed in them, unlike a boy, who is not adorned with such things nor kept in them.

The "upbringing in ornaments" is a metonymy (kinayah) for weakness in confronting difficulties, according to the customary association attached to it. The meaning is: there is no benefit in God taking daughters who have no capacity to help, so that taking them brings Him no increase in honour, according to their customary understanding. This is a persuasive, rhetorical argument (ihtijaj iqna'i khitabi).

The apparent meaning of "khisam" (dispute) is contention and disputation by speech and argument, so the meaning is: a woman does not reach the capacity to make her argument clear. It is reported from Qatadah: "No woman has spoken while having an argument without turning it against herself." And also from him: "one who is brought up in ornaments" refers to the young girls, whom they thereby deride. All the exegetes have followed this interpretation.

The meaning upon it is: they are not capable of defending themselves by speech, and so, a fortiori, they are not capable of what is more severe than that in war; that is, there is no use in taking them as children.

In my view it is also permissible to understand "khisam" as fighting and defending by hand, for the word "khasm" is applied to a combatant. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], which was explained as referring to a group of Muslims with a group of polytheists who fought on the day of Badr.

So the meaning of "not clear" (ghayr mubin) is: not assured of victory. Some Arabs, when they were given the good news of the birth of a daughter, said: "By God, she is not a good child: her crying is her weakness, and her help is theft."

The purpose of this is to expose their false belief, and that they do not properly employ reflection regarding their beliefs; otherwise, when they attributed sonship to God, they would not have attributed to Him the sonship of females, while they themselves regard females as things disliked and weak.

The pronoun in "and he is in dispute" is masculine in agreement with the wording of the relative pronoun "man" (who).

"Hilyah" is a noun for what is adorned with, that is, what one is decorated with. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you extract from it ornaments that you wear﴾ [al-Nahl: 14].

The majority read "yanshа'" (yanshaʾu) with a fatha on the ya' and sukun on the nun. Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yunasha'" (yunashshaʾu) with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the nun and a shaddah on the shin, meaning: he is brought up and raised in ornaments.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 19:

﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿And they have attributed to Him a portion from His servants﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 15]. That was repeated, with the preceding statement ﴿Has He taken daughters from what He creates?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 16] serving as its substitute, so that the rebuke upon them could be built on their statement: ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ This is by way of inductive reasoning (istiqra') to invalidate their claim, since it had already been invalidated at the outset by its contradiction of rational proof and by its contradiction of the perfection that is due to God. Thus its invalidation was completed here by the fact that it is not grounded in sensory evidence.

The clause ﴿who are with the Most Merciful﴾ is a qualifier (ṣifah) of the angels.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Jaʿfar and Yaʿqub read ʿinda (عِنْدَ) with ʿayn, a nun with a fatḥah on the dal. The "nearness" (ʿindiyyah) here is nearness of honour (tashrif), meaning those who are counted in the sacred presence (ḥaḍrat al-qudus) through the sanctification of God. They receive the command from God without intermediary, and they are constantly devoted to His worship, so it is as though they are in the presence of God. This is like His saying: ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and those with Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord are not too proud to worship Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 206]. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Adam and Moses disputed before God, the Mighty and Majestic," the hadith. So the nearness is figurative (majaz), and the indicator (qarinah) is the status of that to which ʿinda is attached.

The rest read ʿibad al-Rahman (عِبادُ الرَّحْمَنِ), with ʿayn, then a btill after which is an alif, then a dal with a ḍammah, meaning: those who are honoured servants. The attribution to the name al-Rahman conveys their honour, as He said: ﴿Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26]. The servitude is a special servitude, namely the servitude of closeness, as in His saying: ﴿So they denied Our servant﴾.

The clause ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) between the clause ﴿And they have made the angels﴾ and the clause ﴿And they say: Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20].

Nafi' and Abu Jaʿfar read with two hamzahs, the first with a fatḥah and the second with a ḍammah, and the shin of (اشْهِدُوا) with a sukun, in the passive voice. The manner of pronouncing the two hamzahs follows the rule of the two hamzahs in Nafi''s reading. On this reading the hamzah is interrogative, and it is for denial and rebuke. The passive form (ṣīghat al-nāʾib ʿan al-fāʿil) was used rather than the active form because the agent is known to be God, Exalted, since the upper world in which the creation of the angels took place is attended only by those whom God commands to attend. Do you not see what is related in the hadith of the Night Journey, the words of each angel assigned to a gate of the heavens to Gabriel when he asks for entry: "Who are you? He said: Gabriel. He said: Who is with you? He said: Muhammad. He said: Has he been sent for? He said: Yes. He said: Welcome, and excellent is the coming; he has come and the gate was opened for him."

The meaning: Did God cause them to witness the creation of the angels? Like His saying: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Kahf: 51].

The rest read it with an opened hamzah, then an opened shin, in the form of the verb. The hamzah is then the interrogative of denial, entering upon the verb (shahida), meaning: they were not present at the creation of the angels, like His saying: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ [al-Saffat: 150].

The clause ﴿Their testimony will be recorded﴾ is a substitutive clause (badal al-ishtimal) for the clause ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾, because that denial includes a threat. This is a report used in the sense of a warning. The recording of the testimony is a metaphor (kinayah) for the certainty of punishment for their lying, as already mentioned above in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 4], and from it His saying: ﴿We will record what they have said﴾. The sin in sanaktub is for emphasis of the threat.

By "their testimony" is meant their claim that the angels are females, and it is called testimony in mockery of them.

The questioning is a questioning of threat and warning with punishment, and it is not one that requires an answer, like His saying: ﴿Then you will be questioned that Day about the bliss﴾ [al-Takathur: 8]. From it is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

*That is more awe-inspiring to me when I speak to him, though it was said that you are reported and questioned.*

That is: questioned about what preceded from you of denial, which is known to the questioner.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 20:

﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them. They have no knowledge of that; they merely guess."﴾ It is coordinated with the sentence ﴿And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say: "They were created by the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 9], for it is an argument for the Oneness of God the Exalted and for the fact that the objects they worship do not deserve to be worshipped. Here is related what they considered to be their excuses when the proof was established against them, by which they intended to confound the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims. They say: "If God had willed, we would not have worshipped the idols," meaning: if God did not love for us to worship them, God would have turned us away from worshipping them. They imagined that this was decisive against the Prophet's ﷺ argument against them, because they had heard from his religion that God is the One who disposes of events, so they interpreted it in a way other than what was intended. The pronoun of the third person in ﴿ma 'abadnahum﴾ refers to something known from the context and from the mention of the act of worship, because they used to worship idols, and that was the majority, while some of them worshipped the jinn. God the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ [Saba': 41].

Ibn Mas'ud said: A group of the Arabs used to worship the jinn, and some peoples worshipped the angels, such as Banu Mulayh (with a damma on the mim, a fatha on the lam, and an unpointed ha), who were a tribe of Khuza'ah. The masculine plural pronoun is used as a generalization (taghlib) and does not refer to the angels, because they used to claim that the angels were females; had they meant the angels, they would have said: "ma 'abadnaha" or "ma 'abadnahunna."

This is the correct meaning of the verse. Similar is related from Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj, and al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyyah adopted it. Among the exegetes, some made the referent of the pronoun "the angels," and perhaps what led them to that is that this statement follows the report of their saying about the angels that they are females; but the juxtaposition of one statement with another does not necessitate the unity of their senses. On this interpretation went the author of al-Kashshaf, and it is far from the wording, because of the masculinity of the pronoun as you know, and from reality, because among the Arabs only small groups worshipped the angels, along with the idols and the jinn, and that was not the general religion of the Arabs. The source of this view is the confusion of the common people and the masses since the Age of Ignorance between the will (mashi'ah) and the volition (iradah), and between approval (ridha) and love (mahabbah). The Arabs used to say: "God willed" and "If God wills," and Tarafah said:

"If my Lord had willed, I would have been Qays ibn 'Asim, and if my Lord had willed, I would have been 'Amr ibn Martad."

On that they built a confusion between the will of God in the sense of the attachment of His volition to the occurrence of a thing, and between His will which He ordained in the order of the world, by attaching effects to their causes and the connection of outcomes to their influences, which God arranged by decree when He created the world, organized it, and established for it customs and laws that do not depart from their course except when God wills to alter their order for another wisdom.

So the will of God in the first sense is indicated by what He established of the order of the conditions of the world and its people. And His will in the second sense is indicated by His legislations which His messengers were sent with.

This confusion between the two wills is the source of the error of the people of misguidance among the nations, and the source of the bewilderment of the ignorant and deficient among the Muslims regarding the meaning of qada' and qadar and the meaning of obligation (taklif) and address (khitab). We have explained that at His saying the Exalted: ﴿Those who associated partners will say: "If God had willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything." Likewise denied those before them until they tasted Our might﴾ [al-An'am: 148], in the surah of al-An'am.

From this statement issued by them one expects a conditional syllogism: that it be said: "If God had willed, we would not have worshipped the idols, on the evidence that God is the One who disposes of our affairs and the affairs of all creatures. But we did worship the idols, on the evidence of observation; so God has willed that we worship the idols."

They were answered regarding their statement by His saying the Exalted: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾, meaning: they have no basis or proof for their analogy, because the antecedent of the conditional syllogism, which is: ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾, is built on conflating the creative will with the legislative will, so their analogy was devoid of knowledge, which is certainty. Therefore God said: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾, meaning: by their saying that, ﴿knowledge﴾; rather it is from the ignorance of sophistry and confusion.

The reference of "that" is to the speech reported by His saying: ﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed."﴾

The clause ﴿They merely guess﴾ explains the clause ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾.

Al-khars: conjecture and assumption for which there is no proof; God the Exalted said: "Killed be the conjecturers" (qutila al-kharrasun).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 21:

﴿Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they are holding fast to it?﴾ This is an *idrab intiqali* (a transitional "rather"/"or" shift), conjoined to the clause: "They have no knowledge of that." So after he negated that their saying, "Had the Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them," was based on the proof of reason, he moved on to negating that it was based on the proof of transmission (*naql*) from one who informs of the realities of things, which are among His affairs.

He brought in the particle *am* ("or") rather than *bal* ("rather") for the shift, because *am* indicates a following interrogation, and it is a rhetorical denial. The meaning is: "We did not give them a Book before it." The pronoun in "before it" (*min qablihi*) refers to the Qur'an mentioned at the beginning of the surah, in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 4]. In this there is a third, implicit praise of the Qur'an, since it implies that the Qur'an brings only the truth to which one holds fast.

This is a preparation for the transition to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they said: Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22].

The *min* in *min qablihi* is *za'idah* (an emphatic, superfluous particle) to strengthen the meaning of *qabla* ("before"). The pronoun attached to *qabla* is the pronoun of the Qur'an, and no antecedent for it has preceded in the wording, but it is apparent from the implication of His saying: "a Book."

*Mustamsikun* is an intensive form of *mumsikun* (holding). It is said: *amsaka bi-l-shay'*, when one grips a thing firmly with one's hand, and it is used figuratively to mean persistence upon a thing, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 43].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 22:

﴿Nay, but they say: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are guided along their footsteps."﴾ This is an idrab (a turning away, i.e. a transition in discourse) of nullification (ibtal) from the preceding speech, namely His the Exalted's words: ﴿So they hold fast to it﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 21]. It is therefore a nullification of the thing negated, not of the negation itself; that is, they have no knowledge in what they say, nor any transmitted report. This statement is thus delivered in the manner of censure directed at them, since they did not compare what the Messenger brought them with what they received from their fathers. For it is the nature of the rational person to distinguish what is presented to him of divergent views and to measure it against the standard of truth.

Here "ummah" (community) means religion (millah) and creed (din), as in His the Exalted's words in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿Indeed this your ummah is one ummah﴾ [al-Anbiya': 92], and in the verse of al-Nabighah:

"And would one who has a religion (ummah) sin while he is obedient?"

That is, one who has a religion.
The "ʿala" (upon) is a metaphor of the subordinate (istiʿarah tabiʿiyyah) for association and possession.

His words "﴿upon their footsteps﴾" are the predicate of "inna" (indeed), and "muhtadun" (guided) is a second predicate. It is also permissible that "﴿upon their footsteps﴾" be connected to "muhtadun" by implying in "muhtadun" the meaning of "sa'irun" (travelling), that is, they have no proof for their worship of idols except the imitation of their fathers, and this is what they say when disputing, since they have no proof other than that.

They regarded following them as guidance, because of the intensity of their deception by their fathers' conditions, to such a degree that they do not reflect on the clash of their conditions with the truth.

[صفحة ١٨٨]

﴿And thus We did not send before you a warner into any town but its affluent ones said: "Indeed we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps."﴾

This is a parenthetical clause (jumlah mu'taridah) that consoles the Prophet (ﷺ) over the adherence of the polytheists to the religion of their fathers. The demonstrative refers to what was mentioned in their saying, "Indeed we found our fathers upon a religion," meaning: and like their saying that, the affluent ones of the towns to which the messengers were sent before you said the same.

The waw is either conjunctive (li-l-'atf) or parenthetical (li-l-i'tirad). (In reality, the parenthetical waw only conjoins the parenthetical clause to the clause preceding it by a verbal conjunction.)

The intended meaning is that this is the disposition (shanshanah) of the people of misguidance, both earlier and later. They are alike in it, just as they are alike in its source, which is shallow, mistaken reasoning. As God the Exalted says: ﴿Did they bequeath it to one another? Nay, they are a rebellious people﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 53], meaning: rather, they shared in its cause that prompted it, which is transgression.

This also contains consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding what he met from his people, since the messengers before him met the same as what he met.

The particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) is connected to the saying, "﴿its affluent ones said﴾." It was placed before its complement for the sake of emphasis on this resemblance and to create anticipation for what follows the demonstrative.

The clause "illa qala mutrafuha" (except that its affluent ones said) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because the exception here is from unspecified circumstances. The meaning is: We did not send to the people of any town in any state of theirs except in the state of a saying that its affluent ones uttered: "Indeed we found our fathers..." etc.

Al-mutrafun is the plural of al-mutraf, one who has been given luxury (taraf), that is, blessing. It was mentioned earlier in God's saying: ﴿Return to what you were made affluent in﴾ [al-Anbiya': 13] in Surat al-Anbiya'.

The meaning is that they are like the Quraysh in their conceit over the blessing they enjoy, that is, in their insolence over God's blessing upon them. The comparison therefore implies that they are like the earlier nations in the cause of conceit, which is what they possess of blessing, until they forgot their need of God the Exalted. God the Exalted says: ﴿Leave Me with the deniers, possessors of blessing, and give them a little respite﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11].

[صفحة ١٨٩]

The description of the present polytheists is related as their describing themselves as being guided by the traces of their fathers, while the description of the earlier peoples is related as their describing themselves as following their fathers. This is because the sayings of the earlier peoples were many and varied, and what unites their varied sayings is that they were imitation of their fathers. Therefore, reporting their sayings falls under reporting speech in substance (hikayat al-qawl bi-l-ma'na), and reporting speech in substance is a method of relating statements that frequently occurs in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 24:

﴿Say: "Even if I brought you better guidance than that which you found your fathers following?"﴾ The majority (al-Jumhur) read (qul) ("Say") in the imperative form addressed to a single person, so it is a command to the Messenger ﷺ to say it in reply to the words of the polytheists: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided.﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 22].

Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read (qala) ("he said") in the past-tense form attributed to a third-person masculine singular, so the pronoun refers back to the warner (nadhir) of those who said: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, adherents.﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 23]. From the two readings it follows that all the messengers answered their peoples with this reply. On both readings, the verb (qul) or (qala) comes detached, not conjoined, because it occurs within the setting of a dialogue, as has been explained more than once, including His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The majority read (ji'tukum) ("I have come to you") with the first-person singular pronoun (ta' al-mutakallim). Abu Ja'far read (ji'nakum) ("We have come to you") with the nun of the first-person plural pronoun of association. Abu Ja'far is among those who read (qul) in the imperative form, so the pronoun in (ji'nakum) refers to the Prophet ﷺ who is addressed by the verb (qul), in order to magnify him ﷺ from his Lord, exalted is He, who addressed him with His words: (Say).

The waw in His saying (awa-law) is a conjunctive waw joining the commanded speech to their speech, and this type of conjunction is among what is called ʿatf al-talqin (the conjunction of instruction). An example of it is His saying, exalted is He, concerning Abraham: ﴿He said, "And of my offspring?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The hamza is for the interrogative of affirmation (al-istifham al-taqriri) mixed with denial. It was placed before the waw for the sake of priority of position (al-taṣdir).

(law) is conditional of extremity (law al-wasliyya), and law al-wasliyya requires emphasis to the utmost extent of the meaning of its condition, as has been explained previously at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Even if he ransomed himself with it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91] in Surat Al 'Imran. That is: even if I brought you guidance better than the religion of your fathers, would you remain upon the religion of your fathers and abandon what is better?

The purpose of the interrogation is to make them affirm this, in order to invite them to consider what they followed their fathers in, perhaps what the Messenger called them to is better than what they have.

Forming the superlative (ism al-tafdil) from guidance (al-hady) is a loosening of the reins for them so that they may reflect. It treats what their fathers were upon as though it contained some guidance, in order to lure the addressees' attention so that they may apply themselves to reflection, like His saying: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in manifest error.﴾ [Saba': 24].

* * *

﴿They said, "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."﴾ This is a substitute (badal) for the clause ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, adherents.﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 23], because that includes the meaning: "We will not follow you and abandon what we found our fathers upon." The pronoun in (qalu) refers back to (mutrafuha) ("its affluent ones"), because the position of the clause ﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 25] specifies that these speakers were the ones on whom the vengeance fell; therefore the polytheists against whom the threat was directed are not among them.

Their saying "with which you have been sent" may be a direct quotation of their words; their applying the term "sending" to the call of their messengers is a mockery, like His saying: ﴿What is this messenger who eats food?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. It may also be a quotation in meaning, and they only said "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you claim you have been sent," while what they were sent with is the affirmation of the oneness of God (tawhid al-Ilah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 25:

﴿So We took vengeance upon them; so look at how was the end of the deniers.﴾ This is a consequence (tafri') of the statement ﴿They said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in what you have been sent with"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 24]. That is: We took vengeance upon them immediately after [1] their open declaration of denying the messengers. This is a threat of vengeance against those who resembled them in their speech, namely the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Al-intiqam (vengeance) is an ifti'al form from al-naqm, which means requiting with evil. The ifti'al form here is for mere emphasis (mujarrad al-mubalaghah). It is said: naqima (like 'alima and daraba), when one repays evil with evil. In a proverb: "He is like the al-Ara'am: if left alone, he bites; and if killed, he takes revenge." Al-Ara'am is a kind of snake which the Arabs believe is from the jinn. If a person leaves it, it leaps upon him and stings and kills him; and if a person kills it, it takes revenge through its venom and causes the death of its killer. This is one of the superstitions of the Arabs.

The intended meaning of vengeance is their extermination and annihilation. This was mentioned in His saying: ﴿So We took vengeance upon them and drowned them in the sea﴾ [al-A'raf: 136], in surah al-A'raf.

Accordingly, the looking in His saying ﴿so look at how was the end of the deniers﴾ is the looking of reflection and contemplation upon what Allah related to His Messenger of their reports, like His saying: ﴿He said, "We will see whether you were truthful or were among the liars"﴾ [al-Naml: 27], in surah al-Naml. It is not looking with the eyes, since the Prophet did not witness the state of vengeance upon them.

It is also possible that the address is general, not to a specific person, meaning: to everyone who is able to reflect.

And "kayfa" (how) is an interrogative about the state, and it has suspended the verb of looking from its object.

[Page 192]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verses 26–27:

﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free of what you worship,"﴾ ﴿"except He who originated me, for He will guide me."﴾ When God reminded them of the past nations and compared their situation to theirs, He presented to them examples of this, including the stances of the messengers with their peoples, among them the story of Abraham, peace be upon him, with his people.

He began by mentioning Abraham and his people in order to refute the claim of the polytheists: ﴿"Indeed, we found our fathers following a community, and indeed we are guided by their footsteps"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. This is because the most fitting of their forefathers for them to follow is their father, whom they boast of being descended from, namely Abraham.

The clause ﴿And when Abraham said﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with the general discourse preceding it, from His saying ﴿"And We did not send a warner before you to any town..."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23] up to His saying ﴿And when Abraham said﴾. This is a conjunction of one theme with another theme.

The word (idh) is an adverbial of time governed by an omitted verb, whose implied sense is: "Remember when Abraham said." Similar instances are numerous in the Qur'an, as was previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will place upon the earth a successive authority"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning is: remember the time when Abraham said to his father and his people a plain statement of disavowal of the worship of idols.

Abraham's father was singled out for mention before his people, though he was only one of them, out of concern for mentioning him, because Abraham's disavowal of what his father worshipped is more indicative of avoiding the worship of idols, to the extent that it is not tolerated, even if the one who worships them is the nearest of people to the one who worships God alone, such as a father. It also serves to make the report of Abraham's speech an exemplar for refuting the polytheists' saying ﴿"And indeed we are guided by their footsteps"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. God said: ﴿"There has already been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, 'Indeed, we are free of you and of what you worship besides God'"﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4], meaning: it was not for you to follow your polytheist fathers, and why did you not follow the best of your fathers, who is Abraham?

The word al-baraʾ (disavowal), with a fatḥah on the bāʾ, is a verbal noun on the pattern fiʿāl, like al-ẓamāʾ (thirst) and al-samāʿ (hearing). It may be used as a predicate and as an attributive, in the dialect of the people of al-ʿĀliyah, which is the area above Najd extending to the land of Tihamah beyond Makkah. As for the people of Najd, they say barīʾ.

The exception in His saying ﴿except He who originated me﴾ is an exception (istithnāʾ) from (mā taʿbudūn, "what you worship"), with (mā) being a relative pronoun. That is, [the exception is from] those whom you worship. Abraham's people were polytheists like the polytheists of the Arabs. We have expounded upon this previously at His saying: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods?"﴾ [al-Anʿam: 74].

He based on this His saying ﴿"for He will guide me"﴾, because His saying ﴿"Indeed, I am free of what you worship"﴾ implies the meaning: "Indeed, I have been guided to the falsity of your worship of idols by a guidance from God."

The sīn of futurity (sīn al-istiqbāl) indicates that he informed them that God's guidance to him had been established and would continue in the future. It is understood that it is already present now, from the implication of the discourse (fahwā al-khiṭāb).

The emphasis of the statement with (inna) is directed at the condition of his father and his people, because they deny that he is now upon guidance. Thus they deny that he will be upon guidance in the future.
