**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 28:**

﴿And He made it a word remaining among his descendants, that they might return﴾. It is coordinated with "when Abraham said" (idh qala Ibrahim), meaning he proclaimed that statement among his contemporary people, and made it a word remaining among his descendants, who transmit it to their contemporaries among the nations. He enjoined it upon his sons, and that they should enjoin it upon their sons. The Exalted said in Surah al-Baqarah: "﴿When his Lord said to him, 'Submit,' he said, 'I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.'﴾ [2:131] ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons in this, and Jacob: 'O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims.'﴾ [2:132]" By that bequest Abraham preserved the monotheism of Allah in worship and divinity among his descendants, who spread it among the people. For this reason Joseph said to his two companions in prison: ﴿O my two companions of prison, are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ [12:39] and said to them: ﴿Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah and who, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ [12:37] ﴿And I follow the religion of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. It was not for us to associate anything with Allah.﴾ [12:38] up to His saying: ﴿But most of the people do not know.﴾ [12:40]

The pronoun of the nominative in "ja'alaha" refers to Abraham, and this is what is apparent from the context and suits His saying ﴿so that they may return﴾ [12:62 as cited], and because the name of Allah (the Majesty) has not preceded so that the pronoun of "ja'alaha" could refer to it.

In al-Kashshaf it is related that it was said: the pronoun refers to Allah, and al-Qurtubi affirmed this, and it is the apparent meaning of the words of Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi.

The accusative pronoun in His saying "wa ja'alaha" refers to the preceding speech. The pronoun is feminine by interpreting the speech as "kalima" (word), in view of its second object being the noun kalima, because speech is called kalima, as in the saying of the Exalted in Surah al-Mu'minun: ﴿It is a word he is saying﴾ [23:100], meaning the statement of the disbeliever ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [23:99] ﴿that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind﴾ [23:100]. The Exalted also said: ﴿Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾ [18:5], which is their saying that Allah has taken a son. He, the Exalted, has said: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons in this﴾ [2:132], meaning with his saying ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [2:131], so He returned to it a feminine pronoun according to the interpretation of (kalima).

Know that speech is called kalima only when it is a saying that circulates on tongues and is taken as an example, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The truest word ever spoken by a poet is the word of Labid: Surely everything other than Allah is vain," or when the speech is made a slogan, as in their saying "La ilaha illa Allah is the word of Islam." The Exalted said: ﴿They indeed uttered the word of disbelief﴾ [9:74].

So the meaning: Abraham made his statement ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾ [43:26] ﴿except He who created me﴾ [43:27] a slogan for his descendants, meaning he made it, and what is synonymous with it, a statement remaining among his descendants through the passage of time, so the descendants of Abraham are never without those who believe in Allah and reject idols.

The particle of place (fi) indicates that this word was not cut off among the descendants of Abraham without generalizing among the descendants. If "descendants" is meant as the totality of his descendants, then the word of monotheism was not cut off from the Jews, and was cut off from the Arabs after they adopted the worship of idols, except those among them who became Jews or Christians. If it is meant as every single descendant, then the Arabs were never without someone upholding the word of monotheism, such as the Christianized among them, like the Christianized tribes and Waraqah ibn Nawfal, and like the monotheists (hanifs) such as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl and Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt. This is because "fi" comes for partitive meaning, as we mentioned in His saying ﴿and provide for them therein and clothe them﴾ [4:5] in Surah al-Nisa', and Sabrah ibn 'Amr al-Faq'asi said from the Hamasah:

"And we drink with its price and gamble."

The descendants ('aqib) are the offspring who are not separated from their origin by a female, meaning Abraham made the word of monotheism remain among his descendants by enjoining it upon them, hoping that they would return, meaning that they would remember monotheism by it when rust covers their hearts, or they would find the worship of idols good, as the people of Moses said: ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾ [7:138], so they would be guided by that word when time is too narrow to spread out the proof. This is the nature of speech that is made a slogan for something, for it becomes a established principle whose truth and correctness have become clear, so its recalling dispenses with repeating the proof for it.

The clause "that they might return" is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause "﴿and made it a word remaining among his descendants﴾", because his making the word ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾ [43:26] remain among his descendants was for purposes beneficial to them, of which: he hoped by it that they would return to abandoning the worship of idols if they were tempted by worshipping them, or would remember by it giving up the worship of idols if they worshipped them. So the meaning of "return" is to go back to what that word indicates. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And We seized them with the punishment so that they might return﴾ [43:48], meaning that they might return from their disbelief.

The particle (la'alla) is for expressing hope, and the hope here is undoubtedly Abraham's hope, so it is necessary to presume the meaning of a statement issuing from Abraham by expressing his hope, by estimating: he said, "perhaps they will return," or "saying: perhaps they will return."

"Return" is used metaphorically for changing a newly arisen belief to a previous belief, comparing the abandoning of the newly arisen belief and adopting the earlier belief to the return of the traveler to his homeland or the return of the one who strives to his house.

The meaning: everyone who has deviated from it returns to it. This hope of his has been fulfilled among some of his descendants and not among others, as the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "And from my offspring?" He said, "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers."﴾ [2:124], meaning the polytheists. Among those in whom Abraham's hope was fulfilled, likely, is the pillar of the lineage of the Prophet (ﷺ), and they only concealed their religion out of taqiyya before their people. I have expanded the discussion on this meaning and on the condition of the people of the interval (ahl al-fatrah) in this verse in my treatise "The Purity of the Prophetic Lineage from Defects."

In His saying ﴿and made it a word remaining among his descendants﴾ there is an indication that the oneness of Allah was not unknown to the polytheists. It follows that the call to knowledge of the existence of Allah and His oneness had reached most nations through what they had transmitted of the sayings of the earlier messengers, and among those nations were the Arabs. Therefore the polytheists are rightly held accountable for associating partners before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), because they neglected to consider what was widespread among them, or were heedless of it, or turned away. So the people of the interval are held accountable for abandoning monotheism in this world and are punished for it in the Hereafter. On this is based what is reported in authentic narrations about the punishment of 'Amr ibn Luhayy, who instituted the worship of idols, and what is reported that Imru' al-Qays, bearer of the banner of the poets, will be taken to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, and other things. This is what is fitting to be the view of the People of the Sunnah who say: the knowledge of Allah is obligatory by the Shari'ah, not by reason, which is the well-known position of al-Ash'ari, and those among them who say that the polytheists of the people of the interval are eternally in the Fire for their polytheism.

As for those who say that the knowledge of Allah is obligatory by reason, which is the saying of all the Maturidis and some of the Shafi'is, there is no difficulty for their view.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 29:

﴿Nay, I gave enjoyment to these people and their fathers until there came to them the Truth and a clear Messenger.﴾ This is an idrab (a turning away, a change of subject) from His saying "﴿so that they may return﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 28], and it is an idrab of nullification (idrab ibtal), meaning: what Ibrahim hoped for, namely that some of his descendants would return to the word which he enjoined them to uphold, did not come to pass. For the earliest nation of his descendants did not return to his word, and these are the Arabs who associated partners with God and worshipped idols.

After (bal) there is an omitted statement, indicated by the nullification and what follows the nullification. The estimated omitted statement is: "Nay, these people and their first forefathers did not return to monotheism, did not disavow the worship of idols, and did not adhere to the injunction of Ibrahim."

The clause "I gave enjoyment to these people and their fathers" is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), answering an implied questioner who asks what God did to them as a consequence of their neglect of Ibrahim's injunction, and why He did not uproot them. As He said: "﴿And We never sent before you a warner into a town but its affluent ones said, 'We found our fathers upon a religion...'﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 23], up to His saying "﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 25]. It was answered that God gave them enjoyment by allowing them to remain until a messenger came to them with the truth, and this was for a wisdom known to God, connected to which is the existence of the Arabs for a long time without a messenger, and the delay of the coming of the messenger until the time in which he appeared.

Through this resumption the transition was achieved to what appeared from the polytheists after the coming of the Messenger ﷺ of their monstrous immersion in turning away from monotheism, which their father had held. Thus the placement of (bal) in this verse is more eloquent than its placement in the verse of Labid:

"Nay, you do not remember Nawar, though she has departed and its ties and cords have been severed."

For his transition was abrupt (iqtidab), whereas here it is a fine transition (takhallus hasan).

"These people" (ha'ula') is a reference to something not mentioned in the speech. I have inferred that the terminology of the Qur'an is to mean by such a term the polytheists of the Arabs, and I have not seen anyone who was guided to point this out. I had mentioned it at His saying "﴿And We brought you as a witness against these people﴾" [al-Nisa': 41] in Surat al-Nisa' and in other places.

By "their fathers" is meant their forefathers who instituted the worship of idols, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy and those who worshipped them after him. The enjoyment of their fathers was a preparation for the enjoyment of these people, and therefore the goal of the enjoyment was the coming of the Messenger, for his coming was to these people.

The enjoyment here is enjoyment through respite and non-uprooting, as the goal indicates in His saying "﴿until there came to them the Truth and a clear Messenger﴾."

By "the Truth" is meant the Qur'an, as His saying indicates: "﴿But when the Truth came to them, they said, 'This is magic'﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 30], and His saying "﴿And they said, 'Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of the two cities, a great one?'﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 31]. This verse is a praise returning to the Qur'an, connected to the praise of it with which the surah opens.

When the Qur'an came upon the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ, the enjoyment ended, and they were seized with punishment gradually, until there was the punishment of the Day of Badr and the Day of Hunayn, and God guided to Islam those who remained on the Day of the Conquest of Makkah and during the days of the delegations. This is in the sense of His saying "﴿And nations, We will give them enjoyment, then there will touch them from Us a painful punishment﴾" [Hud: 48] in Surat Hud.

The Truth that came to them is the Qur'an, and the clear Messenger is Muhammad ﷺ. His description as "clear" (mubin) is because he made guidance clear, established the proofs, and brought the most eloquent speech. Thus the clarity relates to the meanings of his religion and the wording of his Book.

The wisdom in that is that God willed to honour this group from the descendants of Ibrahim by rescuing them from the states of polytheism and misguidance to the paths of faith and Islam, and by following the most excellent of messengers and the most excellent of laws, so that He might make up for what a nation of Ibrahim's descendants had neglected in following their father, until the honour of answering his supplication is completed for his call.

The purpose of this is an increase in respite for them, so that perhaps they may remember, as He said: "﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it and be conscious of God that you may receive mercy﴾" [al-An'am: 155]; "﴿Lest you say, 'The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study﴾" [al-An'am: 156]; "﴿Or you say, 'If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them.' But there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord and guidance and mercy. So who is more unjust than one who denies the signs of God and turns away from them? We will repay those who turn away from Our signs with the worst punishment for what they used to turn away﴾" [al-An'am: 157].

From His saying "﴿And He made it a word remaining among his descendants﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 28] up to His saying "and their fathers" one infers that the forefathers of the Prophet ﷺ in his lineage did not conceal polytheism, and that they were a portion of the descendants of Ibrahim among whom his word remained, and that they did not openly oppose their people out of fear of trial. There is no wonder in this, for changing evil was only made obligatory by the Law, and they had no law.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 30:

﴿When the truth came to them, they said: "This is sorcery, and we are disbelievers in it."﴾

This is an expression of wonder at the state of their heedlessness. That is, they had some excuse before the coming of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Qur'an, because long-lasting heedlessness has a veil that turns neglect into ignorance. So the proper course was that they should awaken when the truth and a clear Messenger came to them, and then remember the word of their father Ibrahim (Abraham). But when the truth came to them, they said, "This is sorcery," that is, they said to the Messenger, "This is a sorcerer," and so they increased in rust upon rust (ray'an 'ala ray'in).

The statement is therefore used for the purpose of wonder, not to inform of the occurrence of this utterance from them, since that is known to them and to the Muslims.

Page 199
In the sequencing of the extended clause with this statement there is an indication that their enjoyment (of worldly provision) was about to come to an end.

So the sentence ﴿When the truth came to them, they said, "This is sorcery"﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿until the truth came to them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 29]. The particle (lamma) here is temporal, so it has the force of the terminal (hatta) as if it were said: "I gave enjoyment to these people and their fathers, then when the truth came to them immediately after that enjoyment, they did not come to their senses from their heedlessness and said, 'This is sorcery.'" That is, before the coming of the truth they were polytheists out of heedlessness and laxity, and when the truth came to them they became polytheists out of obstinacy and arrogance.

The clause ﴿and we are disbelievers in it﴾ is a second statement (maqul thani). That is, they said, "This is sorcery, so we shall not turn to it," and they said, "We are disbelievers in it," that is, in the Qur'an, whether it is sorcery or otherwise. That is, they assumed it to be sorcery, then went further and said, "We are disbelievers in it," that is, disbelievers that it is from Allah, whether it is sorcery, or poetry, or the fables of the ancients. For this meaning they emphasized the statement with the particle of emphasis, so as to make the Messenger (ﷺ) despair of their faith.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 31:

﴿And they say: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"﴾ It is coordinated with the clause "﴿They say: This is sorcery﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 30]. It therefore falls within the scope of the answer of (lamma) (the temporal "lamma," meaning "when"), and likewise occupies the position of expressing wonder, i.e., after they began to offer pretexts for rejecting the truth, when they said of the Qur'an: "This is sorcery." Since their saying that implies that the one who brought the Qur'an is a sorcerer, the discourse moved on to mention another of their attacks upon the Messenger (ﷺ), namely that he was not one of the great men of the two towns.

(Law wa-lawla) (lawla, "why not / if only not") originally is a particle of urging, but it is used here, by way of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal) through the relation of necessary concomitance, to mean the negation of his being a messenger, because urging toward the achieving of something that is definitively known not to occur entails certainty of its non-occurrence.

The two towns are Makkah and al-Ta'if, because they are the largest villages (qura) of Tihamah, the land of those who spoke these words. As for Yathrib, Tayma' and the like, they are from the land of the Hijaz.

Thus the definite article in "al-qaryatayn" is for prior reference (al-'ahd). They made the pillars of fitness for leadership over peoples two things: the greatness of the one who is to be made chief, and the greatness of his town. They therefore do not submit except to one who is from the most renowned tribes in the most renowned villages, because villages are the abode of the affairs of tribes, their sustenance and their trade. The word "'azim" (great) is used figuratively for the one who holds nobility among his people, as though he were great in essence.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that they meant by the great man of Makkah al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, and by the great man of al-Ta'if Habib ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi. And from Mujahid that they meant by the great man of Makkah 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, and by the great man of al-Ta'if Kinana ibn 'Abd Yalil. And from Qatada that they meant al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi.

Then it is possible that they uttered this expression reported of them in the Qur'an without having named two specific persons, and it is possible that they named two persons and described them with these two attributes, so the Qur'an confined itself to mentioning the two attributes concisely, with an indication of what they used to qualify for the selection for prophethood, as a way of ridiculing their opinion.

The two men they meant were possessors of wealth, because abundance of wealth was among the constituents of the attribute of nobility, as is reported of the Children of Israel, their saying: "﴿and he has not been given abundance of wealth﴾" [al-Baqarah: 247].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 32:

﴿Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord? It is We who distribute among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and We raise some of them above others in rank, so that some of them may take others in service. But the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.﴾

This is a denial directed at them, against their saying ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a man of importance from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. When they set themselves in the position of one who chooses among the kinds of people for the message from God, they have made that choice their own rather than God's. It follows from their statement that the selection for the message is in their hands. Therefore the pronoun (hum), which is made the subject, is placed before the predicate verb, to convey the sense of exclusivity (ikhtisas), and the denial is directed at this restriction. This is a refutation of their statement and a correction of their presumption.

[Page 201]

Since the selection for the message is a mercy both for the one chosen for it and for the people to whom he is sent, their presumption in this matter is described as a distribution of God's mercy made by them, through their choosing whom to select for it and determining who is qualified to convey it to those who are to receive it.

The address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the word "Lord" (al-Rabb) is attached to his pronoun, as an indication that God supports him, to console him. Their statement ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a man of importance from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31] was meant to belittle him, so God elevated his station by directing the denial at them, by turning to him in address, and by showing that God is his Lord, that is, the one who manages his affairs and arranges them.

The clause ﴿It is We who distribute among them their livelihood﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for the denial and negation implied by it, and an argument supporting it. That is: since We distribute among people their livelihood, so that they are directed in their affairs in the manner We have arranged for them of the order of life, and since the arrangement of this is for God, exalted, with His perfect wisdom, He made some of them strong and some weak, some rich and some needy, and He made some of them serve others in their work, in accordance with the requirements of the necessities of life. By this He raised some of them above others, and made some of them need others and be made to serve them.

If they are in this condition in the management of the livelihood of this world, then the same holds for the establishment of some of them rather than others for conveying the message, for that is the greatest of human affairs. This is the direction of the argument.

The word "sukhriyyan" may be read with a ḍammah or a kasrah on the sin, both being dialectal forms (lughatan). In the well-known recitations (al-qira'at al-mashhurah) it is read only with a ḍammah on the sin. Ibn Muhaysin read it in the anomalous recitation (al-shadh) with a kasrah on the sin. It is a noun for the thing that is made subject (musakhkhar), that is, one compelled to work without his choice, and also a noun for one who is mocked (yusakhar bihi), that is, one who is ridiculed, as stated in al-Raghib's Mufradat, the Asas, and the Qamus. It has been explained here in both senses, as al-Qurtubi said. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Both are dialectal forms with the meaning of subjugation, and there is no involvement of the meaning of mockery in this verse." No one other than him said this, and al-Raghib's statement is open to interpretation. al-Tabari restricted it to the meaning of subjugation. The correct view is that both meanings are intended in this verse. The choice of the word "sukhriyyan" in the verse rather than any other, because it bears both meanings, is one of the aspects of its inimitability (i'jaz). It may therefore mean that some of them employ others in the affairs of their lives, since man is civil by nature (madani), that is, in need of the help of one another. On this basis al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explained it, and al-Suddi, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said likewise.

[Page 202]

Thus the lam in "li-yattakhidh" is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), giving the cause of the act of "qasamna" (We distributed). That is: "We distributed" among them their livelihood, that is, the means of their livelihood, so that some of them may seek help from others, and thus they come to know one another and gather together because of the need of some of them for others, so that tribes and cities are formed from this.

On this reading, the phrase "some of them others" is general, applying to every person among people, since there is no one who does not make use of another, and who is not himself made use of by another.

It is also permissible that the word be a noun derived from mockery (al-sukhriyyah), which is ridicule. al-Qurtubi related this without naming its sayer. In that case the lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-‘aqibah), like the verse ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. On this reading the verse contains an allusion (ta'ridh) to the polytheists who mocked the believers, like His statement, exalted is He, "So you took them as objects of mockery" in the surah Qad Aflaha al-Mu'minun. The word "sukhriyy" in the sense of mockery also occurs in other verses, such as His statement ﴿So you took them for mockery until they caused you to forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 110], and His statement ﴿Did we take them for mockery, or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ [Sad: 63]. Perhaps what led some exegetes away from explaining the verse of surah al-Zukhruf in this sense is their objection that the taking of some of them as mockery by others should be the cause of God's act in raising some of them above others in ranks. But the interpretation of the word is broad in its parallels and similar contexts. The interpretation of the meaning of the lam is clear.

The clause ﴿But the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾ is a concluding appendix (tadhyil) to the response to them. In this concluding appendix there is a second refutation of them: the wealth which they made the pillar of selection for the message is less than the mercy of God, and so it is better than what they accumulate of wealth, which they made the cause of preference when they said ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a man of importance from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. Wealth is something its owner gathers for himself, and so it is not like God's choosing of a servant to send him to people.

The mercy of God is His choosing of His servant to convey His message to people. It is the mercy mentioned in His statement ﴿Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾. The meaning is: if they are not the distributors of even the least of their conditions, then how could they distribute what is better than the most important of their affairs?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 33–35:

Page 203
﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community, We would have provided for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses and stairways on which to ascend, and doors for their houses and couches on which to recline, and ornaments of gold. But all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the worldly life. And the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous.﴾

(Law) is a particle of prohibition due to existence, meaning a conditional particle indicating that the non-occurrence of its consequent is due to the occurrence of its condition. This implies that God intended to prevent the occurrence of "that mankind would become one community," that is, He intended to guard against the content of its condition.

Since it has been established that among their character is the glorification of wealth and of the wealthy, and their reckoning that this is the foundation of virtues, and they did not concern themselves with the purification of souls, and since God had nullified their making wealth the cause of superiority by two refutations, through His words ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32] and His words ﴿But the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32], He followed this by informing them that wealth and affluence have no share with God, the Exalted. For God gave everything its creation and made for things their realities and their measures. Often wealth belongs to the disbelievers and to those who have no portion of good. Thus it is established that wealth is a distribution from God among people, for which He made causes that He arranged within the system of social orders, and made for it effects appropriate to it. How far apart it is from the gifts of pure souls and good inner natures! Wealth is, for the most part, a source of gratifying desires and a means for boasting and haughtiness. As for the gifts of good souls, they are sources of benefit to their possessors and to the community. Among the people of evil there are rich and poor, and among the people of good there are similar, so the disparity between the effects of acquiring wealth and the effects of psychological virtues becomes evident.

From this belittling of wealth there results a third refutation of what they based their saying upon: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two towns?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. So this sentence is a conjunction upon the sentence "﴿But the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 32].

As for "the people" (al-nas), it may be intended to mean all of mankind, so the definite article would be for totality, that is, all of humanity. And "community" (ummah) is a group of humans distinguished from others by unity in lineage, religion, or a known condition. So the meaning of "that mankind would become one community" may signify: were it not that humanity would become upon one religion, which was the prevailing condition of them at that time, namely disbelief and the rejection of the idea of the Hereafter. On this is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The meaning upon this is: Were it not that all people would become disbelievers, We would have singled out the disbelievers with wealth and luxury and left the Muslims, for what We have stored up for them of the good things of the Hereafter. Then feeble-minded people would suppose that disbelief has an effect in attaining wealth, which God made a reward for those He named disbelievers, so they would follow the religion of disbelief, due to their imagining a necessary connection between the happiness of life and disbelief. The people of the earlier generations were people of illusions and errors, who made concomitance have the ruling of causation. Thus the meaning reverts to: Were it not for avoiding what would lead to the general spread of disbelief and the extinction of faith, We would have made wealth exclusively for the people of disbelief. That is, God does not love the extinction of faith among people, and He did not decree the unity of people upon one creed by His words ﴿And they will not cease to differ﴾ [Hud: 118] ﴿except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them﴾ [Hud: 119]. That is, God was gentle with the servants, so He suspended what would lead them to the vanishing of guidance among them; that is, He left among them a glimmer of the light of guidance.

It may also be (and this is the preferable view in my opinion) that the definite article in "the people" is for a known reference, intending by it some groups of humanity, namely the people of Makkah, and most of them, in the manner of conventional totality, and on the pattern of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 173]. The meaning of their being "one community" would be their unity in wealth.

The meaning: Were it not that a nation among the nations would become entirely people of wealth, which would contradict what God decreed of the inclusion in every land, every tribe, and every nation of rich and needy, for establishing the order of civilization and for the need of some of them for others: this for his wealth, that for his craft, and another for the capacity of his body—We would have made those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, namely the people of Makkah, equal in wealth and luxury. And on both possibilities, the meaning is summarized that the Wise Disposer does not give wealth and luxury any weight, so He does not withhold them from those who deviate from the path of truth and perfection. Thus the speech requires an omitted presumed term, its estimate being: "But people would not be equal in richness, because We did not make that so, since We decreed in the order of human existence

Page 205
that no nation, tribe, or people of a town should be all rich with none in need among them, for that would lead to the dissolution of the order of society and the cessation of the need of some of them for others, so their community would perish; and God willed their survival until a term they will reach."

This is supported by making the object of the verb "disbelieves" specifically the attribute of "the Most Merciful," for the Makkan polytheists denied the attribute of "the Most Merciful," and said, "And what is the Most Merciful?" and the reproach against them for this has been repeated in many verses.

The meaning of "We would have made for those who disbelieve" is: We would have arranged within the order of human society the causes of wealth connected with disbelief in God, such that disbelief would be a cause and a means of richness. Had God willed that, He would have prepared for it its causes in people's minds and in the methods of their financial dealings. This indicates that God prevented the causes of generalizing disbelief on earth out of kindness toward faith and its people, although He did not prevent the occurrence of partial disbelief, few or many, in preservation by Him, exalted is He, of the law of the ordering of effects upon their causes.

This is one of the offshoots of the distinction between approval and will: He does not approve for His servants disbelief, "and had your Lord willed, they would not have done it."

The "lam" in His words "for their houses" is like the "lam" in His words "for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful," meaning: We would have made for the houses of those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful; so His words "for their houses" is a substitute of inclusion for "those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful." He explicitly repeated the governing element for emphasis, as they did in the substitute of the one asked about in such as: "Who is this, Sa'id or 'Ali?" They joined the substitute with an interrogative particle and did not say "Who is Sa'id or 'Ali?" This was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And from the palm trees, from its spathe, clusters hanging low﴾ [al-An'am: 99] in Surat al-An'am.

The point of this substitution is to attach the prepositional phrase initially to the verb of making, then to give attention to mentioning "those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful" in this context, whose purpose is to couple them with the displays of wealth in a context of belittling. Then He mentions what the like of which is rare to find, of silver and gold. And since the entire report was strange, it was fitting that it be arranged in the style of summary followed by detail.

The reciters, the majority, read "suqfan" with a damma on the sin and a damma on the qaf, the plural of "suqf" with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the qaf, which is the structure extending over the walls of the house, covering the space of the house. This was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿So the roof fell upon them from above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 26] in Surat al-Nahl. This plural has no parallel except "rahn" and "ruhun," and there is no third to them.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read it "saqfan" with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the qaf, in the singular. The intended sense of the singular is the genus, by the indication of His words "for their houses," as if it were said: "for every house a roof."

"Zukhruf" is adornment. God said: ﴿The embellished speech as deception﴾ [al-An'am: 112] in Surat al-An'am. So here it is a conjunction upon "saqfan" as a plural for many beauties, and it is also applied to gold, because gold is adorned with, as in His words: ﴿Or you have a house of gold﴾ [al-Isra': 93]. Thus "wa-zukhrufan" is a conjunction upon "saqfan" with the interpretation: "We would have made for them gold," that is, their roofs, stairways and doors would have been of silver and gold, variegated, because that is more striking in its coloring.

Silver is mentioned first because it is more abundant in ornaments and more beautiful in color, and gold is placed last because it is rarer in jewelry; and because its word is more fitting for pausing, since its final letter is tanwin which turns into an alif in pausal form, which suits the prolongation of the voice, and this is more eloquent in pausing.

It is permissible that the word "zukhrufan" be used in both its meanings as a shared term, so no question arises about specifying the roof and the stairways for silver.

"Ma'arij" is the plural of "mi'raj," which is the stairway by which one ascends to the heights.

The meaning of "yazhharun" is they ascend, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So they were not able to scale it﴾ [al-Kahf: 97], that is, to climb over it.

"Surur" with two dammas is the plural of "sarir," discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿On couches facing one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 44] in Surat al-Saffat. The purpose of describing them with the clause "upon which they recline" is to indicate that they are given this splendor together with its use in the ease of life and freedom from fatigue.

The intended meaning is that the stairways, the doors and the couches are of silver, so the description is omitted from the conjoined items because of what the first conjoined item was described with.

Then it closes with His words: ﴿And all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾, that is, all that has been mentioned of roofs, stairways, doors and couches of silver and gold is the enjoyment of this world, which does not return to whoever is given it as eternal happiness. As for eternal happiness, God has stored it up for the righteous, and it is not like the trappings and excess adornment which fall in with diverse souls and abound among the people of base and lowly souls. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires: women and sons, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, livestock and tillage. That is the enjoyment of the worldly life, but with Allah is the best return﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 14].

The majority read "lamma" with a light mim, so the "in" before it is a lightened form of the emphatic "inna," and the "lam" entering upon "lamma" is the lam distinguishing between the negative "in" and the lightened "in," and "ma" is a superfluous particle for emphasis between the annexed and the annexed-to.

ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and Hisham, from Ibn ʿĀmir, read "lamma" with a heavy mim, so it is "lamma," sister of "illa" which is specific to occurring in a context of negation, so the "in" is negative, and the estimate is: "And all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the worldly life."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 33–35:

Page 203
﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community, We would have provided for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses and stairways on which to ascend, and doors for their houses and couches on which to recline, and ornaments of gold. But all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the worldly life. And the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous.﴾

(Law) is a particle of prohibition due to existence, meaning a conditional particle indicating that the non-occurrence of its consequent is due to the occurrence of its condition. This implies that God intended to prevent the occurrence of "that mankind would become one community," that is, He intended to guard against the content of its condition.

Since it has been established that among their character is the glorification of wealth and of the wealthy, and their reckoning that this is the foundation of virtues, and they did not concern themselves with the purification of souls, and since God had nullified their making wealth the cause of superiority by two refutations, through His words ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32] and His words ﴿But the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32], He followed this by informing them that wealth and affluence have no share with God, the Exalted. For God gave everything its creation and made for things their realities and their measures. Often wealth belongs to the disbelievers and to those who have no portion of good. Thus it is established that wealth is a distribution from God among people, for which He made causes that He arranged within the system of social orders, and made for it effects appropriate to it. How far apart it is from the gifts of pure souls and good inner natures! Wealth is, for the most part, a source of gratifying desires and a means for boasting and haughtiness. As for the gifts of good souls, they are sources of benefit to their possessors and to the community. Among the people of evil there are rich and poor, and among the people of good there are similar, so the disparity between the effects of acquiring wealth and the effects of psychological virtues becomes evident.

From this belittling of wealth there results a third refutation of what they based their saying upon: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two towns?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. So this sentence is a conjunction upon the sentence "﴿But the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 32].

As for "the people" (al-nas), it may be intended to mean all of mankind, so the definite article would be for totality, that is, all of humanity. And "community" (ummah) is a group of humans distinguished from others by unity in lineage, religion, or a known condition. So the meaning of "that mankind would become one community" may signify: were it not that humanity would become upon one religion, which was the prevailing condition of them at that time, namely disbelief and the rejection of the idea of the Hereafter. On this is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The meaning upon this is: Were it not that all people would become disbelievers, We would have singled out the disbelievers with wealth and luxury and left the Muslims, for what We have stored up for them of the good things of the Hereafter. Then feeble-minded people would suppose that disbelief has an effect in attaining wealth, which God made a reward for those He named disbelievers, so they would follow the religion of disbelief, due to their imagining a necessary connection between the happiness of life and disbelief. The people of the earlier generations were people of illusions and errors, who made concomitance have the ruling of causation. Thus the meaning reverts to: Were it not for avoiding what would lead to the general spread of disbelief and the extinction of faith, We would have made wealth exclusively for the people of disbelief. That is, God does not love the extinction of faith among people, and He did not decree the unity of people upon one creed by His words ﴿And they will not cease to differ﴾ [Hud: 118] ﴿except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them﴾ [Hud: 119]. That is, God was gentle with the servants, so He suspended what would lead them to the vanishing of guidance among them; that is, He left among them a glimmer of the light of guidance.

It may also be (and this is the preferable view in my opinion) that the definite article in "the people" is for a known reference, intending by it some groups of humanity, namely the people of Makkah, and most of them, in the manner of conventional totality, and on the pattern of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 173]. The meaning of their being "one community" would be their unity in wealth.

The meaning: Were it not that a nation among the nations would become entirely people of wealth, which would contradict what God decreed of the inclusion in every land, every tribe, and every nation of rich and needy, for establishing the order of civilization and for the need of some of them for others: this for his wealth, that for his craft, and another for the capacity of his body—We would have made those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, namely the people of Makkah, equal in wealth and luxury. And on both possibilities, the meaning is summarized that the Wise Disposer does not give wealth and luxury any weight, so He does not withhold them from those who deviate from the path of truth and perfection. Thus the speech requires an omitted presumed term, its estimate being: "But people would not be equal in richness, because We did not make that so, since We decreed in the order of human existence

Page 205
that no nation, tribe, or people of a town should be all rich with none in need among them, for that would lead to the dissolution of the order of society and the cessation of the need of some of them for others, so their community would perish; and God willed their survival until a term they will reach."

This is supported by making the object of the verb "disbelieves" specifically the attribute of "the Most Merciful," for the Makkan polytheists denied the attribute of "the Most Merciful," and said, "And what is the Most Merciful?" and the reproach against them for this has been repeated in many verses.

The meaning of "We would have made for those who disbelieve" is: We would have arranged within the order of human society the causes of wealth connected with disbelief in God, such that disbelief would be a cause and a means of richness. Had God willed that, He would have prepared for it its causes in people's minds and in the methods of their financial dealings. This indicates that God prevented the causes of generalizing disbelief on earth out of kindness toward faith and its people, although He did not prevent the occurrence of partial disbelief, few or many, in preservation by Him, exalted is He, of the law of the ordering of effects upon their causes.

This is one of the offshoots of the distinction between approval and will: He does not approve for His servants disbelief, "and had your Lord willed, they would not have done it."

The "lam" in His words "for their houses" is like the "lam" in His words "for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful," meaning: We would have made for the houses of those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful; so His words "for their houses" is a substitute of inclusion for "those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful." He explicitly repeated the governing element for emphasis, as they did in the substitute of the one asked about in such as: "Who is this, Sa'id or 'Ali?" They joined the substitute with an interrogative particle and did not say "Who is Sa'id or 'Ali?" This was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And from the palm trees, from its spathe, clusters hanging low﴾ [al-An'am: 99] in Surat al-An'am.

The point of this substitution is to attach the prepositional phrase initially to the verb of making, then to give attention to mentioning "those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful" in this context, whose purpose is to couple them with the displays of wealth in a context of belittling. Then He mentions what the like of which is rare to find, of silver and gold. And since the entire report was strange, it was fitting that it be arranged in the style of summary followed by detail.

The reciters, the majority, read "suqfan" with a damma on the sin and a damma on the qaf, the plural of "suqf" with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the qaf, which is the structure extending over the walls of the house, covering the space of the house. This was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿So the roof fell upon them from above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 26] in Surat al-Nahl. This plural has no parallel except "rahn" and "ruhun," and there is no third to them.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read it "saqfan" with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the qaf, in the singular. The intended sense of the singular is the genus, by the indication of His words "for their houses," as if it were said: "for every house a roof."

"Zukhruf" is adornment. God said: ﴿The embellished speech as deception﴾ [al-An'am: 112] in Surat al-An'am. So here it is a conjunction upon "saqfan" as a plural for many beauties, and it is also applied to gold, because gold is adorned with, as in His words: ﴿Or you have a house of gold﴾ [al-Isra': 93]. Thus "wa-zukhrufan" is a conjunction upon "saqfan" with the interpretation: "We would have made for them gold," that is, their roofs, stairways and doors would have been of silver and gold, variegated, because that is more striking in its coloring.

Silver is mentioned first because it is more abundant in ornaments and more beautiful in color, and gold is placed last because it is rarer in jewelry; and because its word is more fitting for pausing, since its final letter is tanwin which turns into an alif in pausal form, which suits the prolongation of the voice, and this is more eloquent in pausing.

It is permissible that the word "zukhrufan" be used in both its meanings as a shared term, so no question arises about specifying the roof and the stairways for silver.

"Ma'arij" is the plural of "mi'raj," which is the stairway by which one ascends to the heights.

The meaning of "yazhharun" is they ascend, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So they were not able to scale it﴾ [al-Kahf: 97], that is, to climb over it.

"Surur" with two dammas is the plural of "sarir," discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿On couches facing one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 44] in Surat al-Saffat. The purpose of describing them with the clause "upon which they recline" is to indicate that they are given this splendor together with its use in the ease of life and freedom from fatigue.

The intended meaning is that the stairways, the doors and the couches are of silver, so the description is omitted from the conjoined items because of what the first conjoined item was described with.

Then it closes with His words: ﴿And all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾, that is, all that has been mentioned of roofs, stairways, doors and couches of silver and gold is the enjoyment of this world, which does not return to whoever is given it as eternal happiness. As for eternal happiness, God has stored it up for the righteous, and it is not like the trappings and excess adornment which fall in with diverse souls and abound among the people of base and lowly souls. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires: women and sons, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, livestock and tillage. That is the enjoyment of the worldly life, but with Allah is the best return﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 14].

The majority read "lamma" with a light mim, so the "in" before it is a lightened form of the emphatic "inna," and the "lam" entering upon "lamma" is the lam distinguishing between the negative "in" and the lightened "in," and "ma" is a superfluous particle for emphasis between the annexed and the annexed-to.

ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and Hisham, from Ibn ʿĀmir, read "lamma" with a heavy mim, so it is "lamma," sister of "illa" which is specific to occurring in a context of negation, so the "in" is negative, and the estimate is: "And all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the worldly life."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 36:

﴿And whoever turns blind to the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he becomes his companion.﴾

The surah began by extolling the Qur'an and describing it as a reminder (dhikr) and a clear exposition for mankind, and by describing the obstinacy of the polytheists in turning away from it and averting from it. They were informed that Allah does not abandon their admonition and their argumentation, because Allah calls to the truth and promises it.

It elaborated on describing the contradiction in their beliefs, perhaps they would awaken from their veil, and on alerting them to the proofs of the truth of what the Messenger (ﷺ) calls them to with this Qur'an. Their doubts were exposed, in that they have no reliance except on what their first, misguided forefathers were upon. They were warned of the approaching end of their enjoyment and respite. This was concluded with further clarification, and the discourse arrived at what they said about the Qur'an and the one who brought it, in His saying ﴿And when the truth came to them, they said, "This is magic"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 30] up to His saying "great", and what was appended to it of complements. Here the discourse returns to the consequences of their diverting their minds

Page 208

from reflecting upon the Qur'anic call. Their turning away was thus a cause for Allah to subject to them devils who accompany them and never cease to divert them from considering the truth and the proofs of right guidance. This is a subjugation required by the order of the generation of branches from their roots, so the blindness of their insights to perceiving the manifest truth is not to be wondered at. This is from the sunnah of existence in the generation of things from their elements: misguidance grows and is generated in souls and takes firm hold of them time after time, until it becomes a nature upon the heart, and coverings upon it and a seal over it. The action of Satan is not weakened except by the repetition of the call to the truth, and by admonition and warning. From the flint of reminder, sparks of light are struck; perhaps they illuminate and meet the strength of the light of truth in a moment of the devil's weakness, and then the angelic power prevails over the satanic power, and its possessor awakens from the sleep of his misguidance.

He alluded to this by His saying "﴿Shall We then withhold the reminder from you, turning away, if you are a people who exceed the bounds?﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 5], as was previously mentioned there. Were it not for this, no one astray would ever desist from his misguidance, and the guidance of the guiders would not benefit the minds of those addressed.

So the clause "﴿And whoever turns blind to the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾" is coordinated with the clause "﴿And when the truth came to them, they said, 'This is magic'﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 30], and so on.

His saying ﴿whoever turns blind to the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ is a parable of their state in displaying their failure to understand the Qur'an, like their saying ﴿Our hearts are under coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness﴾ [Fussilat: 5], by the state of one who is blind to a thing that is visible to the eye.

Ya'"shu" (يَعْشُ) is the present tense of ʿashā, like ghazā, ʿashwan with a waw: when one looks at a thing with a glance that is not fixed, resembling the glance of al-A'shā. As for al-ʿashā (العشا) with a fatha on the ʿayn and the shīn, it is the noun for weakness of the eye in seeing things; it is said ʿashiya with a yā', like ʿaraja, when there is an affliction of ʿashā in his sight, and its verbal noun is ʿashan with a fatha on the ʿayn and with the short vowel, like ʿaraj.

The verb is originally waw-final: ʿashā yaʿshū. It is also said ʿashiya yaʿshā when ʿashā becomes an affliction for him, because the verbs of ailments often come in the pattern fiʿil with a kasra on the ʿayn, like maridha.

And ʿashiya, its yā' is converted from a waw because of the kasra of the form of ailments.

Page 209

So the meaning of "wa man yaʿshu" is one who looks at the Qur'an with a glance that is not firmly settled, that is, one who has no portion except hearing the words of the Qur'an without reflection and without intent to benefit from its meanings. So the hearing of the Qur'an together with not benefiting from it is compared to the glance of one who looks without contemplation.

The verb yaʿshu is transitive with ʿan (عَنْ), which denotes separation, because it was made to imply the meaning of turning away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful; otherwise the proper construction of ʿashā is with ilā (إلى), as al-Hutay'a said:

"Whenever you come to him, you will see him at the light of his fire; you will find the best fire there, and the best kindler."

One does not say ʿashawtu ʿan al-nār except with the same kind of implicit meaning found in this verse. So the explanation of whoever explained "yaʿshu ʿan dhikr al-Raḥmān" as meaning "yuʿriḍu" (turns away) intended to convey the sense in terms of transitivity with ʿan; and the denial by whoever denied that ʿashā can mean aʿraḍa intended to deny that this be an original meaning of the verb ʿashā, thinking that explaining it as turning away is an explanation of the meaning of the verb and not of its transitivity with ʿan. So the dispute between the two groups is verbal.

"Dhikr al-Raḥmān" is the Qur'an, referred to as dhikr in His saying ﴿Shall We then withhold the reminder from you, turning away﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 5]. Its annexation to al-Raḥmān is an annexation of honour, and this is a fifth praise of the Qur'an.

Al-taqyīḍ (التَّقْيِيض) means facilitating and preparing a thing to accompany another thing in work until it completes it. It is derived from a solid noun, qayyada al-bayḍa, that is, the shell surrounding what is inside the egg of the yolk, because the qayd (قَيْض) accompanies the egg and does not separate from it until the chick emerges from it, and so what was made available to it as qayd is completed.

The form tafʿīl here denotes making, like ṭayyana al-jidār (he plastered the wall), and like azarahu, that is, he clothed him with an izar, and daraʿū al-jāriya, that is, they clothed the girl in a dir'. Its original sense here is comparison, that is, we make him like a qayd for him; then it became common until it became an independent meaning. It was previously mentioned in His saying ﴿And We appointed for them companions﴾ [Fussilat: 25] in Surat Fussilat, so what is here is joined to it.

The pronoun in (لَهُ) came singular because each one of those in whom the condition is fulfilled has a devil, and not all of them have one single devil. Among the benefits that have been cited in explaining this verse is what the author of Nayl al-Ibtihaj bi-Tatrīz al-Dībāj mentioned in the biography of the grandson Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, known as Ibn Marzūq. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 37:

﴿And indeed they (the devils) turn them away from the way, while they think that they are guided.﴾ It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in His saying "so he is to him a companion" (fa-huwa lahu qarin), meaning: accompanied by a turning away from the way.

The pronouns in "innahum" and "yasudduna" (they turn away) refer back to "shaytanan" (a devil), because it fell among the elements of the verb that is the response of a conditional clause, and so it acquired generality, following the generality of "man" (whoever) in the conditional context, since it is among the forms of generality. This is like the indefinite noun in a conditional context, on which the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) differ regarding its generality. But it does not apply here, because the generality of "shaytanan" follows the generality of "man," since the parts of the response of a conditional clause take the ruling of the parts of the conditional clause. So the indicator of the generality of the indefinite noun here leaves no room for doubt about it, because of the indicator itself, not because of the mere occurrence of an indefinite noun in a conditional context.

The accusative pronoun in "yasudduntahum" (they turn them away) refers back to "man" (whoever), because the conditional "man" is general. It is as if it were said: "Whoever is blind to the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for them devils, for each one a devil."

The pronouns in "﴿wa yahsabuna annahum muhtadun﴾" (and they think that they are guided) refer back to what the accusative pronoun in "yasudduntahum" referred to, meaning: and those turned away from the way think themselves to be guided.

Pronouns may resemble one another, so the context returns each pronoun to its referent, as in the saying of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"We returned, and had it not been for us, their host would have surrounded the Muslims, and they would have seized what they had gathered."

The pronoun in "ahrazu" (they seized) refers to the group of polytheists, and the pronoun in "jammahu" (they gathered) refers to the Muslims. And the plural pronoun in His saying, exalted is He, "﴿wa 'amarūhā akthara mimmā 'amarūhā﴾" [al-Rum: 9], in Surat al-Rum.

The definite article in "al-sabil" (the way) is the definite article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins). "Al-sabil" means: the broad, extended path that leads to the sought goal.

The condition of those who are blind to the remembrance of the Most Merciful, and the state of the devils' companionship with them, has been likened to the state of one who asks a people for guidance to a road that leads to his aim, but they misguide him, turn him away from the way, and lead him into the deserts of bewilderment by deceit and trickery, while he thinks he is proceeding to where he will reach his goal.

So the clause "﴿wa yahsabuna annahum muhtadun﴾" is coordinated (ma'tufa) upon the clause "wa innahum," so it has the sense of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "fa-huwa," and the linking element is the circumstantial waw. The estimated meaning is: and those turned away think that they are guided by them to the way.

"Al-ihtida'" (being guided) means: knowledge of the path that leads to the intended destination.

﴿Until, when he comes to Us, he says: "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts! Wretched is the companion."﴾ (*Ḥattā*) is *ibtidā'iyyah* (introductory, marking a new stage), and it indicates causation that is a *ghāyah majāziyyah* (a metaphorical end). Its use here involves a *isti'ārah tab'iyyah* (a dependent metaphor).

There is no indication in the verse that the turning away from the path continues permanently, or that the two companions assume they are guided until both perish. A disbeliever may believe, and then the turning away and the assumption end. So do not be misled by the claim of those who assert that the true end (*ghāyah ḥaqīqiyyah*) is never separated from *ḥattā* in all of its uses.

Nāfi', Ibn Kathīr, Abū Bakr on the authority of 'Āṣim, and Abū Ja'far read *jā'ānā* with the alif of the dual pronoun, referring to the one who turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful and his companion, that is, his devil. The pronoun in *qāla* is singular because it refers only to the one who turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful. That is, the disbeliever says this in regret over having followed the devil and obeyed his command.

[Page 213 ends; page 214 begins here.]

The majority (*al-Jumhūr*) read *jā'anā* in the singular form, and the implied pronoun in *qāla* refers to "the one who turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful." That is, one of them says it, namely the one who turns away. So the meaning is one under both readings, because the dual reading clearly states that the devil came together with his disbelieving companion, and that the one expressing regret is the disbeliever. The singular reading implies the devil's coming from his words *"Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts,"* since he knows that his companion devil is present from the other's address to him with *"between me and you."*

*Yā* is originally a particle of calling, but it is often used to express anguish (*talahhuf*), as in the phrase *yā ḥasratan* ("Alas, what regret!"). Here it expresses anguish and regret.

*Al-mashriqān* means "the east and the west." The term "east" (*mashriq*) is used to represent both, because it comes more readily to mind, as souls long for the sunrise after darkness.

What is meant by "east" and "west" is either the place where the sun rises and sets on the horizon, or the direction of the earth from which the sun appears when it rises and disappears when it sets, as it appears to some inhabitants of the earth. Under both interpretations, this is a figure of speech for extreme distance.

*Bu'd* ("distance") is grammatically annexed to *al-mashriqayn* in the dual, with the implied sense "distance that belongs to both of them," that is, exclusive to them, interpreting *bu'd* as mutual separation. This is an eloquent concision produced by the form of *taghlīb* (the dominance of one term) and by the annexation. Its equivalent would be to say "the distance of the east from the west and the west from the east," so the phrase *al-mashriqayn* stands in place of six words.

His words *fa-bi'sa al-qarīn* ("wretched is the companion"), after he wished to be separated from him, are followed by a reproach. The disbeliever reproaches his devil, who was his companion, and by this he alludes to escaping accountability and placing responsibility on the devil who misled him.

The purpose of narrating this is to depict the terrible consequences of this companionship, which the companions had delighted in. This is the case with every companionship built on a deed with a bad outcome. This is in line with the words of God Most High: ﴿The intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67].

The purpose is to warn people against bad companions and to censure the devils, so that people will shun them, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾ [Fāṭir: 6].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 39:**

﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged, that you will be sharing in the punishment.﴾ The apparent meaning is that this sentence is joined (ma'tuf) to the sentence ﴿He will say: "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts!"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 38], and that there is an omitted statement indicated by the verb ﴿came to us﴾, which signals that the two groups have been present for the reckoning. Such a presence implies a exchange of words. When the two groups are present and one of them disowns the other, seeking to escape accountability, as was indicated earlier, then God says: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, that you will be sharing in the punishment.﴾

The address is directed to those who turned away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, and to their devils.

In this statement there is an allusion to an unstated speech, and the implied sense is: "Do not shift the blame onto your companions, for you are held accountable for obeying them, and they are held accountable for misleading you, and you are sharing in the punishment." ﴿And it will not benefit you that you are sharing in the punishment﴾, because the punishment of one group does not lighten the punishment of another, as God the Exalted said: ﴿For their first ones: "Our Lord, these led us astray, so give them a double punishment of the Fire." He will say: "For each is double, but you do not know."﴾ [al-A'raf: 38].

The occurrence of the verb "will benefit you" within a context of negation indicates the negation of any benefit whatsoever in sharing the punishment, since it does not lighten the punishment of the partner. As for what people commonly do, namely finding consolation in seeing someone like themselves afflicted with a calamity, that is one of the illusions of mankind in the present life. Perhaps God made this a mercy for them in the world. But the Hereafter is the realm of realities, not illusions. It is in this illusion that the words of al-Khansa' came:

*"Were it not for the abundance of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself."*

Al-Jumhur read *annakum* with a fatḥa on the hamza of *anna*, making the verbal noun (maṣdar) the subject (fā'il). Ibn 'Amir read *innakum* with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption (isti'naf, a new independent sentence), and in that case the pause would fall at His saying *idh zalamtum*.

Page 215

The subject (fā'il) of "will benefit you" is a pronoun referring back to the wish expressed in their words "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts," meaning: "Your wishing will not benefit you, nor will your escape."

As for *idh* (إذْ), its original nature is an ambiguous adverb of past time, specified by the clause to which it is added. It moves out of its adverbial function toward something close to it through extension (tawassu'), or toward something resembling it through metaphor (majaz). Here it is a metaphor for the sense of causation (ta'lil), since the cause or reason of a thing is likened to a time-adverb in its being necessarily attached to it. The sense of causation among the meanings of *idh* is mentioned in *Mughni al-Labib* (Ibn Hisham), but he did not attribute it to any of the imams of grammar and lexicography.

Al-Zamakhshari allowed that *idh* could be a substitute (badal) for *al-yawm* ("today"). He interpreted the statement by taking the verb *zalamtum* ("you wronged") to mean "it became clear that you wronged," that is, he used the past tense in the sense of "it became manifest." He compared this to the verse of Za'id ibn Sa'sa'a al-Faq'asi:

*"When we are traced in lineage, a base woman did not bear me, and you (fem.) did not find any escape from acknowledging this."*

That is, "it became clear that a base woman did not bear me." Ibn al-Hajib followed him in his *Amali*. Ibn Jinni said: "I repeatedly consulted Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) about His saying *"And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged"*, to the end of the verse, questioning the substitution of *idh* for *al-yawm*. The final outcome of what I gathered from him was that this world and the Hereafter are equal in God's judgment and knowledge, so it is as if *al-yawm* were past, or as if *idh* were future." And he said: "This is a weak and flawed answer."

I say: In this verse, there gather indicators of three tenses: *lan* (never), which negates the future; *al-yawm* ("today"), which is a noun for the present time; and *idh*, which is a noun for past time. All three are bound to the verb "will benefit you," and their implications conflict with one another. The negation in the future conflicts with the restriction by *al-yawm*, which refers to the present. *Idh* conflicts with the negation of benefit in the future, and it also conflicts with the restriction by *al-yawm*. Therefore al-Zamakhshari and others undertook to resolve the conflict between the implication of *idh* and the implication of *al-yawm* by interpreting the meaning of *idh*, as you have seen. But neither he nor anyone else undertook to resolve the conflict between the implication of *al-yawm*, which indicates present time, and the implication of *lan*, which is the occurrence of negation in the future. In my view, to resolve this, *al-yawm* should be taken as an adverb of time for the judgment and the announcement, meaning: it has been decided today that the benefit of your sharing in the punishment is permanently negated from now on, as in the words of Miqdam al-Dubayri:

*"No friend will ever be sincere to me for ten years, [a friend who] has tasted the dressing of wounds, or visited the grave."*

From the convergence of these three indicators in the verse there results a remarkable antithesis (tibaq) between three opposed meanings within the single sentence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 40:

﴿Can you then make the deaf hear, or guide the blind, and those who are in manifest error?﴾ This is a consequence (tafri') of the clause ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36], because that clause indicates their deep immersion in error and the difficulty of their disengagement from it, since the companionship of the devils for them necessitates that. So the discourse moved from that to consoling the Prophet ﷺ regarding the distress and anguish he suffers over them in their insistence on disbelief and misguidance. It also contains an allusion to despair of the guidance of most of them.

The interrogation is for denial: that the Messenger's ﷺ eagerness for their guidance would be effective among them, when God has decreed their misguidance and brought about its causes. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed God does not guide those who lead astray﴾ [al-Nahl: 37]. Since the Messenger's ﷺ state, in repeatedly calling them, is like the state of one who thinks he is able to convey the reminder to their hearts, he was placed in the position of one who thinks so, and he was addressed with an interrogation of denial. The interrogation was applied to a statement containing a restrictive construction (qasr) through the fronting of the predicate subject over the verbal predicate, together with placing the pronoun before the particle of denial. This is an emphatic restriction and a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb), meaning: you do not make them hear, nor do you guide them; rather God makes them hear and guides them if He wills. This is similar to ﴿Can you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99].

Among the subtle meanings of the verse is that God described their state of turning away from the remembrance with ʿashaʾ (dimness of sight), which is a gaze that does not distinguish the shape of the thing looked at. Then He described them here as deaf and blind, indicating that deliberately contriving to justify error and trying to support it turns its owner into a greater error, not that the acquiring of a trait comes without the trait itself, and that states (aḥwal) turn into fixed dispositions (malakat). This is the meaning of the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "A servant continues to lie until he is recorded with God as a great liar." That is, until it becomes certain that lying has become a disposition for him. Since their turning away was a withdrawal from listening to the Qur'an and from reflecting on the signs, their state resembled the state of the deaf and blind, as he had prepared for this with His saying ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36].

[Page 217]
As we have mentioned there, the connection between their being described as dimsighted and what is in this transition to describing them as deaf and blind has become apparent.

The conjunction of ﴿and those who are in manifest error﴾ carries the sense of a concluding generalization (tadhyil), because it is more comprehensive than each of the deaf and the blind considered separately. Moreover, since deafness and blindness are figurative (majaz), their application to what is heard and seen may be partial in a particular situation, so describing them as being in manifest error is a warning to the generality of states. It is also, at the same time, a nurturing of the metaphor (tarshih lil-istiʿara), because the combination of deafness and blindness is more evident as error.
