Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verses 41–42:

﴿So whether We take you away, indeed We will take retribution against them,﴾ ﴿or We show you that which We promised them, for indeed We are Omnipotent over them.﴾ This is a derivative (tafri') from the sentence "﴿Can you make the deaf hear?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 40]" through to its end, which implicitly contains the foundation (ta'sis) of their guidance, and which explicitly consoles the Prophet (ﷺ) for his excessive eagerness in calling them. So here comes the confirmation of a promise of retribution against them. Its meaning is: a promise of the manifestation of the religion, whether during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ) or after his death, and a warning to them of punishment in this world before the punishment of the Hereafter. To fulfil these two purposes, two matters are mentioned in this sentence: retribution against them without doubt, and that this occurs during the lifetime of the Messenger (ﷺ) or after his death. The derived clause is "indeed We will take retribution against them" and what is mentioned with it, so what is meant by it is the certainty of that under every circumstance.

"Imma" (إمّا) is two connected words, originally "in" (إنِ), the conditional particle, and "ma" (ما) is an added particle after "in." The "n" of "in" is assimilated into the "m" of the particle "ma," and the addition of "ma" is for emphasis. It is common for the conditional verb after "in" followed by "ma" to take the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid) for further emphasis. They write it with a hamza, a mim and an alif, following the way it is pronounced.

The "taking away" (al-dhahab) here is used to mean death, by the indication of His saying "or We show you that which We promised them," because death is separation from the living, so causing death is like removing him, that is, making him disappear. For this reason death is expressed as "transfer" (al-intiqal). The meaning is: "whether We cause you to die, indeed We will take retribution against them after your death."

Page 218

The word "muntaqimun" (مُنْتَقِمُونَ) has been used for future time, using the active participle (ism al-fa'il) in the sense of the future. This is a common metaphor, equal to the literal usage, and the indication is His saying "whether We take you away."

What is meant by "that which We promised them" is the retribution derived from His saying "indeed We will take retribution against them." God Almighty has indeed shown him retribution against them by the killing of their chiefs on the day of Badr. God Almighty said, "﴿On the day We will strike with the greatest assault; indeed, We will take retribution.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16]" and "the assault" is the assault of Badr.

The clause "indeed We will take retribution against them" is the answer of the condition, and it is connected with the particle "fa" (فَ) because it is a nominal sentence. It was formed in this way only to indicate the stability and continuance of the retribution. As for the clause "﴿indeed We are Omnipotent over them﴾," it is the evidence for the answer of the clause "﴿or We show you that which We promised them﴾," which is conjoined to the conditional clause, because God's power over them is not appropriate to be dependent upon His showing the Messenger (ﷺ) the retribution against them. So the answer is necessarily omitted, for the purpose of inspiring awe. Its estimate is: "or whether We show you that which We promised them, which is the retribution, you will see a retribution from which they will not escape, ﴿indeed We are Omnipotent over them﴾," that is, we are now able to exercise power over them. So the active participle is used for the time of the present, which is its literal meaning.

It is not correct for the clause "﴿indeed We will take retribution against them﴾" to be evidence for the omitted answer, because it would become: "or whether We show you the retribution against them, indeed We will take retribution against them."

The fronting of the two prepositional phrases "minhum" and "'alayhim" before their complements is for the sake of giving them importance, in the firmness of the retribution and the power over them.

The promise here has the meaning of a warning, by the indication of His saying before it "indeed We will take retribution against them." When the object of a promise (wa'd) is mentioned, its use is valid for both good and evil, and when its object is not mentioned it refers to good. As for a warning (wa'id), it is always for evil.

Al-iqtidar (الِاقْتِدارُ) means intensity of power, and "iqtadara" is more emphatic than "qadara." The author of al-Qamus (the dictionary) neglected to point this out.

These two conditionals and their answers contain five emphatic elements: the added "ma," the energetic nun, the emphatic particle "inna," the nominal sentence, and the fronting of the complement before "muntaqimun."

Page 219

The benefit of the alternation in this condition is to generalise both states: the state of the Prophet's (ﷺ) life and the state after his death. The intended meaning is the time of those two states, because the purpose is to fix the time of the retribution against them.

The meaning is: We will take retribution against them in this world, whether you are alive or after your death. That is, retribution against them is our affair and not your affair, because it is on account of their turning away from our command and our religion. Perhaps this is to dispel the Prophet's (ﷺ) or the Muslims' impatience at the delay of the retribution against the polytheists, and because the polytheists were waiting for the Prophet's death so that they would be relieved of his call. So God informed him that He would not let them escape retribution even if he died. God related their saying, "﴿We wait for him to suffer the misfortunes of time.﴾ [al-Tur: 30]" So in this warning is the casting of terror into their hearts, because of what they hear.

The fronting of the two prepositional phrases "minhum" and "'alayhim" before their complements is for the sake of giving them importance, in the firmness of the retribution and the power over them.

The promise here has the meaning of a warning, by the indication of His saying before it "indeed We will take retribution against them." When the object of a promise (wa'd) is mentioned, its use is valid for both good and evil, and when its object is not mentioned it refers to good. As for a warning (wa'id), it is always for evil.

Al-iqtidar (الِاقْتِدارُ) means intensity of power, and "iqtadara" is more emphatic than "qadara." The author of al-Qamus (the dictionary) neglected to point this out.

These two conditionals and their answers contain five emphatic elements: the added "ma," the energetic nun, the emphatic particle "inna," the nominal sentence, and the fronting of the complement before "muntaqimun."

Page 219

The benefit of the alternation in this condition is to generalise both states: the state of the Prophet's (ﷺ) life and the state after his death. The intended meaning is the time of those two states, because the purpose is to fix the time of the retribution against them.

The meaning is: We will take retribution against them in this world, whether you are alive or after your death. That is, retribution against them is our affair and not your affair, because it is on account of their turning away from our command and our religion. Perhaps this is to dispel the Prophet's (ﷺ) or the Muslims' impatience at the delay of the retribution against the polytheists, and because the polytheists were waiting for the Prophet's death so that they would be relieved of his call. So God informed him that He would not let them escape retribution even if he died. God related their saying, "﴿We wait for him to suffer the misfortunes of time.﴾ [al-Tur: 30]" So in this warning is the casting of terror into their hearts, because of what they hear.

﴿So hold fast to what has been revealed to you. Indeed, you are upon a straight path.﴾ When Allah made light for His Messenger ﷺ what he faced of intense eagerness for their faith, and promised him victory over them, He followed that by commanding him to remain firm in his religion and his Book, and not to let his resolve weaken in the call out of distress at their obstinacy in disbelief and their aversion to the truth.

Al-istimsak (holding fast) means an intense grasping, so the sin and the ta' in it are for emphasis.

The command to it is used to request continuance, because a command to do something addressed to one who is already engaged in it does not aim at seeking the act itself but at another meaning. Here it is a request for steadfastness in holding to what has been revealed to him, as indicated by His saying: "﴿Indeed, you are upon a straight path.﴾" This is like how one is supplicated for with someone honoured and esteemed: one says, "May Allah make you mighty and honoured," meaning, "May He continue that," and his saying, "May Allah grant you life," meaning, "May He lengthen your life." From this is His saying, exalted is He, in teaching the supplication: "﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾" [al-Fatihah: 6].

What was revealed to him is the Qur'an.

The clause "﴿Indeed, you are upon a straight path﴾" is a confirmation of the request to hold fast to what was revealed to him and a reason for it.

Page 220

The straight path is acting upon what was revealed to him. It is as if it were said: "It is a straight path," but He turned away from that to "﴿Indeed, you are upon a straight path﴾" in order to convey that the Messenger ﷺ is firmly established in being guided to the purpose of Allah, exalted is He, just as a traveller on a straight road is firmly settled, who in his journey has no hesitation in his course and no fear of going astray in its byways. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He, "﴿Indeed, you are upon the manifest truth﴾" [al-Naml: 79] in Surat al-Naml.

The particle (ʿalā) here denotes figurative elevation meaning firm establishment, as in His saying: "﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾" [al-Baqarah: 5].

This is a reinforcement of the Messenger ﷺ and a praise of him, that he has not swerved by the width of a fingertip from what Allah sent him with, like His saying "Indeed, you are upon the manifest truth." It is followed by the reinforcement of the believers in their faith. This is also a sixth praise of the Qur'an.

[Page 221]

﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people, and you will be questioned﴾. The portion of the Messenger ﷺ in praise and support was mentioned in His saying, "upon a straight path" (43:43), which was made the cause for the command to remain steadfast upon it. Then another cause was conjoined to it, which included mention of the Qur'an's portion of praise and benefit in His saying, "and indeed it is a reminder," and its honouring of him in His saying, "for you." It was followed by the portion of those who follow him and his Book in guidance and benefit, in His saying, "and for your people." Then He alluded to those who turn away from him and those who recklessly oppose him in His saying, "and you will be questioned," together with a hint (tawjih) in the meaning of the word "reminder" (dhikr), namely that this religion brings him and his people a good reputation among the nations; whoever follows it attains his share of that, and whoever turns away from it is counted among the foolish, as will come. This is with an indication of the benefit of the followers in the Hereafter and the harm to those who turn away from it therein, and the confirmation of that by the particle of the future (sawfa).

This verse comprises ten meanings, and for this reason it is richer in meaning than the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Halt, let us weep for the remembrance of a beloved and a dwelling*

which is counted the most eloquent of their speech in brevity, since he stopped, made others stop, wept, and made others weep. He mentioned the beloved and the dwelling in a single hemistich. This verse does not exceed the measure of that hemistich, yet its meanings number ten, whereas the meanings of Imru' al-Qays's hemistich are six, together with what this verse adds through its particularities, namely emphasis by "indeed" (inna) and the lam, metonymy (kinaya), and the embellishment of tawjih (husn al-tawjih, a rhetorical device of double meaning).

The word "reminder" (dhikr) may mean the reminder of the intellect, that is, his being guided to what he did not know, and so it is likened to recalling a forgotten thing. This is what has been explained by the one who is much mentioned, through "admonition" (tadhkir), meaning exhortation (al-maw'iza).

It may also mean the reminder of the tongue, that is, that it gains you and your people a mention (dhikr), and the word in this sense is predominant in the mention of its report.

The meaning is: the Qur'an is the cause of renown, because it gains his people a nobility by which they are mentioned. This interpretation has been related from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of Ibn 'Adi and Ibn Mardawayh. Al-Qurtubi said: "A parallel to this is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾, meaning: the Qur'an is an honour for you and for your people of Quraysh. The Qur'an was revealed in the tongue of Quraysh, so the people of all languages came to need their tongue; everyone who believes in it is thereby ennobled above the people of the other languages."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to present himself to the tribes, and when they said to him, 'To whom will the affair belong after you?' he would fall silent, until this verse was revealed, and whenever he was asked about that he would say: 'To Quraysh.'"

The discourse of al-Kashshaf follows this.

So in the word "reminder" there is the rhetorical embellishment of tawjih. When it is combined with the fact that the mention of him and his people with praise entails the blame of those who opposed them, there is in it an allusion against those who turn away from him. "His people" (qawmuhu) are Quraysh, since they are the ones addressed by the speech, or all the Arabs, since they were ennobled by the Greatest Messenger ﷺ being from among them and by the Qur'an's descent in their language. That nobility has manifested for them in all eras until today, and without it the Arabs would not have had any standing among the great nations that dominate the earth.

This is a seventh praise of the Qur'an.

The question in His saying, ﴿and you will be questioned﴾, is a question of confirmation (taqrir). The questioning of the believers is about the extent of acting upon what they were charged with, and the questioning of the polytheists is a question of rebuke and threat. He, Exalted is He, said: "﴿Their testimony will be written down and they will be questioned﴾" (43:19), and He, Exalted is He, said: "﴿Did there not come to you a warner?﴾" (67:8), up to His saying, "﴿So they will confess their sin; so away with the companions of the Blaze﴾" (67:11).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 45:

﴿And ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Did We appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Merciful?﴾ The command to ask here is a figurative expression (tamthil) for the fame and certainty of the report, as in the words of al-Samaw'al or al-Harithi:

"Ask, if you do not know the people about us and about them,"

and in the words of Zayd al-Khayl:

"Ask the horsemen of Yarbu' about our valor,"

and in His saying: ﴿So ask those who read the Scripture before you﴾ [Yunus: 94], since the Messenger ﷺ was not in doubt so as to need to ask. Otherwise, asking the messengers who came before him is impossible in its literal sense. The meaning is: survey the laws, books and reports of the messengers, and see whether you find in them the worship of gods. In a hadith, "consult your heart" (istafti qalbaka) means: be firm in knowing what is lawful and unlawful.

The clause "Did We appoint" is a substitute (badal) for the clause "ask," and the hamzah is an interrogative particle. It is a denial (inkari), and this denial is the intended purpose of the statement. It is a rebuttal of the polytheists when they said: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers following a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22], meaning: your fathers were not better guided than the earlier messengers, if you claim to reject Our messenger, because he commanded you to single out God alone in worship.

It is also permissible to take the asking as referring to the fame of the report.

The meaning of the statement is: We did not command, through the tongue of any of Our messengers, that gods be worshipped besides Us. This is a response to the saying of the polytheists: ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20].

The "min" in His saying "min qablika" (before you) serves to emphasize the connection of the adverbial phrase with its governing word.

[p. 223]

The "min" in His saying "min rusulina" (of Our messengers) is an explanation (bayan) of "qablika" (before you).

Thus the meaning of "Did We appoint" is: We did not appoint that, that is, the appointing of legislation and command; that is, We did not command that gods be worshipped besides Us.

He described "gods" with "worshipped" (yu'badun) in order to negate that God would be pleased with the worship of others, let alone that anyone else could be a god like Him. This is because the polytheists used to worship idols, and in their beliefs they were scattered: some of them made the idols gods associated with God; some claimed that they worshipped them so that they would bring them near to God (zulfa); and some claimed them to be their intercessors with God. When this verse negated that He had appointed gods to be worshipped, it refuted all these far-fetched claims.

"Gods" (alihah) is treated as if it referred to rational beings, so it is described with the plural form used for rational beings in His saying "worshipped" (yu'badun). Similar usage occurs frequently in the Qur'an, following what was prevalent in the Arabic language, since they regarded them as rational and knowing beings.

Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read "wa-sal" (and ask) with the hamzah lightened.

Allah mentioned at the beginning of the surah His saying: ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples? And no prophet came to them but that they used to mock him. So We destroyed those who were greater than them in strength, and the example of the earlier peoples has passed.﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 6]. After that he related a reminder about Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with his people, and what branched from that concerning the conditions of the people of polytheism. When that was concluded, it was followed by a comparison of the condition of the Messenger (ﷺ) with the tyrants of his people and their mockery, with the condition of Musa with Fir'awn and his chiefs. For examples (mathal) and parallels (naza'ir) have a role in bringing out truths and depicting two situations in a way that leads one to anticipate that what was the outcome of one of the two situations would befall the people of the other. Fir'awn and his chiefs met Musa with extreme disbelief, with mockery of him, and with belittling him, since he was not possessed of pomp, nor adorned with the finery of wealth. This was fitting to His saying:

[p. 224]
﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 45]. The verse prepared the setting for presenting the example of some of the Messengers who brought a great law before Islam.

The purpose of this story is His saying within it: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took retribution from them and drowned them all﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 55], ﴿and We made them a precedent and an example for the later ones﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 56], for the later ones here means the deniers, the chieftains of Quraysh.

Among what is specifically intended from it here is His saying "and his chiefs," that is, the great men of his people, for this resembles the condition of Abu Jahl and his like. And His saying: ﴿So when he brought them Our signs, behold, they laughed at them﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 47] (is intended), because their condition in that is similar to the condition of Quraysh indicated by His saying: ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples? And no prophet came to them but that they used to mock him﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 6], and His saying after that: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is despicable?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 52], because they resembled, in this, the condition of Abu Jahl and the like in their saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 31]. However, the words of the leaders of Quraysh were closer to courtesy than the words of Fir'awn, because their messenger was from among their own people, so they did not entirely abandon the aspect of modesty, whereas Fir'awn's messenger was a stranger to them. And His saying: "﴿Why are not bracelets of gold cast upon him?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 53]" (is intended) because it resembles what was contained in the saying of the chieftains of Quraysh: "a man of importance from the two cities," for the greatness of those two men lay in abundance of wealth. For this reason, something like it is not mentioned in other accounts of the mission of Musa (peace be upon him) apart from this story. And their saying: "O sorcerer, call upon your Lord for us" is similar to His saying about Quraysh: ﴿This is sorcery, and we are disbelievers in it﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 30]. And His saying: "﴿So We drowned them all﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 55]," which indicates that Allah destroyed them all, is a warning of what occurred in the eradication of the chieftains of Quraysh at the Battle of Badr.

Thus two lessons were derived from this story. The first: that disbelievers and the ignorant cling to such doubts in rejecting the superiority of the excellent, and they cling to spider's threads of incidental matters that have no bearing on the worth of pure souls.

The second: that Fir'awn, possessor of purely worldly grandeur, became subdued and defeated, victory being given over him to the one he had belittled. A parallel to this verse has preceded more than once.

[p. 225]
And (idha) is a particle of surprise (harf mufaja'a), meaning that it indicates that what follows it occurred unexpectedly, so the sentence in which it is used begins with it, conveying the occurrence of an event in the manner of a sudden surprise. The sentence containing (idha) is the answer (jawab) to the particle (lamma), and it is a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya), whereas (lamma) requires that its answer be a verbal sentence (jumla fi'liyya), because what is in (idha) of the meaning of surprise takes the place of a verbal sentence.

As for laughing (al-dahk): it is a metonymy (kinaya) for belittling the signs and denying them. Therefore it is not necessary that every one of those present must have laughed, nor that this occurred at the sight of every sign, since perhaps some of them do not call for laughter.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 48:

﴿And We did not show them any sign but that it was greater than its sister, and We seized them with punishment that perhaps they would return.﴾

The more apparent view is that the clause ﴿And We did not show them any sign but that it was greater than its sister﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The waw is the waw of the circumstantial clause, and the exception is from circumstances, and what follows (illa, "except") is in the position of a circumstantial clause. It dispenses with the waw because illa is sufficient for the connection.

The meaning is that they treat lightly the signs that Musa brought while they are in a state in which they are great and magnificent signs; they only treat them lightly out of obstinacy and stubbornness.

The phrasing nurihim (we show them) in the present tense is to evoke the situation (istihdar al-halah).

The meaning of hiya akbaru min ukhtiha ("it is greater than its sister") may be that every sign that comes is greater than the one before it, so there is an omitted qualifier understood from the context, i.e., "greater than its earlier sister," like His saying ﴿He seizes every ship by force﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], i.e., every sound ship. This entails that the signs are ordered in greatness according to the lateness of their times of appearance, because bringing one sign after another arises from not being deterred by the preceding sign.

It may also bear what the author of al-Kashshaf said: that the signs are described as great, not by their being varied in it. This is the usual practice with things that are close in excellence while their ranks differ in it slightly, i.e., people's opinions differ in preferring them. On this basis people built their speech, saying: "I saw men, some of whom are better than others," and perhaps a single man's opinions about them differ, so at one time he prefers this and at another time he prefers that. From this is the verse of the Hamasah:

Whoever you meet from among them, you say: "I have met their chief,"
Like the stars by which the night traveller journeys.

Al-Anmariyyah also preferred among her accomplished sons, then said: "When I looked at their ranks, close together and slight in difference, I was bereaved of them if I knew which of them is best; they are like a hollow ring, one does not know where its ends are."

So the meaning is: "And We do not show them any sign but that it is a sign of great indication of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ, which nearly makes them forget the other sign." The "sister" is used metaphorically for similarity in being a sign.

"﴿And We seized them with punishment﴾" is conjoined to the clause "and We do not show them any sign," because the punishment was among the signs.

The punishment: the punishment of this world, which is what pains and is hard, and that is the drought, the lice, the flood, the frogs, and the blood in the water.

The seizing (al-akhdh) means striking/afflicting. The ba' in "bil-adhab" indicates instrumentality (li-l-isti'anah), as you say: "Take the book with strength," i.e., "We began with punishment before total destruction, perhaps that would rouse them from their heedlessness." In this there is an allusion to the people of Makkah, when they were afflicted with the years of drought.

The return (ruju') is used metaphorically for submission and acknowledgment, and it is not like the return in His saying earlier ﴿And He made it a lasting word in his posterity, that perhaps they would return﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 28].

The pronouns of absence in "nurihim" and "akhadhnahum" and "la'allahum" refer back to Pharaoh and his chiefs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 49:

Page 227
﴿They said, "O sorcerer, invoke for us your Lord by what He has covenanted with you. Indeed, we are [truly] guided."﴾
It is conjoined to "﴿And We seized them with the punishment﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 48]". The meaning: when We seized them with the punishment at the hand of Musa, they asked him to invoke Allah to remove the punishment from them.

Their addressing Musa with the description of "sorcerer" was an address of honour, seeking to win his favour, because the sorcerer among them was the one possessing knowledge, and the sciences of their scholars were sorcerous, i.e., possessing hidden causes which none knew except them and their followers. Do you not see the saying of the chiefs of Pharaoh's people to him: "﴿And send to the cities gatherers who will bring you every learned sorcerer﴾" [Ash-Shu'ara: 36-37].

The sorcery was in the hands of the priests, and among its manifestations was the embalming of the dead, by which the corpses remained preserved from decay, and no one after them came to know how it was made.

As for the verse of Al-A'raf, "﴿They said, 'O Musa, invoke for us your Lord'﴾" [Al-A'raf: 134], it does not contradict what is here, because the address is one of insistence, so it is repeated and restated in various ways.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "﴿Yā ayyuhas-sāḥir﴾" without an alif after the ha' in pause, which is apparent in continuation (wasl). In pause, it is read with a fatha without an alif, which is not analogical (qiyasi), but the reading is transmitted (riwayah). Abu Shama (d. 665 AH) explained it by saying that they followed the orthography (al-rasm), but there is room for consideration in this. Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it with the alif retained in pause. Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the ha' in continuation only, and this is the dialect of the Banu Asad. In the Mushaf, the word (ayyuhah) was written without an alif after the ha', whereas the original form should have an alif after the ha', because "ha'" is a particle of alerting which separates "ayy" from its descriptive adjunct in the vocative, so the alif was omitted in the Mushaf orthography out of deference to the reading of the majority. The principle is that the orthography should respect the state of pause.

By "your Lord" they meant the Lord to whom Musa had invited them to worship. The Copts used to think that every nation had its own lord, and they did not deny the plurality of gods; they had many lords, differing in their works and their rank. The beliefs of the Greeks were similar to this.

By "what He has covenanted with you" they meant what He has singled out for you with His knowledge, to the exclusion of others, by which you are able to bring about extraordinary wonders.

Page 228
They used to think that those signs were caused by hidden causes, by analogy with their knowledge of the properties of certain things which the common people do not know, and the priests used to entrust these to their disciples and enjoin them to secrecy.

The covenant (al-'ahd) is entrusting someone with an important matter. Their intended meaning is not prophethood, because they did not believe in it; and since they did not know the reality of the covenant, they expressed it by the relative pronoun and its clause. The "ba'" in His saying "by what He has covenanted with you" is connected to "ud'u" ("invoke") and denotes instrumentality (al-isti'anah). When they saw the signs, they knew that the Lord of Musa was able, and that between Him and Musa there was a covenant requiring the granting of his request.

The clause "﴿indeed, we are [truly] guided﴾" is an answer to an implied statement indicated by "﴿invoke for us your Lord﴾", meaning: if you invoke for us and remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe in you, as in the verse of Al-A'raf: "If you remove from us the torment, we will surely believe in you" [Al-A'raf: 134].

Thus "guided" (muhtadun) is an active participle used in the sense of a promise, and it refers to the future by the context, as shown by His saying "they break [their oath]" (yankuthun). A parallel to this is His saying in Surah Ad-Dukhan, quoting the polytheists: "﴿Our Lord, remove from us the punishment; indeed, we are believers. How will the reminder benefit them?﴾" [Ad-Dukhan: 12], and so on. They called their acceptance of him guidance (ihtida'), because Musa had called what he invited them to guidance (hudan), as in the verse of An-Nazi'at: "﴿And I will guide you to your Lord, so you will fear Him﴾" [An-Nazi'at: 19].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 50:

﴿So when We removed the punishment from them, behold, they broke their word.﴾ That is, the consequence of their supplication and their promise to be guided, once the punishment was lifted from them, was that they broke the promise.

And al-nakth (breaking) is the undoing of a firmly tied rope. It was mentioned before in His saying ﴿So when We removed from them the punishment for a term which they were to reach, behold, they broke their word﴾ [al-A'raf: 135] in Surat al-A'raf, and it is a metaphor for breaking a covenant.

The discussion of the structure of this sentence is like the discussion of His earlier saying ﴿So when he brought them Our signs, behold, they laughed at them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 47].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 51:

Page 229
﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people, saying: "O my people! Does not the dominion of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flow beneath me? Will you not then see?"﴾
When He removed the punishment from them through the supplication of Musa, and Pharaoh and his chiefs concealed their breach of the promise they had made to Musa that they would be guided, Pharaoh feared that his people would follow the call of Musa and believe in his message. So he openly reminded his people of the greatness of his own self, in order to keep them firm in obedience to him, and so that he would not convey to them what he had asked of Musa, and what had resulted from Musa's supplication in removing the punishment, and so that they would suppose that the lifting of the punishment was a mere coincidence, since his people had not been informed of what had passed between him and Musa regarding the request to remove the punishment.

And al-nida' (the proclamation) is raising the voice. Its attribution to Pharaoh is a metaphor in the rational sense (majaz 'aqli), because he is the one who ordered the proclamation among his people. The proclamation of important matters issuing from kings and commanders was entrusted to designated criers (munadun), and they sometimes proclaimed matters which the people were meant to know. Among this is what is related in the words of God Most High in Surat Yusuf: ﴿Then a crier called out: "O caravan! Indeed you are thieves."﴾ [Yusuf: 70], and His words Most High: ﴿So Pharaoh sent heralds into the cities, "Indeed these are but a small band, and indeed they have enraged us."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 53].

In the thirtieth maqama of al-Hariri there occurs: "When he sat down, as if he were the son of rainwater, a crier called out from the side of the in-laws, and by the sanctity of Sasan, teacher of teachers, and exemplar of beggars, that none concluded this honored contract, on this bright and marked day, except the one who wandered and roamed, and grew old in the hillock, so that is a proclamation for announcing the contract."

The clause "qala" etc. explains the clause "nada", and the rational metaphor in "qala" is like that in "﴿wa-nada Fir'awnu﴾".

The Pharaoh spoken of in this story is Minephtah the Second.

Al-anhar (the rivers): the branches and channels of the Nile, because of their greatness each one of them was treated as a river, so they were pluralized as anhar, though they belong to one river, the Nile. If the seat of this Pharaoh's rule was the city of Memphis, then the demonstrative in His words "﴿wa-hadhihi al-anhar﴾" refers to the Nile's branches, which begin near Cairo, where the Nile divides into two great branches: the branch of Damietta

Page 230
and the branch of Rosetta, known as the Delta. I reckon that it is the one that was called the branch of Tanis, because Tanis was in that region and was submerged by the sea. It has other small branches, each one of which is called a tara (canal), like the Ismailiyya canal, and there are other branches called al-Riyah. If the seat of his rule was Thebes, which is near the city of (Abu) today, then the reference is to the streams of the Nile and its well-known branches among the people of the city, as though they were visible to their eyes.

The meaning of His words "﴿tajri min tahti﴾" may mean that he claimed the Nile flows by his command, so "min tahti" is a kinaya (metonymy) for subjugation, like His words Most High: ﴿They were under two of Our righteous servants﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10], that is, they were in their wedlock. People say: "such-and-such town came under King so-and-so." It may also mean that he intended the Nile flows through his kingdom from the lands of (Aswan) to the sea, so "min tahti" is a metaphor for control over the Nile's courses, like the metaphor in His words Most High: ﴿Your Lord has made beneath you a stream﴾ [Maryam: 24], according to the interpretation of sarriyyan as a river. Such talk used to pass over the common folk because of the simplicity of their minds.

It is also possible that the intended meaning of the rivers is the outlets of the waters which watered the city and the gardens around it, and that the distribution of the waters was by his command through dams and reservoirs. He then boasts that if he wished, he could cut off the water from them, in the manner of Yusuf's words: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?﴾ [Yusuf: 59]. Then "min tahti" means from beneath my command, that is, they flow only by my command. It has been said that the rivers used to flow beneath his palace.

The interrogative in "a-fa-la tubsirun" is rhetorical (taqriri), and the affirmation is expressed through a negation, to secure their acknowledgment, to the point that the one posing the question presents them with the denial, so they do not deny.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 52:

﴿Am ana khayrun min hadha alladhi huwa maheenun wa la yakadu yubeen?﴾ [Am ana khayrun min hadha alladhi huwa maheenun wa la yakadu yubeen] — "Or am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself?"

(Am) here is disjunctive (munqati'a), meaning (bal) for the transitional turning away (idrab intiqali). The implied sense is: "Rather, am I not better..." The interrogative that must be understood after it is affirmative (taqriri), i.e., a rhetorical question seeking confirmation. Its purpose is to belittle the standing of Musa in their souls by means of accidental attributes that are not decisive. He moved from magnifying his own status to displaying the gulf between himself and Musa, who had come to disparage their religion and their people's worship of him, and so he said: "I am better than this." The demonstrative here is for belittlement. The relative pronoun is used to claim that the content of the relative clause is something known about Musa.

Al-maheen, with a fatha on the mim, means the humble and weak. He intended that Musa was a stranger, not of the noble household lineages in Egypt, and had no family to be proud of. This is sophistry and sedition, since the occasion was not one of victory such that the one standing in it would be disparaged for having few supporters, nor one of boasting such that its holder would be belittled for his weak condition.

By his words "﴿wa la yakadu yubeen﴾" he pointed to the stammer and hesitancy in Musa's speech, as God related in the verse about Musa: ﴿And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent in tongue than me, so send him with me as a supporter to confirm me﴾ [al-Qasas: 34], and in the other place: ﴿And loosen a knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech﴾ [Ta-Ha: 27]. The occasion of Musa on that day was not one of oratory, teaching or admonition, such that lack of eloquence would be a defect in his work. Rather, it was one of argument and proof, so it sufficed that he be able to convey his meaning, even with difficulty. God removed that from him when he devoted himself to calling the Children of Israel, as He said: ﴿You have been given your request, O Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha: 36].

Perhaps Pharaoh said this because of what he knew of Musa's condition before God sent him, when he was in Pharaoh's house, and so he mentioned that aspect of his condition to remind the people of an ancient matter. The Pharaoh in whose time Musa was sent is (Minphtah II), the son of (Ramesses II), in whose days Musa was born and raised at his court. This implies that Minphtah knew Musa, and for this reason he said to him: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you stayed among us for years of your life?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18].

As for our Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), when he was sent to a nation possessed of eloquence and rhetoric, and his miracle was the Qur'an, which was inimitable in its rhetoric and eloquence, and the attribute of the Messenger was eloquence, so that he would have a lofty standing in the souls of his people.

As for the meaning of ﴿wa la yakadu yubeen﴾, it means "and he almost cannot express himself." The discussion of a similar construction has already been presented under His words, exalted is He, ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they almost did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 53:

Page 232
﴿Then why have bracelets of gold not been cast upon him, or angels not come with him in procession?﴾

When his description of Musa as one who is "despised" and who "can hardly express himself" implied that he (Fir'awn) denied that Musa had a claim to the message from God, Fir'awn followed this with his words, "Why have bracelets of gold not been cast upon him," as an escalation in denying that he is a messenger from God. Fir'awn, due to his ignorance or feigned ignorance, imagined to his people that the message has an emblem like the emblems of kings.

"Lawla" (why not) is a particle of urging, used here for challenge, as in His words: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31].

"Al-ilqa'" means throwing, and it is used here in the sense of sending down: that is, "Why have bracelets of gold not been cast upon him from the sky," meaning, "Why has the Lord not invested him with them so as to make him a king over the nation?"

Al-Jumhur read "asawiratun," while Hafs from 'Asim and Ya'qub read "Asworatun" (أسْوِرَةٌ).

"Al-asawiratu" is the plural of "aswar," a linguistic variant of "siwar" (bracelet). The original plural form is "asawir," lightened by dropping the extended vowel of the kasra, then the ha' was added as a substitute for the dropped letters, as it was added in "zanadiqa," the plural of "zindiq," whose correct plural is "zanadiq." As for "siwar," its plural is "asworatun."

"Al-siwar" is a broad ring of gold or silver encircling the wrist. Among most nations it is an adornment of free women. For this reason the proverb came: "Had she been a woman with a bracelet, she would have slapped me," meaning, "Had she been a free woman, she would have slapped me." It was said by one of the captives whose slave-girl slapped him, belonging to a people of whom he was a captive. The bracelet was an emblem of kings in Persia and Egypt, where the king would wear two bracelets. The Pharaohs also had as an emblem the wearing of two bracelets or bracelets of gold, and they sometimes placed two on the wrists and two others on the upper arms. When Fir'awn imagined that the rank of messengerhood is like kingship, he took the absence of what is among their kings' emblems as a sign of the absence of messengerhood.

"Aw" (or) is for alternation, meaning: if bracelets of gold are not cast upon him, then let angels come with him in groups, bearing witness to his messengerhood.

Page 233
I have not found that they affirmed the existence of angels in the sense known among the people of divine religion. Perhaps Fir'awn mentioned the angels in deference to Musa, since perhaps he had heard from him that God has angels or something similar in the context of the call; so he wished to silence him by bringing with him the angels who would appear to him.

"Muqtarinin" (accompanying) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "al-malaika" (the angels), meaning, accompanying him. This circumstantial clause emphasizes the meaning of "ma'ahu" (with him), lest the sense of companionship be taken to mean that the angels support him by speech, from the expression "qarantuhu bihi faqtarana" (I joined him with it, and he joined), meaning joined with Musa, which is the joining of a helper with his helper.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 54:

﴿So he made light of his people, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were a defiant people.﴾ That is, Pharaoh's call to his people, and the effect of his deception upon the chiefs (al-mala') among them, led them to hasten to obey him after they had been prepared to follow Musa when they saw the signs. So "al-khiffah" (lightness, levity) is used metaphorically for moving from a state of reflection, of casting off obedience to Pharaoh and being reluctant to follow him, to hastening to comply with him, just as a thing becomes light after being heavy.

The meaning returns to this: he made light their minds, and they hastened to affirm what he said, after they had affirmed Musa in their souls when they saw his signs, both their descent and their elevation. What is meant by "qawmahu" (his people) here is a part of the people, namely those who attended the assembly of Musa's call; these were the chiefs (al-mala') who were in the company of Pharaoh.

The sin and the ta' in "istakhaffa" are for emphasis in the sense of "akhaffa" (to make light), like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Only Satan caused them to slip﴾ [Al-Imran: 155], and the saying: "This is an act that provokes the anger of the forbearing."

The clause "﴿Indeed, they were a defiant people﴾" stands in the position of the cause (ʿillah) for the clause "so they obeyed him," as is the case with "inna" when it comes in a context other than emphasis. For their being defiant (fasiqin) is a clear matter, since it is necessary that Musa came to them and called them to abandon what they were upon of worshipping idols; so in this context it does not require emphasizing their being defiant, i.e., disbelievers. The meaning: they were light only in obeying the head of disbelief, because of the nearness of their time of disbelief, for they used to deify Pharaoh. When there arose in them a doubt regarding his affair through the sending of Musa, peace be upon him, they did not delay in returning to obedience to Pharaoh for the slightest reason.

What is meant by "fisq" (defiance) here is disbelief (kufr), as He said concerning them in the verse of al-A'raf: ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiant﴾ [Al-A'raf: 145].

﴿So when they angered Us, We took revenge on them and drowned them all﴾ ﴿and made them a precedent and an example for the later ones﴾.

The events narrated so far are followed by the purpose of the passage, which consists of three sequential matters, each following from the one before: the retribution (al-intiqam), then the drowning (al-ighraq), then taking them as a lesson (al-i'tibar) for the nations after them.

Al-asaf (translated here as "anger") is anger mixed with grief and distress. The verb ﴿āsafūnā﴾ ("they angered Us") is applied to the conduct of Pharaoh and his people, because it is an act that brought about God's retribution against them, a retribution like that of one who is angered. They disobeyed His messenger and insisted on their polytheism after the signs of truth had become manifest through Musa (peace be upon him).

Thus the word ﴿āsafūnā﴾ is used metaphorically (isti'ara, metaphorical borrowing) to mean "they disobeyed Us," on the basis of resemblance. The meaning is: when they disobeyed Us with the disobedience of a servant toward his lord who had favored him, by ingratitude for the blessing. God is exempt from being described with asaf in the literal sense, just as He is exempt from being described with anger in the literal sense. So the meaning is interpreted as: God treated them as a master treats a servant who has angered him, leaving no way open for his master's mercy.

The verb asifa is intransitive, and it was made transitive by the prefix hamza (ta'diya).

In the phrase ﴿when they angered Us﴾ there is ellipsis (ijaz), because their being angered had not been mentioned before, so that it could be shown to have been the cause of the retribution against them. The conditional particle of time being attached to it indicates that it had already taken place. The implied sense is: they angered Us, and when they angered Us, We took revenge on them.

The meaning of intiqam has been explained earlier, at the words of God, ﴿so indeed We will take revenge on them﴾ (Al-Zukhruf 43:41).

The fa' in ﴿fa-aghraqnāhum﴾ is coordinated with ﴿We took revenge on them﴾, even though their drowning is itself the revenge upon them. This is either because the verb "We took revenge" is interpreted as "We decreed revenge upon them," so that the coordination with fa' is like its use in the words of God, ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:82). Or the fa' may be considered superfluous, to emphasize the causation of "they angered Us" for the drowning. The underlying structure would then be: "We took revenge on them; We drowned them," with the clause "We drowned them" explaining the clause "We took revenge on them," and the fa' added to emphasize the sense of explanation. Or the fa' may be considered coordinating the clause "We took revenge" with the clause that precedes it, ﴿so he made light of his people﴾ (Al-Zukhruf 43:54), so that the sense is: "[he made light of his people] and so We drowned them all." In that case the clause ﴿We took revenge on them﴾ is an interjection placed between the clause that is the basis and the clause derived from it. A similar construction was mentioned earlier, at the words of God, ﴿So We took revenge on them and drowned them in the sea﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:136).

It follows from their drowning that God made them a precedent (salaf) for other people, meaning that they would come after them.

The word salaf, with fatha on the sin and fatha on the lam according to the recitation of the majority (qira'at al-jumhur, the widely adopted reading), is the plural of salif, like khadam for khadim and haras for haris. The salif is one who precedes others in existence, in action, or in place. Since retribution has been mentioned, the intended meaning of salaf here is one who precedes in receiving retribution. That is, those who come after them will suffer the same as what they suffered.

Hamza alone, and al-Kisa'i, read ﴿salafan﴾ with damma on the sin and damma on the lam. It is the plural of salif, a name for the group that has gone before and passed away.

Mathal means an equal and a similar. It is said mathal with two fathas, just as shabah is said, meaning "one who resembles." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: mathal is singular in form but is used to mean the plural. The word mathal is used metonymically (kināya) for its necessary implication, meaning: We made them a lesson for the later ones, who know that if they do as they did, they will suffer the same as what befell them.

It is also possible that mathal here means a strange and remarkable account that travels among people as proverbs travel, meaning: We made them an account for the others, which they will recount and by which their narrator will admonish them.

The meaning of "the later ones" (al-akhirin) is the people who are the last of those similar to them at the time of this speech. It is therefore determined that they are the polytheists who deny the Messenger (ﷺ). These are the last of the nations resembling the people of Pharaoh in worshipping idols and in denying the Messenger. The meaning of the speech is: We made them a precedent for you and an example for you, so take admonition from that.

The phrase ﴿for the later ones﴾ is connected to ﴿a precedent and an example﴾ by way of tanazu' (contention, the grammatical device in which one governing word is claimed by two governors).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verses 57–58:

Page 236
﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Are our gods better, or is he?" They did not cite him to you except for argument. Rather, they are a quarrelsome people.﴾
He joins a story from among the tales of their disbelief and obstinacy to what came before of their statements, which took place in a dispute from them with the Prophet ﷺ.

This is a preface and introduction before His saying, ﴿And when Jesus came with clear proofs (al-bayyinat)﴾, which is the purpose of joining this discourse to the mention of the mission of Moses, peace be upon him.

The conjunction of the speech with "lamma" (when), which indicates that its answer occurs at the occurrence of its condition or its timing, requires that the content of the condition of "lamma" is known to occur and its time is known. So it is an allusion to an event that took place on account of a case, such as someone who gave an example for a state of Jesus' affairs. Moreover, their saying "﴿Are our gods better, or is he?﴾" may have occurred in the course of the dispute concerning Jesus, and it may be merely the reporting of another doubt from among the doubts of their beliefs. So in this verse there is a general statement which is clarified by what the Prophet ﷺ and the believers know of the dispute that took place with the polytheists, and it is further clarified by His saying, ﴿He is only a servant on whom We bestowed favour, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 59]. This verse is among the most obscure of the Qur'an's verses in its intended meaning.

The people of tafsir have differed regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse and what clarifies its generality, in three opinions which az-Kashshaf mentioned, and he added a fourth possibility from himself. The most apparent of the opinions is what Ibn 'Atiyya related from Ibn 'Abbas, and what he mentioned in al-Kashshaf as a second and third explanation: that when the polytheists heard from the Prophet ﷺ the statement, "﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like that of Adam﴾" [Al 'Imran: 59], and that his creation without a father is no more wondrous than the creation of Adam without a father or a mother, or that this happened before the revelation of Surat Al 'Imran (since that surah is Madani and Surat az-Zukhruf is Makki), they said: "We are better guided than the Christians, because they worship a human being, while we worship the angels." That is, they were repelling what the Prophet ﷺ had used to rebuke them, that his duty was to rebuke the Christians. Then the saying of the Exalted, "﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example﴾", was revealed. Perhaps they said that out of ignorance of what the Qur'an had come with in refutation of the Christians.

Page 237
What most of the exegetes adopted is that the occasion of its revelation is the allusion to what preceded in Surat al-Anbiya' at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98], when 'Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara, before his Islam, said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Is this specific to us and our gods, or to all the nations?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "It is for you and your gods and for all the nations." He said: "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'ba! Do you not claim that 'Isa ibn Maryam is a prophet, and the Christians have worshipped him? If 'Isa is in the Fire, then we are content that we and our gods be with him." So those polytheists who were present rejoiced at his words, and the people of Makkah raised a clamour over that. Then Allah the Exalted revealed, ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us will be kept far from it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101], in Surat al-Anbiya'. And this verse was revealed alluding to their obstinacy.

Some exegetes add to the narration of Ibn al-Zib'ara's words: "The Banu Mulayh worshipped the angels, so if 'Isa and the angels are in the Fire, then we are content." Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 59:

﴿It is nothing but a servant upon whom We bestowed favor, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel.﴾ When there was mention of what alludes to the story of the dispute of Ibn al-Zib'ara (ibn al-Zib'arā) in His saying, ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98], and the cause of his dispute was that 'Isa had been worshipped besides God, He did not let the speech end without following it with an affirmation of the servanthood of 'Isa on this occasion, to show the flimsiness of the opinion of those who claimed his divinity and worshipped him, namely the Christians, out of eagerness to establish the truth through argument.

'Isa has been restricted to servanthood by the method of qasr al-qalb (a restrictive construction that corrects a mistaken belief) in reply to those who claimed he was a god. That is, he is nothing but a servant, not a god, because divinity is incompatible with servanthood. Then His saying "upon whom We bestowed favor" indicates that he was distinguished by the blessing of prophethood, meaning that he has no special excellence over the rest of the Messengers. And his being created without a father was only an irhas (a preparatory sign heralding a prophet).

As for His saying "and We made him an example for the Children of Israel," it is a refutation of the doubt of those who deified him, who imagined that his being created by a word from God indicates that he is a part of God and therefore deserving of divinity. That is, his creation in his mother's womb without any male approaching her was a wondrous lesson for the Children of Israel, because their faith in the unseen had weakened and a long time had passed since the sending of Messengers. So God sent 'Isa as a renewer of faith among them, a proof through his miracles of the greatness of God's power, and a restorer of God's honoring of the Children of Israel, since He placed among them prophets. This was to be a cause of the strengthening of faith among them, and a manifestation of the excellence of the people of merit who believed in him, and a [demonstration] of the obstinacy of those who, because their own interests prevented them, refused to acknowledge his miracles. So they showed hostility toward him and strove to punish and kill him, but God protected him from them and raised him up from among them. Some people were guided by him, and others were led into trial by him.

So the word "example" (mathal) here means a lesson, as in His saying just before: ﴿We made them a precedent and an example for the later people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 56].

And in His saying "for the Children of Israel" there is an indication that 'Isa was sent only to the Children of Israel, and that he did not call anyone other than the Children of Israel to follow his religion. Those non-Israelites who followed him in the ages of disbelief and polytheism only adopted his call because it rescues them from the darknesses of polytheism, idolatry and ta'til (the denial of God's attributes).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 60:

﴿And if We willed, We would have made among you angels to succeed one another on the earth.﴾

When the preceding verse pointed to refuting the error of those who claimed that 'Isa, peace be upon him, was the son of Allah, the Exalted, by restricting him to being a servant of Allah whom Allah favoured with prophethood, and a lesson for the Children of Israel, this was followed by refuting what resembles that error, namely the error of some of the polytheists in claiming that the angels are the children of Allah, the Exalted, whose report precedes in His saying ﴿And they have attributed to Him from His servants a portion﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 15] and the verses after it. So it is indicated that the angels are servants of Allah, the Exalted, whom He placed in the upper worlds, and that if He willed, He would have made them inhabitants of the earth in place of humankind. That is, their being among the people of the upper worlds was not necessary for them in essence; it is only a status by the appointment of Allah, the Exalted, just as He appointed inhabitants for the earth. And if Allah willed, He would have reversed it, making the angels on the earth in place of people. So Allah's honouring them by dwelling in the upper worlds does not necessitate their being the sons of Allah, nor does it require divinity for them, just as the honouring of 'Isa with the blessing of prophethood, and his distinction by being created without a father, did not require divinity for him. Rather, it is by the appointment and creation of Allah.

The condition of (law, "if") was made a verb in the future tense, to indicate that this willing has never ceased to be possible, by which the angels could be given residence on the earth in compensation.

The meaning of (min, "from") in His saying "minkum" ("from among you") is the substitutive sense of exchange, like that in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Are you satisfied with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38].

The prepositional phrase is attached to "ja'alna" ("We made"), and it was placed before the object of the verb for emphasis on the meaning of this substitution (badaliyyah, the sense of "in place of"), so that the hearers' understanding may deeply reflect upon it.

The clause "﴿fi al-ardi yakhlufun﴾" ("﴿to succeed one another on the earth﴾") explains the content of the prepositional phrase up to His saying "minkum," and the object of "yakhlufun" was omitted because "minkum" indicates it. The placing of this prepositional phrase first is for emphasis on what more clearly shows that the clause is an explanation of the content of "minkum."

This is the correct interpretation of the verse, and it is the path taken by the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun). The attempt by the author of al-Kashshaf to read "minkum" in the sense of origin and connection does not fit the context of the verses.

[Page 242]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 61:

﴿And indeed, it is a sign (ʿilm) for the Hour, so do not be in doubt about it.﴾ The more apparent view is that this is a continuation (ʿatf) of the clause ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44], and that what lies between them is digressions (mustaṭradāt) and an interjection (iʿtiraḍ) required by the connection of meaning (munāsaba).

When the discussion of refuting the divinity of other than God had been fully elaborated with proofs of God's oneness, the reins were turned back to establishing that the Qur'an is true, returning to the starting point.

This is a statement addressed by God Most High to those who deny the Day of Resurrection, and it may also be part of the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The masculine third-person pronoun in His saying ﴿And indeed, it is a sign for the Hour﴾ refers to the Qur'an, and on this interpretation were al-Hasan, Qatada and Saʿid ibn Jubayr. Thus this is an eighth praise of the Qur'an. The praise of the Qur'an has continued uninterrupted from the beginning of the surah, each part holding onto the others, interspersed with interjections and digressions, and it reaches this final praise by stating that the Qur'an is the most knowledgeable of people about the occurrence of the Hour.

This is interpreted by what preceded it, His saying ﴿with what has been revealed to you﴾, and it is clarified by His saying after it ﴿This is a straight path﴾. Moreover, the occurrence of such a pronoun in the Qur'an referring to the Qur'an is frequent and well known without any antecedent, let alone when it has an antecedent.

The meaning of affirming that the Qur'an is a sign for the Hour is that it came with the final religion that seals the laws, so that after the coming of the Qur'an nothing remains but awaiting the end of the world. This is the meaning of what is related of the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): "I was sent together with the Hour like these two," and he joined the index finger and the middle finger, pointing to them, and the resemblance lies in there being no separation between them.

The attribution of "a sign for the Hour" to the pronoun of the Qur'an is a metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi), because the Qur'an is the cause of knowledge of the occurrence of the Hour, since in it are the varied proofs of the possibility of resurrection and its occurrence.

It is also possible that the use of "ʿilm" in the sense of "muʿlim" (that which imparts knowledge) is an use of the verbal noun in the sense of the active participle, for emphasis (mubalagha), in that it is the one that produces knowledge of the Hour, since no book among the books of the prophets came close to it in this.

This metaphor or emphasis is suited by the consequential particle in His saying ﴿so do not be in doubt about it﴾, because the Qur'an has left no one any doubt that the Resurrection is certain to occur.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatada that the pronoun refers to ʿIsa (Jesus), and they interpreted it as meaning that the descent of ʿIsa is a sign of the Hour, i.e., a cause of knowledge of the Hour, i.e., of its nearness. This is a distant interpretation, for the assumption of an omitted genitive (muḍaf), namely "descent" (nuzul), has no evidence for it, and it is contradicted by the explicit naming of ʿIsa in His saying ﴿And when ʿIsa came﴾ etc.

It is permissible in my view that the pronoun in "innahu" be a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr shaʾn), meaning: the important matter is the people's knowledge of the occurrence of the Hour.

The verb in ﴿so do not be in doubt about it﴾ is made transitive with the particle "bi" by its being construed with the meaning of "do not deny it" (lā tukadhdhibunna), or the particle "bi" has the meaning of "fi" of location.
* * *
﴿And follow Me; this is a straight path﴾. The pronoun of the speaker may refer to God Most High, meaning: follow what I have sent to you of My speech and My Messenger, in keeping with the general run of pronouns from the beginning of the surah, as has been mentioned. Thus the meaning of following God is following His command, His prohibition and His guidance as conveyed by the tongue of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Following God is then a figure of speech (tamthil) for their compliance with what they were called to, by likening the state of those who comply with God's command to the state of travelers on a path shown to them by a guide. This is like His saying in Surat al-Shura ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52] ﴿the path of God, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 53].

It is also possible that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), with the implied "And say: follow Me," and similar to this is frequent in the Qur'an.

The demonstrative in ﴿this is a straight path﴾ refers either to the Qur'an mentioned previously in His saying ﴿And indeed, it is a sign for the Hour﴾, or to what is present in minds of what has been revealed of the Qur'an, or to the religion of Islam known from the context, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153].

The first person ya' has been deleted for lightness, while the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya) remains as an indication of it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 62:

﴿And let not Satan hinder you; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾

When the ears had been made to receive the varied forms of admonition, commands and prohibitions, and in the course of that there ran a warning against persistence in turning away from the Qur'an, and an announcement to them that this would lead them to keep company with Satan, and that matter received its share of clarification, the discourse moved on to forbidding them from allowing Satan to hinder them from this religion and the Qur'an, which they had been called to follow, through His saying ﴿And follow me; this is a straight path﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 61], as an alert that turning away from this religion is among the whisperings of Satan, and as a reminder of Satan's enmity toward humankind, a strong enmity which does not part from driving people to evil deeds so that they fall into punishment, as a way of satisfying his hostility.

The prohibition against following Satan in his hindering them has been phrased as a prohibition of Satan against hindering them, to indicate that they are able to keep themselves from being ensnared in Satan's nets. Thus, forbidding Satan from hindering them is used as a metaphor for forbidding them from obeying him, which is more emphatic than the Prophet ﷺ directing them to it, in the manner of the Arabs' saying: "I will not find you doing such-and-such, nor will I find you in such-and-such a place."

The clause ﴿indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ is a justification for the prohibition against Satan hindering them, for it is the nature of the sensible person to guard against the schemes of his enemy.

Satan's enmity toward humankind arises from the wickedness of his essential nature, together with what has been joined to that wickedness of the incompatibility of the two elements (fire and clay). When incompatibility meets wickedness of disposition, from their combination arises the intent to harm. This enmity was further kindled by an event that accompanied the origin of the human species at its creation, in his story with Adam, as the Qur'an has related it more than once.

The particle (in) (إنْ) here occupies the position of the fa' of causation (فاءُ التَّسَبُّبِ), indicating causality (التَّعْلِيل).

[p. 246]

You already know that the purpose of mentioning Jesus, peace be upon him, is that his story is a continuation of the account of Moses' mission.

The answer to (*lammā*, "when") is not stated, so it is omitted, because the rest of the speech indicates it.

The position of the particle (*lammā*) here is that Jesus' coming with the clear proofs had already become known to the listener from what preceded it, in God's words: ﴿He is only a servant on whom We bestowed favour, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 59], and so on. The meaning is: when Jesus came to them, the factions disputed about what he brought. The answer to *lammā* is therefore omitted, because the intended point is God's words: ﴿So woe to those who did wrong, from the punishment of a painful Day﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 65]. This indicates that the practice of the nations to whom messengers were sent was not different, for no messenger was without a people who believed in him and a people who denied him. Then they were all alike in ascribing partners to God in divinity, through the claims of the Christians that Jesus is the son of God, exalted be He, as His words *"So woe to those who did wrong"* indicate, that is, those who associated partners with God, as is the general usage of the Qur'an. Thus there was a resemblance between the earlier messengers and Muhammad (ﷺ), may God's blessings be upon them all. Therefore the speech contains concision (*ījāz*), indicated by the consequential *fa'* (*fā' al-tafrī'*).

In the story of Jesus with his people there is a warning that association with God (*shirk*) is one of the accidental attributes of the people of misguidance, which soon infiltrates their souls even if it had not previously clung to them. Jesus was sent to a people who did not follow polytheism, since he was sent to the Children of Israel, and all of them were monotheists. When his followers differed among themselves, some factions denied him, and a group affirmed him, and then they did not follow what he had commanded them, they soon came to adopt the creed of associating partners with God.

The clause ﴿He said: "I have certainly come to you with wisdom"﴾ explains the clause ﴿Jesus came with clear proofs﴾. It is not the answer to the condition of *lammā*, whose consequence, in His words ﴿so the factions differed among themselves﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 65], serves as evidence for it.

In the placement of the clause ﴿I have certainly come to you with wisdom﴾ as an explanation of ﴿Jesus came with clear proofs﴾ there is an indication that he opened with this statement, because it is the habit of the people of misguidance to rush toward their ends, even if the basics of the call contradict their beliefs. That is, Jesus did not call them to more than following wisdom and clarifying what they disputed, and he did not call them to anything contrary to the fundamentals of the Torah's law. Nevertheless, his situation did not escape a dreadful turning away from him and denial.

His beginning by informing them that he had come with wisdom and clarification, which is a general description of the nature of his mission, is an encouragement for them to attend to the details of the call that he would later present to them, some of which are based on this introduction, in His words ﴿So fear God and obey me. Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him.﴾

Wisdom (*ḥikmah*) is knowing what leads to the good and restrains from the bad, and here it means prophethood. Its discussion has already been given at God's words ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269] in Surat al-Baqarah. Jesus came to teach them realities of noble morals and admonitions.

His words ﴿and to make clear to you﴾ are conjoined to *"with wisdom"*, because both are connected to the verb *"I have come to you."* The *lām* is the *lām* of causation. Clarification (*tabyīn*) is the revealing of hidden meanings, due to obscurity or misinterpretation. What is intended is what Jesus clarified in the Gospel and elsewhere, of the matters over which the understandings of the Jews differed, concerning the rulings related to understanding the Torah or to determining the rulings for newly arising events.

In this verse he did not mention his statement reported in the verse of Surat al-Nisa', ﴿and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 50], because that he said in another context.

The intent is to narrate what he said to them that was not of a kind that would provoke his people to deny him. They denied him at a time when he had not told them that he had come to abrogate some rulings of the Torah. That is, they denied him while the signs of his truthfulness through the miracles were manifest, and while there was nothing that would raise doubt about him.

As for his saying ﴿some of that about which you differ﴾, it may be because God informed him that the benefit did not require clarifying everything they differed about, but would be limited to some, and the remainder would be completed through a messenger who would come after him and clarify everything that needs clarification.

Or it may be because what was revealed to him of clarification did not include everything whose ruling they differed about, and he awaited its clarification later, gradually, in legislation, as occurred in the gradual prohibition of wine in Islam.

It has also been said that what is intended by ﴿some of that about which you differ﴾ is what the disagreement concerned that related to the rulings of religion, not what was disagreement concerning worldly matters.

In His words ﴿some of that about which you differ﴾ there is a preparation for them to accept what would be clarified to them at that time or later.

This verse indicates the permissibility of delaying clarification in matters that have an apparent meaning, and in matters that return to clarification through abrogation (*naskh*). This question belongs to the foundations of jurisprudence (*uṣūl al-fiqh*).

He followed the general introduction of his speech with His words ﴿So fear God and obey me.﴾ This is a comprehensive statement that includes the details of the wisdom and the clarification of what they differ about, for fear of God (*taqwā*) is awe of God. It has come in a report: "The head of wisdom is the fear of God." And obedience to the Messenger includes the meaning of ﴿and to make clear to you some of that about which you differ﴾. So when they obey him, they act upon what is made clear to them, and the purpose of clarification, which is action, is achieved. More comprehensive than this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Sufyan al-Thaqafi, when he asked him to say to him a statement about Islam about which he would not ask anyone else: "Say: I believe in God, then be steadfast." This is more suitable as a comprehensive word in a law after which no other law is expected to come, unlike the words of Jesus, peace be upon him, *"and obey me,"* which is limited by the period of his existence among them.

The clause ﴿Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord﴾ gives the reason for ﴿So fear God and obey me﴾, because once His sole lordship is established, the command to worship Him follows, since no one fears God except one who acknowledges His lordship and His sole right to it.

The pronoun of separation (*ḍamīr al-faṣl*, here *huwa*) conveys restriction (*qaṣr*), that is, God is my Lord and not other than Him. This is a declaration of divine oneness (*waḥdāniyyah*), even though the people to whom Jesus was sent were monotheists. Yet an innovation appeared among some of their factions who said: ﴿Ezra is the son of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30].

The emphasis of the clause by *inna* serves to increase attention to the predicate, since the addressees did not deny it.

The placement of himself before his people in His words ﴿my Lord and your Lord﴾ is intended to block the means to exaggeration in sanctifying Jesus, and this is among his miracles, because God knew that some factions among his followers would exaggerate concerning him, claiming that he was the son of God in truth, and would go astray through the words of the Gospel in which Jesus says: "Father," meaning God, exalted be He.

From the establishment of God's oneness is derived the command to worship Him in His words ﴿so worship Him﴾, for the one who is singular in divinity is truly deserving of being worshipped.

[p. 247]

The demonstrative in ﴿This is a straight path﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 61] refers to the content of His words *"So fear God and obey me"*, that is, this is the way to reach success with insight and without hesitation, just as the straight path is one whose traveller's course is not confused for the one who walks upon it.
