This consequence is the purpose of narrating the story in a way that draws a comparison between the states of the messengers. That is, after his call, the peoples to whom he was sent disagreed, along with those who adopted his religion in search of guidance.

This consequence (*tafrī'*) points to the omitted answer of *lammā* ("when").

The pronoun in "*baynihim*" ("among them") refers to those to whom 'Isa came, because they are known from the context of the story through the phrase "when 'Isa came," since coming implies coming to him. They were the Jews.

The *min* ("from") may be extra, serving to emphasise the meaning of "*baynahum*" ("among them"), so that the sense is that they disagreed with the disagreement of a single nation. Thus some of them believed in 'Isa, namely Yahya ibn Zakariyya, Maryam, the mother of 'Isa, the twelve Disciples (*al-Hawariyyun*), some women such as Maryam al-Majdaliyya, and a small group. Most of the Jews and their rabbis rejected him, and there was what there was of the plotting of the Jews against him, until God raised him up.

Then the Disciples spread out calling to the law of 'Isa, and peoples in the lands of Rome and Greece followed them. Not long after, they disagreed among themselves about the foundations of the religion, and they split into three sects: the Nestorians, the Jacobites, and the Melkites. The Nestorians said: 'Isa is the son of God. The Jacobites said: 'Isa is God, by way of *hulūl* (indwelling or incarnation). The Melkites, who are the Catholics, said: 'Isa is the third of three, whose totality is the God. These are: the Father, who is God; the Son, who is 'Isa; and the Holy Spirit, who is Gabriel. Thus God, in their view, is three *aqānīm* (hypostases).

The verse includes both disagreements, so the *fa* (then) is used in its literal sense of sequence and in its figurative sense. Its inclusion of the last disagreement is figurative, with the relation of resemblance, likening the sudden emergence of disagreement among his followers, despite the existence of a law that prevents such things, to something that happened right after the mission of 'Isa, even though a long time lay between them, during which their innovation crept in. Using a word in both its literal and figurative senses is common, since the criterion is that the indicator of the figurative meaning should prevent the literal meaning alone from being intended, in verification.

This disagreement is stated here in summary, and its details occur in many verses concerning how the Jews received the call of 'Isa, and verses concerning what the Christians introduced into the religion of 'Isa, such as the claim of his sonship to God and his divinity.

It is also possible that *min* in His words "*min baynihim*" ("from among them") is for origin (*ibtidā'iyya*), attached to "*ikhtalafa*" ("disagreed"), meaning that the disagreement arose from among them, without anyone else introducing it to them. That is, their religion was sound, and then disagreement arose among them.

On this reading, the dispute is specific to the followers of 'Isa, peace be upon him, from among the Christians, since they split into sects and innovated the matter of the sonship of 'Isa to God. Thus the *fa* is purely for figurative sequence.

Following the mention of the disagreement, a threat of punishment is pronounced against those who did wrong, with torment on the Day of Resurrection, as a consequent appendage (*tadhyīl*) to what precedes it. "Those who did wrong" includes all those who associated with God others in His divinity: "Indeed, associating partners with God is a great injustice" [Luqman 31:13]. This is the general usage of *zulm* (wrongdoing) in the Qur'an. It is thus known that the disagreement among the groups led most of them to become polytheists, according to the context and what is known in usage, namely that the appendage must be suited to what it is appended to, so that the appendage encompasses the appended matter and other matters. Accordingly, the generality of this appendage includes the polytheists of the Arabs, who are the intended audience of these parables and lessons. Do you not see that in Surat Maryam there occurs His saying: "Then the groups disagreed among themselves, so woe to those who disbelieved because of the scene of a great Day" [Maryam 19:37]? Here the relative clause is the verb "disbelieved," because the intended meaning in the verse of Surat Maryam is those among the Christians who disbelieved. For this reason it is followed by His saying: "But the wrongdoers today are in clear error" [Maryam 19:38], when the aim was to move on to warning the polytheists after warning the Christians.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 66:

Page 251

﴿Do they await anything but the Hour, that it should come upon them suddenly while they are not aware?﴾

This is a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'naf bayani), as if the one who hears His saying ﴿So woe to those who have wronged, from the punishment of a painful day﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 65] were a seeker of clarification who asks: When will this painful day arrive, and what is this woe? So the sentence ﴿Do they await anything but the Hour, that it should come upon them suddenly﴾ comes as an answer to the first part of the question. The answer to the second part will come in His saying ﴿The intimate friends on that day will be enemies to one another﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67], and in His saying ﴿Indeed, the criminals will be in the punishment of Hell﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 74], and the verses that follow.

The answer has come according to the method of the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), and the meaning is: this punishment is certain to occur without doubt, whether its time of occurrence is near or far, so let not the delay in its coming trouble you. He, exalted is He, said ﴿Say: Tell me, if His punishment comes upon you by night or by day, what is it that the criminals seek to hasten?﴾ [Yunus: 50]. This meaning is also indicated by restricting the coming of the Hour with the qualifier "suddenly", for a thing that is not preceded by any sign has no known time of arrival.

"Yanzurun" (they await) means "yantazirun" (they expect), and the interrogation is one of denial: that is, after they associated partners with Allah, they await nothing for the punishment to take place except the arrival of the Hour. The Day is expressed by "the Hour" as an allusion to the swiftness of what takes place in it.

The definiteness of "al-sa'ah" (the Hour) is definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd).

"Al-baghtah" (suddenness) means "al-fajah" (the unexpected), and it is: the occurrence of a thing without anticipation.

"An ta'tiyahum" (that it should come upon them) is a substitute for "al-sa'ah" in a substitution of identity (badal mutabiq), for the coming of the Hour is the very Hour, since the designation of the Hour is the arrival of the appointed time, and "al-hulul" (arrival) is the figurative coming intended here.

The clause "wa hum la yash'urun" (while they are not aware) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object pronoun in "ta'tiyahum". And "al-shu'ur" (awareness) is knowledge of the occurrence of a thing that has occurred.

Since the implication of "baghtah" requires the absence of awareness of the Hour's occurrence at the moment it befalls them, the circumstantial clause came as an emphasis (muakkidah) of the clause before it.

[Page 252]

"﴿The close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous.﴾" "﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you today, nor shall you grieve,﴾ ﴿those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims.﴾ ﴿Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, delighted.﴾ ﴿There will be circulated among them platters of gold and cups, and therein is what the souls desire and what the eyes find delight in, and you therein will abide.﴾ ﴿And that is Paradise, which you have been given as an inheritance for what you used to do.﴾ ﴿For you therein is abundant fruit, from which you will eat.﴾"

This is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes) that serves two purposes:

First: to explain some of the terrors alluded to by the general threat in His saying ﴿So woe to those who wronged, from the punishment of a painful Day﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 65].

Second: to admonish the polytheists with what will occur on the Day of Resurrection of terrors for those like them, and to give joy to the believers.

Here, from among the terrors, has been selected what is most fitting to the state of the polytheists in their gathering together against the Messenger (ﷺ) and the religion of Islam, for what gathered them was only their mutual support and affection in disbelief and their boasting of that among themselves in their gatherings and evening conversations. God the Exalted said, relating about Abraham, ﴿And he said, "You have taken only idols instead of God as a bond of affection among yourselves in the life of this world; then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others"﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 25]. And that is the manner (shanshana) of the people of polytheism from before.

In the meaning of this verse is His earlier saying just above, ﴿Until, when he comes to Us, he will say, "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts! Wretched is the companion!"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 38].

Al-akhillāʾ (the close friends) is the plural of khalīl, which is the constant companion. It was said that it is derived from takhallul (penetrating), because he is like one who penetrates his companion and mingles with him. It was discussed in His saying ﴿And God took Abraham as a khalīl﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 125] in Surat al-Nisāʾ. The noun to which "idhh" (when) is added in His saying "yawma idhin" (on that Day) is the element replaced by the tanwīn (nunation); it is indicated by what was mentioned before it in His saying ﴿from the punishment of a painful Day﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 65].

[Page 253]

Al-ʿadū (the enemy) means the one who is hateful; its form is faʿūl in the sense of fāʿil, i.e., ʿādin (one who is hostile). For this reason its use is the same for the singular and other than singular, and for the masculine and other than masculine. It was discussed at His saying ﴿If he is from a people hostile to you﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 92] in Surat al-Nisāʾ.

[Page 255]

It is smaller than the ibrīq (ewer), except that it has no spout and generally no handle. The ibrīq, however, has a handle and a spout.

The description of the akwāb is omitted because the description of ṣiḥāf indicates it, meaning: "and cups of gold."

These cups are for water and for wine.

His saying "mā tashtahīhi al-anfus" (what the souls desire) is general, covering everything to which the appetites of the souls relate in obtaining and attaining it. God creates in the people of Paradise the desires suited to the world of eternity and sublimity.

"Wa taladdhu" (and delights) is the present tense of ladhdha, on the pattern of ʿalima: when one perceives pleasure. This is common in speech, until the verb is treated as transitive, and they say ladhdhahu. The omitted pronoun is the link of the relative clause to the relative pronoun.

The delight of the eyes lies in seeing beautiful forms and colours which gladden the soul. So the delight of the eyes is a means to the delight of the souls. Therefore "wa taladdhu al-aʿyun" is coordinated to "mā tashtahīhi al-anfus" with a coordination in which there is a general and specific relation between the coordinated and the one it is coordinated to. The souls may desire what the eyes do not see, such as conversation with companions and hearing beautiful sounds and music. And the eyes may perceive what the soul had not previously desired to see, or what the soul had desired in taste or hearing, and it is brought to them in beautiful forms, as a completion of the blessing.

[Page 256]

[Page 257]

[Page 255]

It is smaller than the ibrīq (ewer), except that it has no spout and generally no handle. The ibrīq, however, has a handle and a spout.

The description of the akwāb is omitted because the description of ṣiḥāf indicates it, meaning: "and cups of gold."

These cups are for water and for wine.

His saying "mā tashtahīhi al-anfus" (what the souls desire) is general, covering everything to which the appetites of the souls relate in obtaining and attaining it. God creates in the people of Paradise the desires suited to the world of eternity and sublimity.

"Wa taladdhu" (and delights) is the present tense of ladhdha, on the pattern of ʿalima: when one perceives pleasure. This is common in speech, until the verb is treated as transitive, and they say ladhdhahu. The omitted pronoun is the link of the relative clause to the relative pronoun.

The delight of the eyes lies in seeing beautiful forms and colours which gladden the soul. So the delight of the eyes is a means to the delight of the souls. Therefore "wa taladdhu al-aʿyun" is coordinated to "mā tashtahīhi al-anfus" with a coordination in which there is a general and specific relation between the coordinated and the one it is coordinated to. The souls may desire what the eyes do not see, such as conversation with companions and hearing beautiful sounds and music. And the eyes may perceive what the soul had not previously desired to see, or what the soul had desired in taste or hearing, and it is brought to them in beautiful forms, as a completion of the blessing.

[Page 256]

[Page 257]

[Page 255]

It is smaller than the ibrīq (ewer), except that it has no spout and generally no handle. The ibrīq, however, has a handle and a spout.

The description of the akwāb is omitted because the description of ṣiḥāf indicates it, meaning: "and cups of gold."

These cups are for water and for wine.

His saying "mā tashtahīhi al-anfus" (what the souls desire) is general, covering everything to which the appetites of the souls relate in obtaining and attaining it. God creates in the people of Paradise the desires suited to the world of eternity and sublimity.

"Wa taladdhu" (and delights) is the present tense of ladhdha, on the pattern of ʿalima: when one perceives pleasure. This is common in speech, until the verb is treated as transitive, and they say ladhdhahu. The omitted pronoun is the link of the relative clause to the relative pronoun.

The delight of the eyes lies in seeing beautiful forms and colours which gladden the soul. So the delight of the eyes is a means to the delight of the souls. Therefore "wa taladdhu al-aʿyun" is coordinated to "mā tashtahīhi al-anfus" with a coordination in which there is a general and specific relation between the coordinated and the one it is coordinated to. The souls may desire what the eyes do not see, such as conversation with companions and hearing beautiful sounds and music. And the eyes may perceive what the soul had not previously desired to see, or what the soul had desired in taste or hearing, and it is brought to them in beautiful forms, as a completion of the blessing.

[Page 256]

[Page 257]

The definiteness of al-akhillāʾ is the definiteness of the genus, and it conveys a customary (ʿurfī) comprehensiveness: either the close friends from both groups, the polytheists and the believers, or the close friends from Quraysh who are being spoken about. Otherwise, among the close friends who are not believers, there are those between whom there is no enmity on the Day of Resurrection, namely those who did not use their friendship to incite one another to polytheism, disbelief and sins, even though they differ in ranks and degrees on the Day of Resurrection.

"Yawma idhin" (on that Day) is an adverbial complement connected to "ʿadūw" (enemy). The clause "yā ʿibādī" (O My servants) is a direct speech introduced by an omitted verb of saying, indicated by the form of address; that is, "We will say to them," or "God will say to them."

The majority read "yā ʿibādī" with the yāʾ retained according to the original form. Ḥafṣ and al-Kisāʾī read it with the yāʾ of the speaker deleted for lightness. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Abū ʿAlī said: Its deletion is good, because it is in the position of tanwīn, and it has been replaced by it; just as tanwīn is deleted in a singular noun in the vocative, so likewise the yāʾ is deleted here.

Opening their address by removing fear from them is a comfort to them, a favour through rescuing them from its like, and a reminder to them of the cause of the difference of their state from the state of the people of misguidance, for they witness what is done to the people of misguidance and corruption.

"Lā khawfun" (no fear) is in the nominative with tanwīn in all the well-known readings. It was not put in the accusative because the accusative would imply the extra, emphatic min which makes the negation general. Since that emphasis would indicate explicitly that the negation does not intend a single instance, and since the context is not one of hesitation about negating the category of fear from them, because it had not befallen them at that time while it befell others, the sign of their deliverance from it was clear, so there was no need for the noun of "lā" to be put in the accusative. A parallel to this is the saying of the fourth of the women in the Ḥadīth of Umm Zarʿ: "My husband is like the night of Tihāma: neither hot nor cold, neither fear nor boredom." It is narrated with the four nouns in the nominative, because the absence of those states from the night of Tihāma is well known, and she only intended to explain aspects of the resemblance in her saying "like the night of Tihāma."

[Page 254]

In His saying "wa lā antum taḥzanūn" (nor shall you grieve), the subject is mentioned and then the predicate is given as a verbal predicate, to convey emphasis in negating grief from them. Thus the emphasis conveys the strengthening of the negation, not the negation of the strength of true grief with a weak grief. This is the usage found in the very forms of exaggeration, as in His saying ﴿And your Lord is not a wrongdoer to the servants﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 46]. It reassures their souls that grief is negated from them in the future times, since thoughts might arise in them asking whether the security they are in will last for them.

The clause "alladhīna āmanū bi-āyātinā" (those who believed in Our signs) is a qualifying description of the one addressed in "yā ʿibādī" (O My servants). The relative pronoun is used in it, since the relative clause indicates the cause of the negation of fear and grief from them. His saying "wa kānū muslimīn" (and were Muslims) is coordinated to the relative clause.

There is a variation between the two relative clauses: the first is a past-tense verb, while the second is the verb of being (kāna) with a predicate given as an active participle. This is because faith (īmān) is the binding of the heart, which occurs in a single instant, whereas Islam is the carrying out of the five pillars of Islam, as its explanation came in the Ḥadīth of Jibrīl's questioning. It is something that becomes established in the self gradually, so the verb kāna was preferred, which indicates the unity of its predicate with its subject, as if it were from the very fabric of its existence.

Their spouses were coordinated with them in the permission to enter Paradise, as part of the completion of the blessing of enjoying the friendship that existed between them and their spouses in this world.

"Tuḥbarūn" (you will be delighted) is the present form of the passive of ḥubira, from ḥabara-hu, meaning he made him happy. Its verbal noun is al-ḥabr (with fatḥa then sukūn), and the noun is al-ḥubūr and al-ḥabra. It was discussed in His saying ﴿So they, in a meadow, will be delighted﴾ [al-Rūm: 15] in Surat al-Rūm.

The clause "yuṭāfu ʿalayhim bi-ṣiḥāfin" (there will be circulated among them platters...) and what follows is a parenthetical clause between parts of the speech. Therefore there is no shift (iltifāt) in the pronoun "ʿalayhim" (among them); rather, the context calls for the third-person pronoun.

Al-ṣiḥāf is the plural of ṣaḥfa, a round vessel with a wide mouth, whose base tapers to something close to a circle. The ṣaḥfa is a vessel for placing food or fruit, like the ṣiḥāf of the Chinese Faghfūrī, which holds the fill of five persons, and is less than the qaṣʿa (large bowl), which holds the fill of ten. It has been reported that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may God be pleased with him) had platters made according to the number of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), so that whenever fruit or a delicacy was brought to him, he would send some of it to them in those platters.

[Page 255]

Al-akwāb is the plural of kūb (with ḍamma on the kāf), a vessel for drink, of water or wine, of elongated shape, having a short neck; at the top of that neck is its mouth, which is the outlet of what is in it, and its mouth is narrower than its belly. Most often it has no handle by which it is held; it is held by placing the hand on its neck. Sometimes it has a short handle. It is smaller than the ibrīq (ewer), except that it has no spout and generally no handle. The ibrīq, however, has a handle and a spout.

The description of the akwāb is omitted because the description of ṣiḥāf indicates it, meaning: "and cups of gold."

These cups are for water and for wine.

The clause "wa fīhā mā tashtahīhi al-anfus" (and therein is what the souls desire) and what follows is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to Paradise, and it is part of the same speech.

The pronoun in "fīhā" refers to Paradise. His saying "mā tashtahīhi al-anfus" (what the souls desire) is general, covering everything to which the appetites of the souls relate in obtaining and attaining it. God creates in the people of Paradise the desires suited to the world of eternity and sublimity.

"Wa taladdhu" (and delights) is the present tense of ladhdha, on the pattern of ʿalima: when one perceives pleasure. Its verb is intransitive by rule, and it is made transitive to the thing that gives pleasure by the preposition bi, so one says ladhdha bihi. The omission of the preposition and the attaching of the verb directly to the genitive object is frequent, so it becomes accusative by removal of the preposition. This is common in speech, until the verb is treated as transitive, and they say ladhdhahu. From this is His saying here "wa taladdhu al-aʿyun" (and the eyes delight in it), the implied sense being "wa taladdhuhu al-aʿyun." The omitted pronoun is the link of the relative clause to the relative pronoun.

The delight of the eyes lies in seeing beautiful forms and colours which gladden the soul. So the delight of the eyes is a means to the delight of the souls. Therefore "wa taladdhu al-aʿyun" is coordinated to "mā tashtahīhi al-anfus" with a coordination in which there is a general and specific relation between the coordinated and the one it is coordinated to. The souls may desire what the eyes do not see, such as conversation with companions and hearing beautiful sounds and music. And the eyes may perceive what the soul had not previously desired to see, or what the soul had desired in taste or hearing, and it is brought to them in beautiful forms, as a completion of the blessing.

[Page 256]

"Al-anfus" (the souls) is the subject of "taladdhu," and the object is omitted because it is evident from the context.

Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ on the authority of ʿĀṣim, and Abū Jaʿfar read "mā tashtahīhi" with a pronoun suffix referring back to the relative "mā." This is also how it is written in the Medina and Syrian codices. The rest read "mā tashtahī" with the pronoun suffix deleted, and it is likewise written in the Mecca, Basra and Kufa codices. The reports from ʿĀṣim, the reciter of Kufa, are two transmissions: one taken by Ḥafṣ and the other taken by Abū Bakr. The deletion of a connected pronoun, in the accusative, governed by a verb or a participle within the relative clause, is common in speech.

His saying "wa antum fīhā khālidūn" (and you therein will abide) is good news to them of the non-cessation of delight, abundance of provision, and attainment of desires. The nominal sentence is used here, which indicates permanence and stability, as an emphasis on the reality of eternity, to remove the supposition that it means only a long duration.

Fronting the prepositional phrase is for emphasis. Another statement is coordinated to some of what is said to them, aimed at extolling Paradise and the believers, since they were given it on account of their righteous deeds. So Paradise is referred to with the demonstrative for the distant, to magnify its status, though in fact it is present before their eyes.

The clause "wa tilka al-jannatu alatī ūrithtumūhā" (And that is Paradise, which you have been given as an inheritance) and what follows is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) to the speech.

The demonstrative is the subject and "al-jannatu" (Paradise) is its predicate; that is: that which you see is the Paradise you have heard of and been promised to enter.

The clause "alatī ūrithtumūhā bi-mā kuntum taʿmalūn" (which you have been given as an inheritance for what you used to do) is a qualifying description of Paradise.

"Ūrithtumūhā" (you have been given it as inheritance) is used metaphorically for: you have been given it exclusively, not others, by comparing God's giving the believers, exclusively over others, the bliss of Paradise, to a ruler giving the wealth of a deceased to his heir exclusively over other relatives, since the heir is more entitled to it and more deserving of obtaining it.

The bā in "bi-mā kuntum taʿmalūn" (for what you used to do) is causal, and this causality is by the decree and promise of God. His saying "kuntum taʿmalūn" (you used to do) indicates that their deeds by which they merited Paradise were something established and fixed, and that their doing was repeated and renewed, that is, not cut off until their death.

[Page 257]

The clause "lakum fīhā fākihatun kathīra" (for you therein is abundant fruit) is a second qualifying description of Paradise. Al-fākiha means fruits, fresh and dry, and they are among the finest things enjoyed in food, and their flavours are known to every hearer.

The reason for repeating the favour of the blessing of food and drink in Paradise is that this is among the blessings in which human natures do not differ in finding them delightful. For this reason He said "minhā taʾkulūn" (from which you will eat), like His saying ﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit﴾ [al-Anʿām: 141].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verses 74–75:

﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide forever in the punishment of Hell.﴾ ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it despairing.﴾ This sentence has two positions. The first: it completes the detailing of what the threat in His saying, ﴿So woe to those who have wronged, from the punishment of a painful day﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 65], had left in general terms, following the detailing of part of it in His saying, ﴿Do they await only the Hour?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 66], and so on. And in His saying, ﴿The close friends that Day will be enemies to one another﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67], where the completion of its detailing was interrupted by giving attention to mentioning the promise for the believing, God-fearing servants. So in this position it is an explanation of the threat as a whole and a detailing of its generality.

The second position: it is like a explanatory resumption (al-isti'naf al-bayani) prompted by what one hears of the description of the conditions of the believing, God-fearing servants, namely the question: what is the condition of their opposites, the polytheists who did wrong?

Both positions are equal in that the sentence has no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case analysis).

The opening of the statement with (inna) (indeed) is either for emphasis on it, or because the eager questioner who longs for the news is treated as one doubtful of its content, due to his intense desire for it, or in view of what the statement contains of an implicit address to the polytheists while they deny its content, as if it were said: "Indeed, you, O criminals, will abide forever in the punishment of Hell."

The criminals (al-mujrimun): those who commit ijram, which is a great sin. What is meant here by them is the polytheists who denied the Prophet ﷺ, because the context concerns them, and because the sentence is an explanation of the generality of their threat in His saying, ﴿So woe to those who have wronged, from the punishment of a painful day﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 65], and because the answer of the angels, their address with His saying, ﴿We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 78], does not apply to other than the deniers, meaning those averse to Islam and the Qur'an. Thus the mention of "the criminals" is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, to draw attention to the fact that their polytheism is a crime.

The sentence ﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "the punishment of Hell." The verb yufattaru is the doubled form of fatara, meaning to become calm or subside; with doubling, it takes a direct object. The meaning: no one lightens it.

The sentence ﴿and they will be in it despairing﴾ is conjoined (ʿataf) to the sentence ﴿Indeed, the criminals will abide forever in the punishment of Hell.﴾

Al-iylas (iylas) means despair and humiliation. It was mentioned earlier in Surat al-An'am. Al-Zamakhshari added to the meaning of iylas the condition of silence, which no one else mentioned; the truth is that silence is among the necessary implications of the meaning of iylas, not a condition within its meaning.

This is a parenthetical clause within the narration of the state of the guilty ones. Its purpose is to negate that what they were made to endure, namely eternal abiding in the punishment, is something to be regarded as excessive, and to negate any softening of heart toward their condition described in His saying ﴿and they therein will be despairing﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 75].

Here, "injustice" (zulm) means transgression (i'tida'), which is inflicting harm without a legitimate or rational justification. Its negation of God in His dealing with them in that manner is because that treatment was a recompense for their own injustice. Therefore He followed it with His saying ﴿but they were the wrongdoers﴾, meaning the transgressors, since they transgressed against what God commanded of them, namely acknowledging His divinity, and against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when they denied him and defamed him, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿Indeed, association [with Him] is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13] in Surat Luqman.

"Hum" (هم) is a detached pronoun that does not require an antecedent, because it was not brought in to indicate a referent, since the pronoun in "kanu" (كانوا) already indicates the referent. Thus the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) is brought in to convey the restriction (qasr) of the attribute of wrongdoing to the subject of (kāna). Since the conjunction of contrast (ḥarf al-istidrāk) after the negation was already sufficient to convey the restriction, the bringing in of the pronoun of separation serves as an emphasis of the restriction by repeating another form of restrictive construction.

Most of the Arabs treat the pronoun of separation in speech as not occupying a position in i'rab, so it is like a particle. According to the majority of grammarians it is a particle with no place in i'rab; the grammarians of Basra call it faṣl (separator), and the grammarians of Kufa call it 'imād (support).

The reciters agreed on the accusative for al-ẓālimīn (الظالمين) as the predicate of kānū. The Banu Tamim treat it as a pronoun requiring an antecedent and as the head of its clause, a subject (mubtada'), and they treat its clause as occupying the position of i'rab required by what precedes it. On this reading, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and Abu Zayd al-Nahwi recited "﴿wa-lakin kanu hum al-ẓālimūn﴾", where "hum" is a subject and the clause consisting of it and its predicate is the predicate of kānū.

Sibawayh related that Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj used to say "aẓunnu Zaydan huwa khayrun minka" with the nominative "khayrun".

**[p. 260]**

The clause ﴿ونادوا﴾ ("and they will call out") is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in ﴿وهم فيه مبلسون﴾ ("while they are in despair therein," 43:75), or it is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿وهم فيه مبلسون﴾.

Their calling is narrated in the past tense, though it is something that will happen on the Day of Resurrection. This is either because their despair (iblās) in the torment of Hell, which is hopelessness, comes after they have called out ﴿يا مالك﴾ and he has answered them with what he answered, and this is the case if you make the clause "and they called out" circumstantial; or because the future verb is placed in the position of the past to affirm that it will certainly occur, as an interpretation of the speech contrary to what the apparent sense requires. An example is God's saying: ﴿ويوم ينفخ في الصور فصعق من في السماوات ومن في الأرض﴾ ("And on the day the Trumpet is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon," 27:87). This second explanation applies if the clause "and they called out, etc." is coordinated.

**Mālik** is the vocative of the name of the angel appointed over Hell. They addressed him so that he would raise their plea to God, the Exalted, as an intercession.

The lām in ﴿ليقض علينا ربك﴾ ("let your Lord decree an end upon us") is the lām of command, meaning supplication.

Directing a command to an absent person happens only with the sense of conveying a message, as here, or by treating a present person as absent for some consideration, such as honour, as in the vizier's saying to the caliph: "Let the caliph see his opinion."

Qaḍāʾ here means death, as in God's saying: ﴿فوكزه موسى فقضى عليه﴾ ("Moses struck him and dispatched him," 28:15). They asked God to remove life from them so that they might rest from feeling the torment.

They only asked God to cause them to die, and they were answered that they will remain (ṃākithūn), an answer comprehensive of both the negation of death and the negation of coming out. It is therefore a decisive answer to whatever they might ask afterwards.

Among the rare readings (nawādir) related to this verse is what is reported that Ibn Masʿūd read ﴿ونادوا يا مال﴾ with the kāf omitted, as apocopation (tarkhīm). When his reading was mentioned to Ibn ʿAbbās, he said: "How much the people of the Fire were too preoccupied for apocopation!" In al-Kashshāf it is said: "Some of them said: what made apocopation good is that they cut off part of the name because of their weakness and the greatness of what they are in." (ended). By "some of them" he meant Ibn Jinnī, as reported by al-Ṭībī, who said: "There is a secret in apocopation in this place. Because of the greatness of what they are in, their souls became weak and humbled, and their speech became small, so this is one of the places of brevity (ikhtiṣār)."

In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Yaʿlā ibn Umayya: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) reading on the pulpit ﴿ونادوا يا مالك﴾ with the kāf affirmed." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the reading ﴿ونادوا يا مال﴾ was narrated by Abū al-Dardāʾ from the Prophet (ﷺ), so the Prophet (ﷺ) recited both ways. The reading with the kāf affirmed became mass-transmitted (mutawātir), while the other remained transmitted through single narrators (āḥād), so it was not Qur'an.

The clause ﴿لقد جئناكم بالحق﴾ ("We have certainly brought you the truth") to the end of the verse is in the position of a reason (ʿilla) for the clause ﴿إنكم ماكثون﴾ ("you will remain"), considering the whole sentence, which is completed by the contrastive particle (istidrāk) in ﴿ولكن أكثركم للحق كارهون﴾ ("but most of you are averse to the truth").

The pronoun in ﴿جئناكم﴾ ("We have brought you") refers to the angels, and "the truth" (al-ḥaqq) is the revelation that Gabriel brought. Mālik attributed the bringing of the truth to the collective of angels, following the Arabic manner of a group or tribe taking pride in the virtues of some of its members. This manner is well known in Arabic speech, as in the saying of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza:

"We released the shackle of Imruʾ al-Qays from him after his imprisonment and hardship had lasted long."

The aversion to the truth is attributed to most of them rather than all of them, because the polytheists are of two groups. One of them is the great leaders of the religion of disbelief, who bar people from faith by intimidation and enticement, like Abū Jahl when he barred Abū Ṭālib at his deathbed from saying "There is no god but God," and said: "Are you turning away from the religion of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib?" The second group is the masses and the common people, who follow the leaders of disbelief. Many verses point to this, among them God's saying in Sūrat al-Baqara: ﴿إذ تبرأ الذين اتبعوا من الذين اتبعوا﴾ ("When those who were followed disown those who followed," 2:166), and the verses that follow. Thus the first group is the intended meaning of ﴿ولكن أكثركم للحق كارهون﴾, and those people only disliked the truth because it aims at the removal of their authority and the cutting off of their interests.

The placement of ﴿للحق﴾ before ﴿كارهون﴾ is for emphasis on the truth, honouring it, and it also serves to complete the rhyme (fāṣila).

**[p. 260]**

Because of the greatness of what they are in, their souls became weak and humbled, and their speech became small, so this is one of the places of brevity (ikhtiṣār)."

In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Yaʿlā ibn Umayya: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) reading on the pulpit ﴿ونادوا يا مالك﴾ with the kāf affirmed." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the reading ﴿ونادوا يا مال﴾ was narrated by Abū al-Dardāʾ from the Prophet (ﷺ), so the Prophet (ﷺ) recited both ways. The reading with the kāf affirmed became mass-transmitted (mutawātir), while the other remained transmitted through single narrators (āḥād), so it was not Qur'an.

The clause ﴿لقد جئناكم بالحق﴾ ("We have certainly brought you the truth") to the end of the verse is in the position of a reason (ʿilla) for the clause ﴿إنكم ماكثون﴾ ("you will remain"), considering the whole sentence, which is completed by the contrastive particle (istidrāk) in ﴿ولكن أكثركم للحق كارهون﴾ ("but most of you are averse to the truth").

The pronoun in ﴿جئناكم﴾ ("We have brought you") refers to the angels, and "the truth" (al-ḥaqq) is the revelation that Gabriel brought. Mālik attributed the bringing of the truth to the collective of angels, following the Arabic manner of a group or tribe taking pride in the virtues of some of its members. This manner is well known in Arabic speech, as in the saying of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza:

"We released the shackle of Imruʾ al-Qays from him after his imprisonment and hardship had lasted long."

The aversion to the truth is attributed to most of them rather than all of them, because the polytheists are of two groups. One of them is the great leaders of the religion of disbelief, who bar people from faith by intimidation and enticement, like Abū Jahl when he barred Abū Ṭālib at his deathbed from saying "There is no god but God," and said: "Are you turning away from the religion of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib?" The second group is the masses and the common people, who follow the leaders of disbelief. Many verses point to this, among them God's saying in Sūrat al-Baqara: ﴿إذ تبرأ الذين اتبعوا من الذين اتبعوا﴾ ("When those who were followed disown those who followed," 2:166), and the verses that follow. Thus the first group is the intended meaning of ﴿ولكن أكثركم للحق كارهون﴾, and those people only disliked the truth because it aims at the removal of their authority and the cutting off of their interests.

The placement of ﴿للحق﴾ before ﴿كارهون﴾ is for emphasis on the truth, honouring it, and it also serves to complete the rhyme (fāṣila).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 79:

﴿Or have they decided on a matter? Then indeed We are decreeing a matter.﴾

(Am) here is disconnected (munqati'a), serving the transitional iDrab (a shift of topic, in the sense of turning away from one subject to another) while the purpose remains unified. He moved from the topic of the punishment prepared for them on the Day of Resurrection to the disgrace prepared for them in this world.

So the sentence is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the sentence ﴿They await only the Hour﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 66], and so on.

The speech after (am) is an interrogation from which the interrogative particle has been omitted, and it is an interrogation of affirmation and threat, meaning: Have they decided upon a matter?

The pronoun in "abramū" (they have decided) refers to the polytheists who plotted against the Prophet (ﷺ). The pronoun in (inna) is the pronoun of Majesty (Allah).

Page 262

The fa' in His saying ﴿Then indeed We are decreeing﴾ is for consequence (tafriʿ) upon what the interrogation implies, namely the assumption that the object of the question has taken place. Thus the speech reverts in meaning to a conditional: meaning, if they have decided upon a scheme, then indeed Allah is decreeing for them a matter that nullifies the scheme and brings harm upon them. Its parallel and its like in meaning is His saying ﴿Or do they intend a plot? But those who disbelieve, they are the ones who will be plotted against﴾ [al-Tur: 42].

It is related from Muqatil that this verse was revealed concerning the Quraysh's plotting to scheme against the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Dar al-Nadwa, when their affair settled upon what Abu Jahl advised them: that from every tribe a man should emerge, so that they would all share in killing the Prophet (ﷺ), so that the Banu Hashim would not be able to demand retribution for his blood. And Allah destroyed all of them at Badr.

The basic meaning of ibram (decreeing/determining) is a firm killing (al-qatl al-muhkam), and here it is used metaphorically for firmly establishing a plan and resolve upon what they have planned.

The difference between "abramu" and "mubrimun" is that their determining is an occurred act, whereas Allah's determining as recompense for them is a warning that Allah has decreed the nullifying of what they decided, for the active participle (ism al-fa'il) is literally in the time of the present, meaning: We are now decreeing a great matter for them, and that is the creating of the causes of the battle of Badr, in which they were uprooted.

Al-amr: a great and serious deed. The object of "mubrimun" is omitted because what precedes it indicates it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 80:

﴿Do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private consultations? Yes, and Our messengers are with them, recording.﴾ (Am) and the interrogative implied after it in His saying "﴿Do they think﴾" are both like what preceded in His saying "﴿Or have they determined a matter? [Al-Zukhruf: 79]﴾".

The particle (bala) is an answer to the negation in His saying "﴿that We do not hear﴾", meaning: Yes, indeed We do hear their secrets and their private consultations.

Page 263
Al-sam' (hearing) is: knowledge of sounds.
What is meant by the secret (sirr) is what they conceal within themselves of schemes of deceit against the Prophet (ﷺ), and by the private consultation (najwa) is what they confer among themselves in that matter in a hidden discourse.

The clause ﴿and Our messengers are with them, recording﴾ is conjoined so that they may know that God's knowledge of what they conceal is knowledge that has a consequence for them, namely their being held accountable for what they conceal, because the recording of deeds indicates that they will be reckoned for them on the Day of Recompense.

Writing (al-kitaba) may be taken literally, or metaphorically, or as a metonymy for enumeration and preservation.

The messengers (al-rusul) are the guardian angels, because they are sent to trace people's deeds; and for this reason He said ﴿recording, in their presence﴾, like His saying: ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him a watchful observer, ready [to record]﴾ [Qaf: 18], meaning: a watcher who observes his speech.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 43, verses 81–82:**

﴿Say: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of those who worship [him]."﴾ ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾

When the mention of those who did wrong by claiming that the angels are the offspring of God came up in His words, ﴿So woe to those who did wrong, from the torment of a painful day﴾ (Surah al-Zukhruf 43:65), following His words, ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example﴾ (43:57), and following His words before it, ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, into females﴾ (43:19),

He followed this with what awaits them of the terrors of the Resurrection and what He has prepared for those who renounced association with God and embraced faith. God commanded His Messenger to move from the station of warning and threat to the station of argument against the existence of a son for God. This combined a refutation of some polytheists who worshipped the angels with a refutation of those who claimed that some of their idols were daughters of God, such as al-Lat and al-'Uzza. So He commanded him with His words, ﴿Say: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of those who worship [him]."﴾ That is: say to them by way of dialectical argument and confounding them.

[p. 264]
He taught him words indicating that it never escaped him that God has no son, and that it never occurred to him that God has a son. The people to whom he is told to say this are the polytheists who claim that. This is the general purpose of the verse, since it opens with His words, ﴿Say: "If the Most Merciful had a son"﴾, while the hearers know that such a claim finds no acceptance with the Prophet (ﷺ).

The structure of the verse is subtle and difficult, and it contains many meanings. The first and the most preferred of them is: if he knew that God had sons, he would be the first to worship them, that is, he would have the greatest right among you to worship them. This is because he is not less discerning than to know something to be a son of God and not acknowledge its divinity, since the son of God would be emanating from a divine essence, and so would be nothing but a god. And I know that a god deserves worship. The proof is therefore composed of a conditional implication. The condition is hypothetical, and the implication between the consequent and the condition is based on the premise that the speaker is rational, calls to truth and salvation, and so does not accept for himself what would ensnare him. Moreover, he would not accept for them except what he accepts for himself. This is the utmost of sincere counsel to them. With it the argument is completed, and it shows that he is steadfast in the affirmation of the oneness of God.

Plurality is negated by negating its most specific form, which is plurality through paternity and filiation, like the plurality of a family, and this is the root of plurality. Thus the plurality of foreign deities is also negated by indication of the wider meaning (dalalat al-fahwa). A parallel to this is the statement of Sa'id ibn Jubayr to al-Hajjaj. When al-Hajjaj said to him, when he wanted to kill him, "I will replace the world for you with a fire that blazes," Sa'id said, "If I knew that this were up to you, I would not have worshipped any god other than you." Thus he alerted him to his error, since sending into the Fire belongs to the attributes of God, exalted is He.

The conclusion is that this argument is composed of a conditional proposition whose first part, the antecedent, is false, and whose second part, the consequent, is also false, because the falsity of the consequent follows necessarily from the falsity of the antecedent. Like your saying: "If five is an even number, then it is divisible into two equal parts." Here the argument is by means of the falsity of the consequent to establish the falsity of the antecedent, because the Prophet's (ﷺ) being a worshipper of the one alleged to be God's son is something negated by observation, for he has never ceased to forbid them from that. This follows the pattern of the argument in His words, exalted is He, ﴿If there were in them gods other than God, they would both be ruined﴾ (Surah al-Anbiya' 21:22), except that the condition there is marked by an explicit particle of impossibility, whereas here the condition is marked by a particle not explicit in impossibility.

[p. 265]
The purpose of departing from the explicit particle of impossibility here is to make them initially suppose that the assumption of a son for God is a matter open to consideration, and so that the wording of the speech can be directed in such a way that when they reflect on it they find that it negates that God has a son by way of the method of the theologians (al-madhhab al-kalami, the method of scholastic theology). Evidence for this is what al-Zamakhshari narrates in al-Kashshaf: that al-Nadr ibn 'Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy said, "The angels are the daughters of God," and then the verse was revealed, ﴿Say: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of those who worship [him]."﴾ Then al-Nadr said, "Do you not see that he has agreed with me?" Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to him, "He has not agreed with you, but he has said: 'The Most Merciful had no son, and I am the first of the monotheists from the people of Makkah.'" The general sense of this has been transmitted from al-Suddi. So the wording of the verse in this form contains a wonderful brevity, and an invitation to the opponents: if they reflect on it, the face of truth becomes clear to them. If they turn away after that, their turning away is counted as a retreat.

The verse may bear other meanings. Among them: the meaning is, "If the Most Merciful had a son in your claim, then I am the first of those who worship God," that is, the first of those who believe by denying them. This is the view of Mujahid, meaning by the indication of its concluding statement (tadhyil), the sentence ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ and what follows.

Among them: the particle (in) is for negation, not for condition, and the meaning is: "The Most Merciful had no son," and so it is a consequence of this: "I am the first of those who worship God," that is, I declare Him far above having a partner. This is from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Zayd ibn Aslam, and his son.

Among them: the interpretation of "worshippers" (al-'abidin) as an active participle of 'abada, ya'budu, from the pattern of fariha, meaning "he was disdainful and angry." This was said by al-Kisa'i. Nifṭawayh criticized it, saying that the active participle of 'abada, ya'budu is only said as 'abd, and they rarely say 'abid, and the Qur'an does not come with the rare of the language.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "walad" (son) with a fatha on the waw and a fatha on the lam, and the majority read it as such. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (wuld) with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam, as the plural of walad.

As for the clause ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾, it may be a completion of what the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to say, that is: "Say: 'If the Most Merciful had a son,' on the supposition, with the implication that this is a declaration of His transcendence above the actual realization of that." In that case this clause has the status of the consequent in the two parts of the conditional exceptive syllogism.

There is no iltifat (shift of grammatical person) in the pronoun in "yasifun" (they describe), because the implied sense of the speech is: "Say to them: 'If the Most Merciful had a son.'"

It may also be an independent statement from God, exalted is He, to establish His declaration of transcendence above what they say. In that case it stands as an interjection between the clause ﴿Say: "If the Most Merciful had a son"﴾ and the clause ﴿And He is the God in heaven﴾ (43:84). This clause carries the meaning of a concluding statement (tadhyil), because it declares God transcendent above everything they attribute to Him, including the ascription of a son and other things.

Describing Him with lordship over the strongest, most comprehensive, and greatest of existents implies the negation that He has a son, since the benefit of begetting is absent. The creation of the worlds and the order of their growth and continuance has been completed. And from His being their creator it is known that He is not preceded by non-existence, for otherwise He would need a creator to create Him. The non-preceding of non-existence entails that He will not be overtaken by annihilation. So the existence of a son for Him would be pointless.

The meaning is: turn away from them while they are plunging into idle talk and playing in the places of seriousness, when they mock Islam. Al-La'ib (play) means jesting and mockery.

The imperative here is used for threat, of the type of ﴿اعملوا ما شئتم﴾ [Fussilat: 40].

The majority of readers recite "يُلاقُوا" with a damma on the yā' and an alif after the lām, and the form of mufā'ala is figurative in that the meeting is certain. Abu Ja'far recited it as "يَلْقُوا" with a fatḥa on the yā' and a sukūn on the lām, taking it as the imperfect of the unaugmented form.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 84:

﴿And He is the One who is in the heaven a god, and in the earth a god.﴾

It is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers.﴾ [Al-Zukhruf: 81]. The two clauses between them are parenthetical insertions (iʿtirad). The purpose of the coordination is to convey the negation of any partner in divinity absolutely, after the negation of a partner in it by way of sonship. By mentioning the heaven and the earth, the intent is to encompass the realms of governance and creation, because the polytheists made partners for God on earth, namely their erected idols, and made partners for Him in the heaven, namely the angels, when they made them daughters of God, exalted is He. Thus His saying ﴿in the heaven a god, and in the earth a god﴾ is a refutation of both groups in what they claimed of divinity for them.

The apparent construction of this clause would have been for its first part to read ﴿the One who is in the heaven a god﴾ as a description of the Most Merciful from His saying ﴿if the Most Merciful had a son﴾ [Al-Zukhruf: 81]. He deviated from the apparent construction by presenting the clause as coordinated, so that it is independent and not a description, and by introducing in it a subject (mubtada') for the purpose of restricting (qasr) the attribute of divinity in the heaven and in the earth to God, Exalted is He, such that no other shares that with Him, because placing the subject (musnad ilayhi) in definite form and the predicate (musnad) in definite form is one of the methods of restriction. So the meaning is: He, and none other, is the One who is in the heaven a god and in the earth a god. The relative clause ﴿alladhi﴾ ("the One who") is a nominal clause whose initial element has been elided, and its initial element is a pronoun referring back to the referent of the pronoun ﴿Huwa﴾ ("He"). Eliding the initial element of the relative clause is a good usage when the relative clause is long, as here. The estimated sense is: the One who He is in the heaven a god.

Page 268

The two prepositional phrases are linked to ﴿god (ilah)﴾ in view of what it implies of the sense of "one worshipped," since it is derived from alaha, meaning he worshipped, so it resembles a derivative. The linking of the prepositional phrase to it is valid, and its linking to the word ilah is like the linking of an adverbial of place to "sieve" (ghirbal), and stronger than the linking of a prepositional phrase to "kanun" in the verse of al-Hutay'a, who satirizes his mother, from among his verses:

"A sieve when you are entrusted with a secret, and a kanun (brazier) upon those who talk."

﴿And He is the Wise, the All-Knowing.﴾ After God was described as singular in divinity, He was followed by a description as ﴿the Wise, the All-Knowing﴾, as a refinement (tadqiq) of the proof contained in His saying ﴿And He is the One who is in the heaven a god and in the earth a god﴾, since it indicates the negation of the divinity of any other in the heaven and the earth and His exclusive possession of divinity in both, because of what the form of restriction contains of affirming the attribute for Him and negating it from whoever else. So His saying "And He is the Wise, the All-Knowing" is a completion of the proof and an argument for it. For this reason we named it a refinement, since tadqiq in technical usage is mentioning a thing with the proof of its proof, whereas tahqiq is mentioning a thing with its proof. The One described with perfect wisdom and complete knowledge is self-sufficient, free of anything else, and so has no need of a son, nor of a daughter, nor of a partner.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 85:

﴿Blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and with Him is knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿuṭifa) with ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 82]. Its purpose is to follow the declarative (inshāʾ) glorification of God's transcendence (tanzīh) with a declarative praise and exaltation (thanāʾ wa tamjīd).

"Tabāraka" is a statement (khabar) used in the sense of an declarative praise (inshāʾ al-madḥ), because the meaning of tabāraka is that He is characterized by blessing (barakah) in a strong way, owing to what the form tafāʿala indicates of the strong occurrence of the derived action (mushtaqq minhu). Its original use is to indicate the performance of an action by two agents, such as taqātala ("they fought each other") and tamārā ("they disputed"), but it is used to mean merely the repetition of the action, as in tasāmā and taʿālā.

[Page 269]

Barakah is an increase in good.

Lordship (rubūbiyyah) was mentioned together with the glorification of God's transcendence, that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, because lordship requires His transcendence above having a child, which is the subject of the discourse negating it, and above a partner, which is included in His saying ﴿Exalted is He above what they describe﴾. Dominion over the heavens and the earth was mentioned together with the blessing and magnification, because dominion is suited to greatness and the outpouring of good. Therefore, do not be troubled by the fact that ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 82] is sufficient without ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. The aim of the Qur'an is reminder (tadhkīr), and the aims of reminder differ from the aims of argumentation and disputation. Reminder suits drawing attention to the various attributes according to their different aspects, and addressing the seeking of support from His bounty. Furthermore, the form "tabāraka" indicates that blessing is intrinsic to God, Exalted is He, and this requires His independence from increase through taking a child or taking a partner. Thus, in this respect, this sentence is another argument following the argument of His saying ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 82].

His singular lordship over the greatest of existents has been emphasized three times: by His saying "the Lord of the Throne," by His saying ﴿And He is the God in the heaven and the God on the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 84], and by His saying ﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾.

How many distinctive features and subtle points flow to the one who reflects upon the verses of the Qur'an, which none encompasses except the All-Wise, the All-Knowing!

Since His saying ﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ indicates disposal over these worlds for the duration of their existence and the existence of what is between them, He followed it with His saying ﴿and with Him is knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned﴾, to indicate that along with His dominion over the transient worlds, He has dominion over the enduring worlds, and that He is the One who disposes of those worlds and what is in them through bestowing bliss and punishment. So His saying ﴿and with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾ serves as a preparation (tawṭi'a) for His saying ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾, and an incorporation (idmāj) to establish the resurrection (baʿth).

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in "ilayhi turjaʿūn" (to Him you will be returned) serves to emphasize (taqawwī), since the addressees do not affirm that they will be returned to anyone other than Him, for they do not believe in resurrection at all.

As for their saying to the idols ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18], their intention is that they are intercessors for them in the world, or it is by way of disputation (ʿalā sabīl al-jadal). For this reason it is followed by His saying ﴿And those they invoke besides Him have no power of intercession﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 86].

[Page 270]

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read "turjaʿūn" with the second-person prefix (bi-l-fawqiyyah), as a shift (iltifāt) from the third person to the second person, for direct address with threat. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the third-person prefix (bi-l-taḥtiyyah), following the style of the pronouns before it. They all agree that it is in the passive voice (mabnī lil-majhūl).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 86:

﴿Those whom they invoke besides Him have no power of intercession, except those who bear witness to the truth while they know.﴾ When He informed them that to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and that with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, He made known to them that what they worship besides God has no power to intercede for them in this world. This refutes their claim that they are their intercessors (shufa'a') before God.

Since the angels were among those they worshipped besides God, He excepted them by His words ﴿except those who bear witness to the truth while they know﴾, meaning that they are the ones who are granted intercession. This is in the sense of His words ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 26], then He said ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 28]. This has already passed in the commentary on surah al-Anbiya'.

He described the intercessors as those who "bear witness to the truth while they know," meaning that they know the condition of the one who deserves intercession. For He knows that they do not intercede for those whose condition contradicts the condition of one who bears witness to God's truth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 43, verse 87:

﴿And if you were to ask them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they turned away?﴾

After he had thoroughly refuted, through the details that have been presented, the claim that there could be a god other than Allah, he came here with a comprehensive statement refuting their assertion of the divinity of other than Allah, with His words ﴿And if you were to ask them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾.

That is: if you ask them, as a question of affirmation (suʾal taqrir), who created them, they will acknowledge that Allah created them. This is known from the condition of the polytheists, as in the statement of Dimam ibn Tha'laba to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I ask you by your Lord and the Lord of those before you: has Allah sent you?" Because of this, He emphasized that they acknowledge Allah as the Creator, saying "they would surely say, 'Allah'." This is sufficient to show the foolishness of their opinion, for how can one be a god who does not create? He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then remember?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17].

The addressee in His words "if you were to ask them" is the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also possible that the address is to an unspecified person, meaning: if anyone who is able to ask them were to ask them.

Based on this affirmation and acknowledgment, there follows the denunciation and wonder at their turning away from the worship of Allah to the worship of other gods, with His words ﴿So how are they turned away?﴾

"Anná" is an interrogative particle concerning place, so its position is accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarfiyyah), meaning: to what place are they turned?

"Yu'fakūna" means "they are turned away." It is said: afakahu 'an kadhā, ya'fikuhu, from the pattern of ḍaraba, when he turned him away from it. It is put in the passive form because no one turned them away; rather, they turned themselves away from the worship of their Creator. So His statement ﴿so how are they turned away?﴾ is like the Arabs' saying: "Where are you being taken?", meaning: where are you taking yourself? They do not mean that someone took him away and they are asking about that; rather, the meaning is that no one took him away, but he went of his own accord.

﴿Wa-qīlihi yā Rabbi inna hā'ulā'i qawmun lā yu'minūn﴾ (And His saying: "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe.")

Al-qīl is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of qāla. The more apparent view is that it is a noun used in the sense of the object, i.e., al-maqūl (what is said), like al-dhibḥ (what is slaughtered). Its original form is qawl, with a kasra on the qāf and a sukūn on the wāw. The meaning is: "and what he said."

The pronoun attached to qīl refers to the Messenger ﷺ. This is indicated by the context of argument and debate from His saying ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81], by the phrase "yā Rabbi," by his saying ﴿Indeed these are a people who do not believe﴾, and by His answer, ﴿So turn away from them and say: Peace﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 89]. It is preferable that the pronoun be in the third person, as a shift (iltifāt, a change of grammatical person) from address,

[Page 272]

in His saying ﴿And if you asked them who created them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87]. After the argument and the report of their acknowledgment that God is the One who created them, and yet they did not budge from disbelief by the width of a fingertip, the Messenger despaired of their belief. So he said: ﴿My Lord, these are a people who do not believe﴾, turning to God for help concerning them and entrusting the matter to Him, so that His judgment might be carried out upon them.

This is the use of a declarative statement (khabar) to express grief or complaint, and it carries the meaning of a performative utterance (inshā', speech that does not describe but enacts), like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the Messenger says: My Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned﴾ [al-Furqan: 30], meaning they did not act upon it and therefore did not believe. This is supported by the fact that ﴿So turn away from them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 89] follows as a consequence. In the third-person pronoun there is an iltifāt, because the speech had been running in the style of address from His saying ﴿And if you asked them who created them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87]. The apparent expectation would have been: "And your saying: My Lord, etc." What makes this shift good is that it reports something in the Messenger's own soul, so the Messenger is placed in the position of one absent, to show that God does not neglect his call and his complaint, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ [Abasa: 1].

The attribution of qīl to the Messenger's pronoun indicates that this was repeated from him and became known from him with his Lord, meaning he was known for this and for what is similar in meaning, such as ﴿My Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned﴾ [al-Furqan: 30], and His saying ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him say: When is the help of God?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214].

The majority of readers (al-Jumhūr) read "wa-qīlahu" with a fatḥa on the lām, considering it a maṣdar in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) replacing its verb.

The estimated sense: "And he said" (the Messenger) "his saying." The clause is conjoined to the clause ﴿And if you asked them who created them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87], or to the clause ﴿Then how are they turned away?﴾. That is: "And the Messenger said at that time: My Lord, etc." A parallel is the verse of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

"The slanderers walk on either side of her, and their saying is: Indeed you, son of Abī Sulmā, are to be killed."

This is according to the narration of qīlahum with the accusative, meaning: "and they say: their saying." This is the narration of al-Aṣma'ī.

The accusative may also be as the object of the verb "lā nasma'u" (we do not hear), with the estimate: "Yes, and We know his saying." This is the view preferred by al-Farrā' and al-Akhfash. Al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjāj said it is accusative by a verb understood, indicated by His saying ﴿And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 85], meaning: "and He knows his saying."

[Page 273]

ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read "wa-qīlihi" with a kasra on the lām of qīlihi. The genitive may be read in two ways:

First: it is conjoined to "the Hour" in His saying ﴿And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 85], meaning: "and the knowledge of the saying of the Messenger: My Lord." On this view it is a promise to the Messenger of victory and a threat to them of retribution.

Second: the waw is an oath particle (li-l-qasam), and the answer of the oath is the clause ﴿Indeed these are a people who do not believe﴾, meaning that God swore by the saying of the Messenger, "My Lord," exalting the Messenger and his saying, which is an entrusting to the Lord and confidence in Him.

The content of his saying is only "My Lord," meaning that He swore by the call of the Messenger to his Lord, a call of one in distress.

Ibn Hishām, in his commentary on the Ka'biyya, reported from Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī that whoever read it in the genitive was speaking by conjecture and confusion. Ibn Hishām rejected this, since the genitive reading can be justified in a correct manner.

After the call, what it was made for has been omitted, which is indicated by the context of one whose stratagem has failed with them, so he entrusted his matter to his Lord. Then God swore by that word that they will not believe, but God will indeed take vengeance upon them. Therefore He said: ﴿So you will soon know﴾.

The indication by "hā'ulā'" (these) refers to the polytheists of Mecca, as is the common practice of the Qur'an. Describing them as "a people who do not believe" is more indicative of the firmness of unbelief in them than saying "these do not believe."

[p. 274]

﴿So turn away from them and say, "Peace." But soon they will know.﴾ The *fa'* here is *fasihah* (a *fa'* that reveals an implied condition), because it discloses an omitted clause. The sense is: when you have said this and entrusted the matter to Us, then We Ourselves will take retribution from them. "So turn away from them": that is, disregard them, do not grieve over them, and if they argue with you, say to them, "Peace," meaning: we have made peace in the argument and abandoned it.

The origin of "Peace" (*salam*) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) that came in place of its verb. Its original form was the accusative (*nasb*), but it was changed to the nominative (*raf'*) to indicate permanence, as was explained earlier in His words, ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah 1:2].

[p. 275 marker in source appears before the next section in the original sequence; see below]

It is said: *safaha yasfahu* (from the pattern *manaʿa*) means "he turned away and left." It was explained at the beginning of the surah, ﴿Shall We withhold the Reminder from you and turn away [*safhan*]?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:5]. However, the *safh* commanded here is not the *safh* whose occurrence is denounced in His words, ﴿Shall We withhold the Reminder from you and turn away [*safhan*]?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:5].

From this is derived "but soon they will know," as a threat and a warning to them. The object of *ta'lamun* ("you will know") is omitted for the sake of awe, so that their minds may go in every possible direction.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, and Rawh from Ya'qub read *ta'lamun* with the *ta'* (second-person, "you will know"), taking "soon you will know" as part of what the Messenger was commanded to say to them, meaning: "and say, 'Soon you will know.'" The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with the *ya'* (third-person, "they will know"), taking it as a promise from Allah to His Messenger ﷺ that He will take vengeance on those who deny.

What is in this verse of the command to turn away and to make peace in argument, and of the warning, indicates that the discourse in this surah is ending, and this is part of the excellence of the closing passage (*maqta'*).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Surat al-Dukhan**

This surah is named *Ha Mim al-Dukhan*. al-Tirmidhi narrated with two weak chains which support one another, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever recites *Ha Mim al-Dukhan* on a night, or on the night of Friday…" (the hadith).

The two terms function as a single name, because the word *Ha Mim* is not specific to this surah, so it is not counted as a proper name for it. For this reason, the author of *al-Itqan* did not count it among the surahs that have more than one name.

It is named in the *mushafs* and in the books of Sunnah as "Surat al-Dukhan."

The reason it is named "al-Dukhan" (the Smoke) is the occurrence in it of the word *dukhan*, referring to a sign from the signs of Allah with which Allah strengthened His Messenger ﷺ. For this reason it was named after it, out of concern for its importance. Although the word *dukhan* has another meaning which occurs in the surah *Ha Mim Tanzil* in His words, ﴿Then He turned to the heaven, and it was smoke﴾ [Fussilat 41:11], and that surah was revealed before this one according to the known order of the revelation of the surahs, based on the narration of Jabir ibn Zayd, which al-Ja'bari and the author of *al-Itqan* relied upon, the reason for naming does not require it.

It is entirely Meccan according to the majority opinion. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is Meccan; I know of no disagreement concerning any part of it." In *al-Kashshaf* the exception of His words, ﴿Indeed We will remove the punishment a little; indeed you will return﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:15], was mentioned without attributing it to any speaker. Al-Qurtubi did likewise, and al-Kawashi mentioned it as an opinion without attributing it to a specific person.

I think it is an opinion that arose from what its proponent understood, and I will clarify this in its proper place.

[p. 276]

It is the sixty-third surah in the order of revelation according to the statement of Jabir ibn Zayd; it was revealed after Surat al-Zukhruf and before Surat al-Jathiyah, in its present position.

Its verses are counted as fifty-six by the people of Madinah, Makkah, and al-Sham; by the people of Basrah as fifty-seven; and by the people of Kufah as fifty-nine.

* * *

**Its purposes**

The opening of this surah resembles the opening of Surat al-Zukhruf in its tribute to the Qur'an, its honour, and the honour of the time when its revelation began, so that this would indicate that it is from Allah and would point to the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. It then moves on to the point that those who turn away from reflecting on the Qur'an have been distracted from reflection by mockery and slander, so the Messenger's supplication for them to be struck with the punishment of hunger became binding upon them. This is to awaken their insight through sensory proofs, when rational proofs had failed to have effect on them, so that they might know that Allah's answering of His Messenger's ﷺ supplication is evidence that He sent him to convey His purpose.

Then He warned them of a punishment that would befall them in addition to what the Messenger ﷺ had asked for, as support from Allah for him, with something beyond what he had sought.

He set forth for them a parable of peoples like them who disobeyed the messengers of Allah sent to them, and the punishment that befell them was meant to be a lesson for these people: in detail, the people of Pharaoh with Musa and the believers among his people; without detail, the people of Tubba'; and in general, those who came before these.

Since denial of the Resurrection and considering it impossible were among the greatest causes that led them to neglect reflecting on the purpose of Allah, the discourse moved to affirm it and to describe what follows it of punishment for the obstinate and reward for the believers, as warning and encouragement.

Included within it is the excellence of the night in which the Qur'an was revealed, that is, when its revelation began, and that was the Night of Decree (*Laylat al-Qadr*).

Woven into this is what the connections led to of signs of Allah's oneness and of His support for those who believed in the messengers, and of the affirmation of the Resurrection.

It concludes with strengthening the heart of the Messenger ﷺ, with waiting for victory and waiting for the disbelievers to be overcome.
